Chapter 1

Measurement/Unit

49 facts · 8 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (94 points)

Notes

  • A unit of measurement is a definite magnitude of a quantity, defined and adopted by convention or by law.
  • It is used as a standard for measurement of the same kind of quantity.
  • Any other quantity of that kind can be expressed as a multiple of the unit of measurement.
  • To measure physical quantities four systems are in application as follows:

1. CGS System (centimetre - gram - second system):

  • It is a variant of the metric system based on the
centimetre–unit of length
gram–unit of mass
second–unit of time
2.FPS System (foot - pound - second system):
  • It is also known as the British System of measurement.
  • It relates to measuring –
foot–unit of length
pound–unit of mass
second–unit of time

Note: 1 Pound (lb) is equal to 453.59237 grams.

3. MKS system (metre - kilogram - second system):

  • It relates to measuring –
metre–unit of length
kilogram–unit of mass
second–unit of time
4.SI system (International System of Units):
  • It is the modern form of the metric system of measurement.
  • It is the most widely used system of measurement.
  • It was adopted by the 11th General Conference on Weight and Measures (CGPM), held at Paris (France) in 1960.
  • It has seven fundamental or base units.

Definition of Units of SI System:

1. Metre (m):

  • The metre is the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the speed of light in vacuum 'c' to be 299,792,458 m/s.

2. Kilogram (kg):

  • As per old definition, one kg was defined as the mass of Platinum - Iridium prototype kept at the BIPM, Sevres (near Paris). Generally, at 4ºC, the mass of 1 litre pure water is about 1 kilogram.

According to revised definition (which came into force on 20th May, 2019), the kilogram is now defined in terms of the Planck constant. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the Planck constant 'h' to be 6.62607015 × 10–³⁴ kg m²/s. Thus,

h
1 kg =m s

34 

6.62607015 10
3.Second (s):
  • One second equals the duration of 9,192,631,770 periods of the radiation corresponding to the transition between the two hyperfine levels of the unperturbed ground state of Caesium (Cs-133) atom. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the caesium frequency to be 9,192,631,770 Hz, which is equal to s–¹.

4. Ampere (A):

  • As per earlier definition; given two straight parallel conductors of infinite length, of negligible circular cross section and positioned 1 metre apart in vacuum, one ampere was defined as the electric current which passes through both of them makes them attract each other by the force of 2 x 10⁻⁷ newton per metre of length.

According to revised definition (which came into force on 20th May, 2019), the ampere is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the elementary charge 'e' to be

1.602176634 × 10–¹⁹ C (coulomb) or A.s (ampere second). Thus, one ampere is the electric current corresponding to the flow of 1/(1.602176634 × 10–¹⁹) elementary charges per second.

5. Kelvin:

  • As per old definition, the kelvin was the fraction 1/273.16 of the thermodynamic temperature of the triple point of water.

According to revised definition (which came into force on 20th May, 2019), the kelvin is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the Boltzmann constant 'k' to be 1.380649 × 10–²³ kg m²s–²K–¹. Thus,

1.380649 

That means one kelvin is equal to the change of thermodynamic temperature that results in a change of thermal energy kT by

1.380649 × 10–²³ Joule (kgm²s–²).

6. Candela (cd):

  • The candela is the luminous intensity in a given direction of a source that emits monochromatic radiation of frequency 540 × 10¹² hertz and has a radiant intensity in The 22 SI derived units with

7. Amount of Substance - Mole (mol):

  • As per old definition, one mole is the amount of substance composed of as many specified elementary entities (atoms, molecules, ions, electrons, etc.) as there are atoms in 0.012 kg of C-12.

According to revised definition (which came into force on 20th May, 2019), the mole is the amount of substance of a system that contains 6.02214076 × 10²³ specified elementary entities. This number is the fixed numerical value of the Avogadro constant 'N(A)', when expressed in the unit mol–¹ and is called the Avogadro number.

Derived units:

  • These units of measurement are derived from the 7 base units, specified by the International System of Units.
  • Derived units are defined as products of powers of the base units; dimensionless cases use the unit one (symbol 1); decimal multiples/submultiples are formed using SI prefixes (powers of ten).
  • Some of the coherent derived units in the SI are given special names. Below table lists 22 SI units with special names. Together with the seven base units, they form the core of the set of SI units. All other SI units are combinations of some of these 29 units.

Other measures of Length unit:

i.1 millimetre= 10⁻³ metre
ii.1 centimetre= 10⁻² metre
iii. 1 kilometre= 1000 metres (10³ m)
iv. 1 Angstrom (Å)= 10⁻¹⁰ metre
  • A unit of length to measure very small distances like wavelength, atomic and ionic radius or size of molecules and spacing between planes of atoms in crystals.

v. Nanometre –

  • 1 nanometre is one billionth of a metre, equal to 10-9 metre.
  • It is used to measure extremely small objects such as atomic structures or transistors found in modern CPUs. vi. Micron (micrometre) –
  • Micron is the previous name of micrometre.
  • 1 micrometre is equal to 10⁻⁶ m.
  • Micrometre is represented by μm.
  • It is used to measure cell size.

vii. Astronomical Unit –

  • Astronomical unit is usually used to measure distances within our solar system.
  • An astronomical unit (au) is the average distance between Earth and Sun.
  • It equals to approximately 149.6 million kilometre or 1 au = 149,597,870,700 m = 1.496 × 10¹¹ metre.

viii. Light-year –

  • A light-year is a distance that light travels in vacuum in one Julian year.
  • It is a unit of length used to express astronomical distances.
  • 1 light-year is equal to

= 3 × 10⁸ m/s × 365.25 × 24 × 60 × 60s

= 9.46073 (≈ 9.461) × 10¹⁵ metre.

  • Julian year: In Astronomy, a Julian year is a unit of measurement of time defined as exactly 365.25 days of 86400 SI seconds each.

ix. Parsec –

  • A Parsec is an astronomical term used to measure large distances to astronomical objects outside the solar system.
  • A Parsec is defined as the distance at which one astronomical unit subtends an angle of one arcsecond, which corresponds to 648000/π astronomical units (au).
  • 1 Parsec is equal to 3.0857 × 10¹⁶ metre, or
  • 1 Parsec is equal to 3.262 light-years.

Question Bank

Seven fundamental physical quantities: length, mass, time, electric current, temperature, luminous intensity, amount of substance. Force, velocity and work are not among them.

Memory aid LMT + CTL + A: Length, Mass, Time; Current, Temperature, Luminous intensity; Amount of substance.

1 paper question

Power = work ÷ time (rate of doing work); SI unit watt = joule per second; also written in kilowatt (kW).

UP1 paper question

Electric power → watt. Ampere → electric current; volt → electric potential; coulomb → electric charge.

Don't confuse Watt (power) with volt (potential difference).

2 papers question

Force = mass × acceleration; SI unit newton (kg·m/s²); modern definition from Isaac Newton's laws of motion.

1 paper question

Work = force × displacement in the direction of force (a scalar); SI unit joule (= newton metre), also the unit of energy.

UP1 paper question

Frequency → hertz (Hz), the derived SI unit = one cycle per second.

2 papers question

Processor speed → hertz/gigahertz: clock cycles completed per second; 1 GHz = 1 billion cycles per second.

1 paper question

GHz (gigahertz = one billion hertz) on a computer indicates its speed: the clock or processing speed of the central processor.

1 paper question

Resistivity ρ = RA/l; its SI unit is ohm-metre (Ωm). 'Ohm-metre' is the unit of resistivity.

2 papers question

Magnetic field B (magnetic flux density) → SI unit tesla.

1 paper question

1 tesla = 1 weber per square metre (Wb/m²) = 1 newton per ampere-metre; named after Nikola Tesla.

1 paper question

Not matched: radioactivity – curie (old non-SI unit); SI unit is becquerel (Bq). Lens power – dioptre, pressure – pascal, heat – joule are correct.

UP1 paper question

Light-year → unit of distance: the distance light travels in one year ≈ 9.461 trillion km. Must know

Don't confuse A light-year measures distance, not time or speed.

UP8 papers question

Astronomical distances use light-years because the speed of light in vacuum is always the same (not even affected by gravity).

1 paper question

1 parsec = distance at which Earth's mean orbital radius subtends 1 arc second (parallax) ≈ 3.262 light-years ≈ 206265 AU ≈ 30.9 trillion km.

Memory aid PAR-SEC = PARallax of one arc SECond.

UP1 paper question

Different Scientific Apparatus and its Applications

ApparatusApplication
AltimeterAn instrument used to measure the altitude

of an object, mainly in an aeroplane.

Ammeter An instrument used to measure the electric current in a circuit.

Anemometer A device used for measuring wind speed and, in some types, wind force/pressure and/or wind direction.

Actiometer A device used to measure the heating power or intensity of solar radiation.

Accelerometer A device that senses the different types of accelerations or vibrations.

Atmometer A device used for measuring the rate of water evaporation.

Audiometer An instrument used for measuring or evaluating hearing acuity.

Barograph A type of Barometer that records the atmospheric pressure over time in graphical form.

Barometer A device used for measuring atmospheric pressure.

Bolometer A device to measure the power of incident electromagnetic radiation via the heating of a material with a temperature dependent electrical resistance.

Calipers A caliper is a device used to measure the distance between two opposite sides of an object.

Calorimeter A calorimeter is an object used for calorimetry, or the process of measuring the heat of chemical reactions or physical changes as well as heat capacity.

Cardiograph An instrument for recording graphically the movements of the heart.

Chronometer A portable timekeeping device of great accuracy, particularly one used for determining longitude at sea; in watch making, a chronometer is a high-precision watch tested/certified to specific standards.

Colorimeter A device used to measure the absorbance of particular wavelengths of light by a specific solution.

CathetometerAn instrument to measure vertical distance.
CryometerA type of thermometer used to measure the

very low temperature of an object.

Dip Circle A device used to measure the angle between the horizon and the Earth's magnetic field (the dip angle).

Dynamometer A device used for measuring force, Torque or power (e.g., of an engine).

Electroencepha An instrument used to measure/record the

lograph electrical activity of the brain or brain-wave patterns; the recording/test is called an electroencephalogram (EEG).

Electrometer An electrical instrument for measuring electric charge or electrical potential difference.

Electroscope An instrument used to detect the presence and magnitude of electric charge on a body.

Evaporimeter An instrument used for measuring the rate of water evaporation from a wet surface to the atmosphere.

FathometerAn apparatus to measure the depth of the sea.
FluxmeterAn instrument used to measure the magnetic

flux.

Gravimeter An instrument used for measuring gravitational acceleration.

Gyroscope A device used for measuring angular velocity.

Hydrometer An instrument for measuring the relative density of liquids.

Hydrophone An instrument used for recording or listening to under-water sound.

Hygrometer An instrument for measuring the relative humidity of the atmosphere.

Hygroscope An instrument which gives an indication of the humidity of air.

Hypsometer A device for calibrating thermometers at the boiling point of water at a known height above sea level or for estimating height above sea level by the finding temperature at which water boils.

Kymograph A device to record muscular motion, changes in blood pressure and other physiological phenomena.

Lactometer An instrument used to check the purity of milk by measuring its density.

Luxmeter An instrument (illuminance meter) that measure illuminance, i.e., light falling on a surface, in lux.

Lysimeter A device used to measure actual evapo transpiration (evaporation + transpiration) from a cropped/vegetated surface.

Magnetometer It is also known as Magnetic sensor. It is an instrument that measures magnetism-either by magnetization of a magnetic material like a ferromagnet or the direction, strength or relative change of a magnetic field at a particular location.

Manometer A device to measure pressure of liquids or gases.

Microphone Its nickname is mic or mike. It is a transducer that converts sound waves into electrical signals.

Microtome It is a tool used for cutting extremely thin slices of materials, known as sections. Used especially in Biology to observe the sections under a microscope or electron microscope.

Nephoscope An instrument for measuring the altitude, velocity, and direction of movement of clouds.

Odometer An instrument for measuring the distance travelled by a wheeled vehicle.

Ondometer An instrument for measuring the frequency/ wavelength of electromagnetic waves.

Periscope It is an instrument for observation over, around or through an object or condition that prevents direct line of sight observation from the observer's current position.

Phonograph A device for mechanical recording & reproduction of sound.

Photometer An instrument for measuring the intensity of light.

Potentiometer An instrument for measuring voltage by comparison of an unknown voltage with a known reference voltage or to measure the electromotive force (emf) – a differential potential that tends to give rise to an electric current.

Pycnometer A laboratory device used for measuring the density or specific gravity of materials (liquids or solids).

Pyrheliometer It is an instrument for the measurement of direct beam solar irradiance.

Pyrometer A type of remote-sensing radiation thermometer used to measure the high temperature of the surface.

Psychrometer An apparatus used to measure the relative humidity of the atmosphere.

Rain Gauge (Udometer, Pluviometer or Ombrometer) It gathers and measures the amount of liquid precipitation over a set of period.

Radiometer It is a device for measuring the radiant flux of electromagnetic radiation.

Refractometer A device used for the measurement of an index of refraction.

Salinometer An instrument used for measuring the salinity of water.

Saccharimeter An instrument used for measuring the concentration of sugar solutions.

Sextant An instrument which measures the angular distance between two visible objects. It is used to know the height of celestial bodies.

sounds of the heart.

Tachometer An instrument/device used to indicate/ measure the rotational (angular) speed (rate of revolution, usually in rpm) of a rotating shaft/engine. It is widely used in automobiles & planes etc.

Viscometer An instrument used to measure the viscosity of a fluid.

Wind vane An instrument for showing the direction of the wind.

SONAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging) – A technique that uses sound propagation (usually underwater, as in submarine navigation) to navigate, communicate with or detect objects on or under the surface of the water, such as other vessels. Active sonar (which uses the echo principle) transmits sound pulses and listens for echoes; passive sonar only listens and does not emit sound.

RADAR (Radio Detection and Ranging) – Radar is an object - detection system that uses radio waves to determine the range, angle or velocity of objects.

Notes

  • Mechanics: Mechanics is that area of science concerned with the behaviour of physical bodies when subjected to force or displacements and the subsequent effects of the bodies on their environment.
  • Weight: Weight is the force exerted on a body by gravity/ force with which the Earth attracts it.
  • Mass: Mass represents the amount of matter (measure of inertia) in a particle or an object. Mass remains the same everywhere (in Classical Mechanics). It is denoted by 'm'. Difference between Weight and Mass

(kg).

Distance & Displacement:

  • In daily language Distance & Displacement are used in the same sense but in Physics both have a different meaning.
  • The length of a specific path travelled between two points by an object is distance.
  • Displacement is the shortest distance measured from the initial to the final position of an object (along a straight line) and has direction from initial to final position.
  • Travelled distance has only magnitude, while displacement has magnitude along with the direction. It is clear that distance is a scalar quantity and displacement is a vector quantity. In a course of motion, the travelled distance by an object is not zero, but the final displacement may be zero. Displacement of an object will be zero when the moving object comes to its initial point.

Speed & Velocity:

  • Speed is the distance travelled per unit of time. The average speed of an object is obtained by dividing the total distance by the total time taken.

Total travelled distance

∴ Average speed = Total time taken

It is a scalar quantity and its SI unit is metre/second.

  • Velocity is the speed of an object moving in a definite direction.

Displacement

∴ Average velocity = Total time taken

  • The difference between speed & velocity is that speed has the only magnitude without any specific direction, while velocity has both magnitude & direction. Speed is scalar & velocity is a vector quantity.

Acceleration:

  • Acceleration is the change in velocity of an object per unit time.

change in velocity

∴ Acceleration = time taken

⇒ Acceleration

If the initial velocity of object is u & after time t its velocity is v, then

acceleration (a)

Its SI unit is m/sec² or m.sec⁻².

Newton's Laws of Motion:

  • Newton's laws of motion are three physical laws that, together, laid the foundation for classical mechanics. They describe the relationship between a body and the forces acting upon it and its motion in response to those forces.

1. Newton's First Law of Motion –

  • Newton's first law states that every object will remain at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled to change its state by the action of a net external force.
  • Inertia is a tendency of matter by which it continues in its existing state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless that state is changed by an external force.
  • The tendency of an object to resists changes in its state of motion varies with mass. Mass of an object is a measure of its inertia. The more inertia that an object has the more mass that it has. The light object has less inertia.

2. Newton's Second Law of Motion –

  • The second law states that the acceleration of an object depends upon two variables: the net force acting upon the object and the mass of the object.
  • Thus, the acceleration of an object subject to a net external force is directly proportional to the net force, in the same direction as the net force, and inversely proportional to the mass of the object i.e. a = F/m

Where a = acceleration, F = net force & m = mass or F = m × a ⇒ Force (net) = Mass × Acceleration SI unit of force is newton (N).

  • 1 newton is equal to 1 kilogram metre per second square or 1 newton of force is the force required to accelerate an object with a mass of1 kilogram, 1 metre per second, every second. In other words, a force of one newton produces an acceleration of 1 m.s–² on an object of mass 1 kg.

3. Newton's Third Law of Motion –

  • For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.
  • The Force imposed by the first object to other object is known as an action while the force imposed by the second object on the first object is known as reaction. (No cause effect is implied; the two forces act simultaneously and on two different bodies). The size of the force on the first object equals the size of the force on second object. Newton's third law of motion is also known as 'Action Reaction' Law.

Momentum:

  • Momentum is the product of the mass & velocity of an object.

∴ Momentum (P) = Mass (m) × Velocity (v)

  • It is a vector quantity possessing a magnitude and a direction. It's SI unit is kilogram metre per second (kg.m.s–¹).

Change in momentum –

  • The rate of change in momentum of an object is proportional to the imposed force on an object.
  • Rate of change in momentum takes place in the direction in which applied/net force acts. It is the other form of newton's second law of motion.

Force ∝

If an object of m mass has its initial velocity u, then its initial momentum = mu

Its last velocity became v, after the imposing of force (F) for time (t). So, the final momentum of the object = mv

∴ change in momentum = mv – mu mv mu

⇒ F = ma (for fixed mass)

It is the Newton's second law of motion.

Work:

  • A force is said to do work if, when acting, there is a displacement of the point of application in the direction of force. If no displacement occurs after applying force, no work is done.

The value of work is equal to -

work = Force (F) × displacement in the direction of force

or W = F cos θ × s where, W = work F = force

= F × s

s = displacement (when θ = 0° i.e. force and displacement are in the same direction)

If the force (F) is not in direction of displacement, forming θ angle with it, then

work done (W) = F cos θ × s

where, F cos θ is the component of force (F) in the direction of displacement

s

  • Work is a scalar quantity. Its SI unit is joule. One joule is defined as the amount of energy exerted when a force of 1 newton is applied over a displacement of one metre along the direction of the force.

1 joule = 1 newton × 1 metre.

Power:

  • Power is the rate of doing work by machine or anybody.

∴ Power

  • Its SI unit is joule/sec. It is also called watt.
  • Another unit of Power is Horsepower.

1 Horsepower (hp) = 746 watt.

Energy:

  • Energy is the capacity for doing work. Different forms of energy are Mechanical energy, Heat energy, Light energy, Sound energy, etc.
  • It is a scalar quantity. Its SI unit is joule.

Mechanical Energy:

  • Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic & potential energy in an object that is used to do work. The sum of potential and kinetic energy is called mechanical energy.
  • So, mechanical energy = kinetic energy + potential energy Kinetic Energy:
  • The kinetic energy of an object is the energy that it possesses due to its motion. If the mass of the body is m kg and speed v m/sec. then

K.E. mv²

Potential Energy:

  • Potential energy is the energy in a body due to its position. It is clear that if any object under a force is shifted from one position to another position, then during it, done work is stored as the potential energy of the object.

P.E. = mgh where, m = mass of the object

g = gravitational acceleration h = height

  • Elastic potential energy, gravitational potential energy, electrical potential energy etc. are different forms of potential energy.

Chapter 4

Motion Under Gravity

39 facts · 5 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (113 points)

Notes

The Motion of Planets:

  • All the planets including the Earth, move around the Sun in their orbits.
  • A natural satellite (moon) is a naturally formed celestial body in space that orbits a planet or a dwarf planet; even some asteroids can have moons.
  • Planets Mercury and Venus have no natural satellites.
  • Earth has one natural satellite.
  • Mars has two small satellites.
  • Jupiter has 101 known satellites with confirmed orbits (As of 16 March, 2026).
  • Saturn has maximum numbers of known satellites with confirmed orbits i.e. 285 (As of 16 March, 2026).
  • As of 16 March, 2026, Uranus has 29 satellites, Neptune has 16 satellites, and dwarf planet Pluto has 5 satellites. Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion:
  • Johannes Kepler, a German astronomer, propounded three laws about planetary motion around the sun.
  • These laws are as follows:

First Law –

  • All planets move around the Sun in an elliptical orbit, having the Sun at one of the two foci.

Second Law –

  • A radius vector joining any planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in an equal length of time.
  • The second law clears that for the same planet, it moves faster when it is nearer the Sun and slower when it is farther from the Sun.

Third Law –

  • The square of the orbital period of a planet is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit.
  • Kepler's third law states P² ∝ a³. That means, for bodies orbiting the Sun, knowing the orbital period (P) allows estimation of the semi-major axis (a) of its orbit. It means that ifyou know the planet orbit (P = how long it takes the planet to move around the Sun) then you can determine that planet distance from the Sun (a = the semi-major axis of the planet's orbit).

Newton's Law of Gravitation:

  • Newton proposed that all the bodies of the Universe attract each other by a force called gravitational force.
  • Newton propounded following law about gravitation – "The attracting (gravitational) force between two objects is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres."
  • Newton's Law of Gravitation can be expressed mathematically as follows:

If two objects whose masses are m₁ and m₂ respectively, and they are positioned at a distance r, then the attraction of force between them will be

where G is the constant of proportionality known as universal gravitational constant.

  • If the objects mass is unit (m₁ & m₂ both 1 kg.) and distance between them is unit (r = 1 m), then –

F = G

It means that numerical value of gravitational constant (G) equals the force of attraction between two objects with unit mass and positioned at a unit distance.

  • In SI System its value is 6.67430 × 10–¹¹ newton.metre² per kg² (N.m².kg–²/m³.kg–¹.s–²)
  • The value of G was first determined experimentally by Henry Cavendish.

Gravity and Gravitational acceleration of Earth:

  • Gravity is attraction force by which the Earth attracts objects towards its centre.
  • It is a peculiar form of gravitation.
  • When an object is thrown or dropped freely, it falls towards the Earth due to the gravity of Earth and its falling rate is continuously increasing due to the production of acceleration, which is known as gravitational acceleration. It is represented by 'g'. Its unit is metre/second².

Relation between 'g' & 'G':

  • Gravitational acceleration of Earth

  • Value of 'g' does not depend upon the mass of the object.
  • If two objects of different mass are dropped freely (in absence of air) from the same height, equal acceleration will produce in both objects, they will reach at the same time to surface of the earth.
  • Although, in the presence of air their acceleration will vary due to upthrust force (buoyancy) and air resistance/ drag and depends upon the shape of the object, its size, its velocity.
  • Objects may reach at different times on Earth in the presence of air; for similar shapes/sizes, the heavier one is usually less affected by drag, but shape/area can reverse the outcome.
  • The value of'g' differs at different places of Earth surface.
  • The value of 'g' is minimum at equator and maximum at poles.
  • The value of'g' also varies by going upward or downward from the earth surface. In both cases, it decreases. Circular Motion of Satellites:
  • When a satellite revolves around Earth in an orbit, a centripetal force acts on it.
  • This force is gravitational force imposed by Earth on satellite.

Escape Velocity (Escape Speed):

  • Generally when we throw an object upward, it after reaching to a certain height, comes down due to the gravitational force of Earth.
  • Escape velocity (escape speed) is the minimum speed needed for a free object to escape from the gravitational influence of Earth and object never comes back to Earth. In standardized words, it is the minimum initial speed required for an object to reach infinity (i.e., escape from Earth) such that its speed at infinity becomes zero, assuming no air resistance/atmospheric energy loss and no further propulsion after launch.
  • The minimum kinetic energy required for escape velocity is known as escape energy.

  • It is clear that if any object is thrown from the surface of the Earth at the minimum speed of 11.2 km/second, (in ideal no air resistance), that object will move in space and never comes back to the Earth.

Circular Motion and Escape Velocity relation:

  • If the circular orbital speed of a satellite revolving nearby to Earth is Vo and the escape velocity (escape speed) of an object thrown from Earth's surface is Ve, then–

Ve = Vo

  • It is clear that at the same distance from Earth's centre a satellite revolving nearby to Earth, if by any reason, its

speed exceeds by at least (or about 1.414) times its

circular orbital speed (idealised), it will escape into space, leaving its orbit (neglecting drag and other forces). Periodic Motion, Oscillatory Motion and SHM:

  • Periodic motion: motion that repeats itself after equal intervals of time.
  • Oscillatory motion: to-and-fro motion about a mean (equilibrium) position.
  • Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM): an oscillatory motion in which the restoring force (or acceleration) is directly proportional to the displacement from the mean position and is directed towards the mean position.

Examples: a mass attached to a spring; a simple pendulum for small angular displacement.

Simple Pendulum –

  • An ideal simple pendulum consists of a point mass (bob) suspended by a light, inextensible string from a fixed support, oscillating in a vertical plane with negligible friction/air resistance.
  • In a laboratory setup, a small dense bob (often spherical) is tied to a light string that does not stretch appreciably and is suspended from a rigid support/stand.
  • The mass attached at the free end is called the bob.
  • The effective length (l) is the distance from the point of suspension to the centre of mass (centre of gravity) of the bob.

Periodic Time of Simple Pendulum –

  • Periodic Time of ideal simple pendulum is represented by following formula:

(For small angular displacement, typically up to about 15°)

where l = effective length of simple pendulum

g = gravitational acceleration

  • From the above formula, it is clear that for ideal simple pendulum (in small angle model), periodic time does not depend upon the mass of the bob.
  • Time period (T) of the pendulum is directly proportional to under root of effective length.
  • If the effective length of pendulum increases by four times, periodic time will be increased by two times.
  • Time period (T) of the pendulum is inversely proportional to under root of gravitational acceleration (g).

For example - when a pendulum clock is carried on the mountain or in any mine, 'g' value decreases, time period increases and the clock becomes slow.

  • The time period of a hypothetical simple pendulum whose length approximately equal to Earth's radius, is about 84.4 minutes (often discussed as the Schuler period). It is the maximum limit of a simple pendulum on Earth.
  • A seconds pendulum is a pendulum whose time period is precisely 2 seconds.

Chapter 5

Physical Properties of Matter

49 facts · 8 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (96 points)

Notes

  • Matter around us exists in three different states—(i) solid,

(ii) liquid, and (iii) gas.

  • The three states of matter show characteristic mechanical properties (many properties overlap across states):

1. Solids: show elasticity and plasticity. Solids are not perfectly rigid; a force is required to deform their shape or size.

2. Fluids (liquids and gases): liquids and gases can flow and are therefore called fluids; fluids exert pressure (normal force per unit area).

3. Liquids (specifically): show surface tension and capillarity because surface tension is concerned with liquids (gases do not have free surfaces).

4. Buoyancy/floatation (in fluids): an immersed body experiences upthrust (buoyant force); objects float iftheir density is less than the liquid and sink if greater.

Elasticity:

  • Generally, the meaning of a rigid substance is a hard solid which has definite shape and size.
  • But actually these can be stretched, compressed and deformed.
  • Even though a rigid steel rod can be deformed by applying sufficient external force.
  • A force is required to deform the shape or size of a body; deformation may be longitudinal, shear, or volumetric.
  • After removing the force, the body regains original dimensions only if stress is within the elastic limit; otherwise permanent deformation remains.
  • The property of any substance by which it tries to gain its normal shape after being stretched or compressed is called elasticity.

"Ability of an object or material to resume its normal shape after being stretched or compressed" is elasticity.

  • On the basis of the property of elasticity, matters are of two types:

1. Perfectly elastic substance - Matter which resumes perfectly its normal state after withdrawing the applied force.

2. Perfectly plastic substance - Matter which does not resume its normal state after withdrawing the external force, but deformed forever.

  • Really no matter is perfectly elastic nor perfectly plastic but lies between the limit of these two properties.
  • Materials may behave approximately elastic (e.g., quartz) or approximately plastic (e.g., wax) within a certain range; putty and mud are close to ideal plastics.

Stress:

  • During the application of external force on a matter to change its shape or size, an internal reaction force of equal amount is produced in the opposite direction on every section.
  • This force tries to resume a normal state of matter. Stress is the restoring force per unit area developed in the body.
  • If force (F) is applied vertically on a transverse section with the area (A) of matter,

then

Stress = F/A

Its SI unit is newton/metre² (Nm–²), i.e., pascal (Pa). Strain:

  • When the shape or size of a matter is changed by applying an external force, the ratio of change in dimension to the original dimension (e.g. ΔL/L) is known as strain.
  • Since, it is a ratio, hence it is dimensionless or without any unit.

Hooke's Law –

  • For sufficiently low stress/strain (within the linear elastic range/below the proportionality limit) applied stress on the matter is directly proportional to strain developed in it. The ratio of stress and strain is a constant value (proportionality constant), known as elastic modulus; for tensile/compressive stress this is Young's modulus (E). Surface Tension:
  • Surface Tension is the elastic tendency of a fluid surface which makes it to acquire the least surface area possible. It is measured in force per unit length.
  • Its SI unit is newton/metre (Nm–¹).
  • The value of surface tension of any liquid depends upon its nature, temperature and the medium present on another side of the liquid surface.
  • Surface tension decreases with rise in temperature.
  • It becomes zero at the critical temperature.
  • When gravity/airflow effects are negligible compared with surface tension, drops/bubbles are approximately spherical. Small raindrops are roughly rounded, but larger raindrops flatten/distort as they fall.
  • Drops occupy the form in which surface (interfacial) energy is minimum (since creating extra surface area requires energy).
  • If only surface tension acts on a drop (other effects negligible), it minimizes surface area/surface energy and becomes spherical.

Cohesive and Adhesive Force:

  • According to molecular theory, every matter is made up of small particles, known as atoms; in many substances, atoms combine to form molecules. These particles attract each other.
  • Cohesive force is the force of attraction between molecules of the same matter.
  • Adhesive force is the force of attraction between molecules of different matter.
  • The adhesive force between oil and water is less than the cohesive force of water but higher than cohesive force of oil, so when the water dropped on oil surface, its drops occupy spherical shape by shrinking, while when oil dropped on the water surface, it spreads widely in form of the thin film generally.
  • For two immiscible liquids A and B, whether A spreads on B depends on surface and interfacial tensions. The spreading parameter is S = γB − (γA + γAB). If S > 0, A spreads completely on B; if S < 0, it does not (forms droplets/lens instead of a thin film).

Capillarity:

  • A capillary tube is a narrow tube (commonly glass) of very small internal diameter, open at both ends.
  • The rise or fall of a liquid in a narrow tube due to surface tension (with wetting/non-wetting effects) is called capillarity.
  • Liquids that wet glass (acute contact angle) show capillary rise, while liquids that do not wet glass (e.g., mercury in glass) show capillary depression.
  • Example: When a capillary tube is kept standing in mercury, the mercury level in the tube is depressed compared with the level of mercury outside.

Examples of capillarity / capillary effects:

  • In a fountain pen, ink is drawn toward the nib through narrow channels/slits by capillary action.
  • Fuel/oil rises in candle and lamp wicks by capillary action.
  • Blotting paper absorbs spilled liquid due to capillary action in its pores.
  • In plants, water moves upward through xylem mainly due to cohesion–adhesion and transpiration pull; capillarity alone is not sufficient to explain rise to great heights. Viscosity:
  • A liquid is flowing over a rigid horizontal surface AB as shown in the figure. The liquid layer which is in contact with the bottom remains at rest/has zero velocity relative to the surface, but the velocity of the upper layers is increasing. The uppermost layer flows with maximum velocity.
  • In three horizontal layers a, band c, a is with minimum velocity, b has more than a and c is with maximum velocity.
  • The consecutive layers, from bottom to surface try to reduce the relative velocity between adjacent layers.
  • An internal force acts between layers, try to slow down the velocity of the layer which is just above it.
  • An internal force acts on different layers which tries to oppose their relative velocity.
  • This force is known as the viscous force.
  • To maintain the flow of liquid, the external force is applied against viscous force.
  • The property of fluids (liquids and gases), which opposes the relative movement among different layers of fluid, is known as viscosity.
  • Highly viscous liquids like honey and glycerine have greater resistance to flow, so they flow less readily/slower, than low-viscosity fluids.
  • With increase in temperature, viscosity of liquids / generally decreases.
  • The viscosity of gases generally increases with increase in temperature.
  • Viscosity is primarily a property of fluids; solids generally lack viscosity and mainly resist shear elastically, though some solid materials show viscoelastic/creep behaviour. Pressure:
  • Pressure is a scalar quantity equal to normal force per unit area.

Pressure =

SI unit of Pressure is newton/metre²; Nm–² (Pascal; Pa). Pressure within liquid at any point –

  • Hydrostatic (Gauge) pressure at a point, situated at h depth from the free surface of the liquid is –

P(g) = ρgh

where, ρ is density of liquid g is gravitational acceleration.

Absolute pressure in a liquid open to atmosphere is – P = P(a) + ρgh

Upthrust Force:

  • When a body is immersed in a liquid, an apparent loss of weight is observed. This apparent loss is due to a force which is exerted by the liquid on the body in the upward direction. This force is known as the upthrust or buoyant force.
  • The centre of buoyancy (upthrust) is the centre of mass/ centroid of the displaced fluid volume.

Archimedes' Principle:

  • It states that the upward (buoyant) force that is exerted on a body immersed in a liquid, whether fully or partially submerged, is equal to the weight of the liquid that the body displaces and it acts in the upward direction at the centre of mass of the displaced liquid.

Law of Floatation:

  • When a body is in liquid, the following two main forces act on it –
1.The weight (W) of the body acts vertically downward.
2.Upthrust/buoyant force (F) acts vertically upwards on the

body.

  • The value of F (upthrust) is equal to the weight of the liquid displaced by the solid.
  • The sinking or floating of any object in liquid depends upon the relative values of these two forces. Conditions are as follows –

(i) If W > F – resulting force (W – F) will act downward– object will sink.

(ii) IfW = F – the body is in equilibrium; it may float or remain suspended.

(iii) IfW < F – leaving object free, it will start to come upward.

  • How much portion of solid will remain in liquid, it depends upon the relative density of liquid and solid which can be calculated as follows (Applicable for a floating body in equilibrium) –

Volume of submerged solid portion Density of solid =

Two volume of solid Density of liquid

  • From the above equation, it is clear that solid will be submerged less in liquid with high density and will be submerged more in liquid with less density.
  • If densities are equal, the body can remain suspended (neutral buoyancy) when fully immersed.
  • If two liquids are immiscible/form layers, the less dense liquid floats on the more dense liquid.

Optics

120 facts · 31 Must know

Key facts from the book (135 points)

Notes

  • Liquids that wet glass (acute contact angle) show capillary rise while liquid that is not wet glass (e.g.: mercury in glass) sho capillary depression.
  • Visible light is electromagnetic radiation detectable by the human eye. It lies between infrared (longer wavelengths) and ultraviolet (shorter wavelengths).
  • Wavelength range (approx.): about 380–700 nm (≈ 3.8×10–⁷ – 7.0×10–⁷ m). Some texts extend the upper limit to about 760 nm depending on convention.
  • Light is perceived only when light from a source/object enters the eyes. Objects are seen because they emit light or reflect/scatter incident light into our eyes.
  • In a homogeneous medium, under geometrical optics conditions (objects and apertures >> wavelength), light travels approximately in straight lines; light can also diffract (spread/bend) around obstacles and apertures.
  • Light can travel through a vacuum (sound waves cannot).
  • Light shows wave–particle duality (wave-like and particle like behaviour).
  • Thus, light has dual nature:

(a) Particle nature – behaves in the form of particles.

(b) Wave nature – behaves in the form of waves. Speed of light in different media (approx.)

  • The speed of light depends on the medium and is maximum in vacuum.

Refractive Index:

  • The refractive index of a medium is equal to the ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to its speed in that medium.
  • If the refractive index of a medium is η(m) and the speed of light is v and c in that medium and vacuum respectively, then c

η =

m v

  • A higher refractive index corresponds to a lower speed of light in that medium (for the same frequency).
(a) Refractive index of water –1.33
(b) Refractive index of glass –1.50
  • Since the speed of light is maximum in vacuum, so the value of the refractive index of any medium (transparent media for visible light) is typically more than 1 in relation to vacuum; for X-rays it can be slightly less than 1.
  • The ability of a medium to refract light is also expressed in terms of its optical density.
  • A medium with higher refractive index (n) is called optically denser.
  • The speed of light is higher in a rarer medium than a denser medium.

Refraction of Light:

  • Light rays travel in a straight line in a homogeneous medium.
  • When a ray of light travels obliquely from one transparent medium to another with different refractive indices, its direction changes (This phenomenon is called refraction). At normal incidence, the direction does not change (though speed changes).
  • The ray approaching and striking the surface separating two media is called the incident ray.
  • The ray that travels in the second medium after refraction is called the refracted ray.
  • The point of incidence is the point where the incident ray strikes the interface/surface.
  • The normal is the line drawn perpendicular to the interface/ surface at the point of incidence.
  • The angle of incidence (i) is the angle between the incident ray and the normal.
  • The angle of refraction (r) is the angle between the refracted ray and the normal in the second medium.
  • When light goes from an optically rarer medium (lower refractive index) to an optically denser medium (higher refractive index) it bends towards the normal; from optically denser to optically rarer it bends away from the normal.

Examples of Refractive Phenomenon:

(i) An rod/pencil partially immersed in water appears bent/ displaced at the air-water interface when observed from outside.

(ii) A coin in water appears raised above its actual position.

(iii) Twinkling of stars (due to atmospheric refraction). Refraction of light in a Prism:

  • A prism is a transparent refracting medium bounded by to non-parallel plane faces inclined at an angle (angle of prism).
  • Prisms are commonly made of glass (also other transparent materials are used).
  • In the above figure, the light ray AB, after falling on the first refracting surface PQ of the prism, is refracted along BC direction inside the prism, bending towards normal line EBF. Refracted ray BC at second refracting surface PR emerges into air along CD direction bending away from the normal line GCF. Thus, ABCD is the path of light in a Prism.

Dispersion of Light:

  • White light contains all visible wavelengths and is commonly represented as seven colours: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange and Red (VIBGYOR).
  • The splitting/spreading of white light into its constituent colours (wavelengths) is called dispersion.
  • In spectrum violet color is at lower position and the red color is at the upper position.
  • In normal dispersion through a prism, red deviates least and violet deviates most.
  • In vacuum, all colours travel with the same speed.
  • In air and other media, speed is slightly less than in vacuum and depends on refractive index; because refractive index depends on wavelength, different colours have slightly different speeds (the effect is very small in air and larger in glass).
  • Thus the refractive index of any medium differs for different colors of light.
  • Speed of violet light is minimum and speed of red light is maximum in the glass.
  • In glass (normal dispersion), violet travels slower than red; hence refractive index is greatest for violet and least for red, so violet deviates most and red least.
  • Within the visible spectrum, violet has the shortest wavelength and highest frequency, while red has the longest wavelength and lowest frequency.

Critical Angle and Total Internal Reflection:

  • Critical angle (i(c)) is the angle of incidence beyond which rays of light passing through a denser medium to the surface of a rarer medium are no longer refracted but totally reflected.
  • In other words, critical angle (i(c)) is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction is 90°; for i > i(c), total internal reflection occurs.
  • Its value depends upon the nature of both mediums and color of rays.
  • For critical angle light must pass from a denser medium to rarer medium.
  • For glass-air surface the value of the critical angle is approximately 41.14º and for the water-air surface it is about 48.75º.

Rarer medium 90°

  • The complete reflection of light ray reaching an interface with a less dense medium when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle is known as total internal reflection.

  • Mirage formation is a result of the refraction and the total internal reflection of light in the air.
  • Optical fibres and Endoscope function on the principle of total internal reflection.

Reflection:

  • When light falls on the surface it may be absorbed, transmitted or reflected.
  • Reflection is when light bounces off an object.
  • Smooth, polished surfaces give specular (regular) reflection, while rough surfaces give diffuse reflection (reflected rays spread in many directions).
  • Silver is the better reflector of light.

Mirror:

  • A smooth well polished reflecting surface is called the mirror.
  • Mirrors are of two types–

(i) Plane Mirror

(ii) Spherical Mirror

Plane Mirror –

  • A plane mirror is a flat and smooth sheet of glass with a reflective metal layer (silver or aluminium) coated on the back surface and protected by paint.
  • The mirror used to see the face is a plane mirror.
  • Our face image formed in the plane mirror can not be obtained on screen, it can only be observed in the mirror.
  • So, the image formed in a plane mirror is an example of virtual image.
  • Such an image is also known as imaginary or unreal image.
  • The size of the image formed in the mirror is just equal to the size of the object.
  • The image and objects are at the same distance from the mirror at opposite sides.
  • The image is a laterally inverted mirror image of the object. If a person is reflected in a plane mirror, the image of his right hand appears to be the left hand of the image. Spherical Mirror –
  • A spherical mirror is a mirror which has the shape of a piece cut out of a spherical surface.
  • These are of two types –

(i) Concave Mirror

(ii) Convex Mirror

Concave Mirror –

  • Concave mirrors have inwards curved reflecting surface.
  • Dentists use concave mirror for the examination of patient’s teeth producing big images of teeth.
  • Concave mirror are used as a reflector, for obtaining a sharp beam of light in torches, headlight of vehicles and searchlights.
  • Concave mirrors are also used for shaving to get clear image of face, etc.

Convex Mirror –

  • Convex mirrors have outward curved reflective surface.
  • It is used as rear-view side mirrors in vehicles.

Lens:

  • A lens is a transparent (usually homogeneous) material bounded by two surfaces, of which one or both are spherical; the other may be plane.
  • Curved surface may be spherical, cylindrical or elliptical, but these are mostly spherical.
  • Lens is of two types-

(i) Convex Lens

(ii) Concave Lens

Convex Lens –

  • Convex lens is thick in center but thin at corner.
  • Convex lens is also known as a converging lens because it converges the parallel light rays at one point. Its focal length is positive.
  • A convex (converging) lens forms a real, inverted image when the object is beyond the focus; if the object lies between the focus and the optical centre, the image is virtual, erect and enlarged (e.g., magnifying glass).
  • Convex lens is used to correct far-sightedness/ hypermetropia, an eye defect in which near objects are not clearly visible but long-distance objects are clearly visible.

Concave Lens –

  • Concave lens is thin at the centre but thick at the corner.
  • It is also known as a divergent lens because it diverges the parallel light rays. Its focal length is negative.
  • Objects appear smaller and farther through the concave lens and their images are virtual.
  • Concave lens is used to correct near-sightedness/ myopia, an eye defect in which far objects are not clearly visible but near objects are clearly visible.

Scattering:

  • Scattering is the redirection of light in many directions when it interacts with particles or inhomogeneities in a medium.
  • In many everyday cases (dust, smoke, fog, colloids), scattering can be understood as diffuse reflection of light by suspended particles.
  • The wavelength dependence of scattering depends on particle size: very fine particles scatter shorter wavelengths (blue) more effectively, while larger particles can scatter longer wavelengths and may make scattered light appear whitish.
  • The clear sky appears blue mainly because air molecules and other very fine particles scatter shorter wavelengths of sunlight more strongly than longer wavelengths.

Chapter 7

Heat and Thermodynamics

76 facts · 12 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (79 points)

Notes

Heat:

  • Heat is that energy which transfers from one system to another system as a result of their difference in temperature.
  • Its SI unit is joule (J).
  • Generally, calorie is also used as a unit (non-SI) of heat. Temperature:
  • Temperature is a thermal state of an object, which indicates the degree of hotness/coldness of a body and determines the direction of heat flow.
  • Heat always transfer from a substance of higher temperature to a substance of lower temperature.

Measurement of temperature:

  • Thermometer is an instrument used for measuring the temperature.
  • To measure temperature, following temperature scales are commonly used –

(i) Celsius (Centigrade) Scale (°C):

  • A scale of temperature in which (at 1 atm) 0ºC represents the melting point of ice and 100ºC represents the boiling point of water.
  • Historically, the melting point of ice and boiling point of water (at 1 atm) were taken as fixed reference points close to 0°C and 100°C respectively (however they are very close, but not exactly equal in modern thermometry.

(ii) Kelvin Scale (K):

  • Kelvin is the absolute temperature scale.
  • On Kelvin Scale, ice melting point is 273.15K while the boiling point of water is 373.15K.
  • It is clear from above that 0ºC temperature on the Celsius scale is equal to 273.15 K (and 100°C is equal to 373.15 K) on the Kelvin scale.
  • So, temperature on Kelvin scale = temperature on Celsius scale + 273.15

T(K) = t(°C) + 273.15

(iii) Fahrenheit Scale (°F):

  • On this scale (at 1 atm) melting point of ice is 32ºF and boiling point of water is 212ºF is mentioned.

Relation between Celsius and Fahrenheit Scale

  • A temperature is °Cat the Celsius scale and °F on Fahrenheit scale, then

9

t (°F) = t (°C) + 32 5

Equivalently=
59

Temperature effects on matter:

  • On heating (at a given pressure), a solid may change to a liquid (melting), and a liquid may change to a gas (vaporisation/boiling).
  • On cooling, a gas may change to a liquid (condensation), and a liquid may change to a solid (freezing).

(i) Melting:

  • A process in which a solid converts into a liquid on heating.
  • The temperature at which solid matter melts and converts into a liquid at a given pressure (commonly quoted at atmospheric pressure) is known as its melting point. For example – ice melts at 0ºC into water. So, the melting point of ice is 0ºC.
  • Different solids have a different melting point. For example –

The melting point of ice – 0ºC The melting point of wax – ≈ 60ºC

The melting point of Iron – ≈ 1538ºC

  • The melting point of any solid shows the extent of the force of attraction between their particles (atoms or molecules). The high melting point of solid shows that it has a high force of attraction between particles.

(ii) Boiling:

  • Process in which a liquid converts into vapour throughout the bulk of the liquid on heating is known as boiling.
  • The temperature at which a liquid boils and converts into vapour very fastly at a given pressure (commonly at atmospheric pressure) is termed as its boiling point.
  • Different liquids have different boiling points.

For example (at 1 atm) –

Ethanol–78ºC
Water–100ºC
Mercury–357ºC

(iii) Condensation:

  • The condensation process is the change of physical condition of matter from gas to liquid and it is the reverse phenomenon of vaporisation.

(iv) Freezing:

  • It is a phase transition in which a liquid turns into a solid when its temperature is lowered below its freezing point and this process is the reverse of melting.
  • On cooling a liquid, the temperature at which it turns into a solid is known as its freezing point.
  • The freezing point of water is about 0ºC.
  • For a pure substance at a given temperature the freezing point of the liquid and the melting point of solid is the same. For example – water freezes at 0ºC and ice melts at 0ºC i.e. both points are same.

Latent Heat:

  • During a change of state, heat is transferred without change in temperature.
  • Latent heat (for a process) is the amount of heat per unit mass transferred during change of state without temperature change.
  • Latent heat is mainly of two types –

(i) Latent heat of fusion (melting/freezing).

(ii) Latent heat of vaporisation (boiling/condensation). Latent Heat of Fusion –

  • Required energy converting for solid into liquid phase or vice versa, is called latent heat of fusion. The value of latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.34 × 10⁵ joule / kg (Jkg–¹). Latent Heat of Vaporisation –
  • Required energy converting for liquid into vapour is called latent heat of vaporisation. The value of latent heat of vaporisation of water (at 100°C, 1 atm) is 22.6 × 10⁵ joule / kg (Jkg–¹).
  • When water turns into vapour, it absorbs the latent heat. By experiments, it has been observed that burning from steam is more severe than burning from boiling water, although both are at the same temperature i.e. at 100ºC.
  • Steam causes more severe burns than boiling water at the same temperature because when steam condenses on the skin, it releases its latent heat of vaporisation in addition to the heat released as the condensed water cools.
  • Steam at 100°C carries 22.6 × 10⁵ joule/kg more heat than water at 100°C.

Sublimation:

  • On heating when a solid changes directly into gas (without becoming liquid), then that phenomenon is known as sublimation. Direct change from gas to solid (without becoming liquid) is called deposition.
  • Some substances having the sublimation property are Ammonium chloride, Iodine, Camphor and Naphthalene, etc.

Evaporation:

  • The process in which liquid turns into vapours below its boiling point is termed as evaporation. It may occur at room temperature.
  • Wet clothes dry due to evaporation of water.
  • Pond water dries up due to evaporation of water.
  • Increase in temperature increases the rate of evaporation.
  • Evaporation increases with temperature; at the boiling point, vaporisation becomes boiling (bulk phenomenon).
  • In case of low humidity in the air, the evaporation rate is high and water evaporates very soon, while higher humidity in the air, results into a low rate of evaporation. Cooling by Evaporation:
  • When a liquid evaporates, it absorbs heat (latent heat) from its surroundings, producing cooling.
  • A good example of cooling by evaporation is cooling of earthen pots.
  • The earthen pot has many tiny pores in its wall. The water diffuses out from the pores and evaporates continuously. The required heat for evaporation is taken from the water itself, it leads to a lowering of temperature in the remaining amount of water.
  • The sweating process is more in the summer season. Evaporation of sweat provides cooling to our body as it absorbs heat from the skin.
  • Cotton clothes are the best absorbent of water. They absorb the sweat of our body and expose it for easier evaporation.
  • Synthetic clothes such as polyesters are unable to absorb sweat in excess quantity, so these are unable to provide cooling to our body. Due to this reason, cotton clothes are given priority in the summer season.
  • A fan increases evaporation of sweat, so we feel the cooling.
  • In desert room cooler, the cooling effect is produced due to evaporation of water. It cools better in hot and dry days because higher temperature and lower humidity increase the rate of evaporation.

Chapter 8

Wave Motion

41 facts · 6 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (83 points)

Notes

Wave:

  • Wave involves the transfer of energy without net transfer of matter. A wave can be described as a disturbance that travels through a material medium or through vacuum/ space (depending on the type of wave), transferring energy from one location (its source) to another location without net transfer of matter.
  • In classical physics, waves are often grouped into two major types:

1. Mechanical waves (require a material medium).

2. Electromagnetic waves (do not require a material medium).

  • Additionally matter waves or de Broglie waves exist in quantum physics. These waves are associated with the moving particles.

1. Mechanical Waves:

  • A mechanical wave is a wave in which particles of a material medium oscillate about their mean positions and energy is transmitted through the medium.
  • The medium as a whole does not move with the wave; only oscillations and energy transfer propagate.
  • Mechanical waves transfer energy which propagates in the same direction as the wave.
  • Mechanical waves can be produced only in media which possess elasticity (restoring force) and inertia.

Types of mechanical waves –

  • During transmission of a mechanical wave through a medium, the medium particles start to vibrate. On the basis of the direction of particle vibration, mechanical waves are of two types –

(i) Transverse waves

(ii) Longitudinal waves

(i) Transverse Waves:

  • Atransverse wave is a travelling wave in which the particles of the medium oscillate perpendicular (right angled) to the direction of energy transfer (wave propagation).

Examples –

a. Vibration on a stretched string/rope: When one end of the rope is bound with hook and another free end is vibrating upward and downward, the produced vibration in rope particle is perpendicular to the wave direction.

b. Waves in solids (e.g., shear waves in solids).

  • Transverse mechanical waves propagate in solids (which can sustain shear stress) and do not propagate in fluids (liquids and gases) as bulk shear waves.
  • Surface water waves are special: particle motion has both vertical and horizontal components; ocean waves are a combination of longitudinal and transverse motions, and oscillations can extend below the surface with decreasing amplitude.
  • Electromagnetic waves such as light are also transverse waves.
  • In transverse wave, maximum displacement in upward side (highest point) from the equilibrium state is termed as 'crest' while maximum displacement in the downward side (lowest point) is termed as 'trough'. The crest is the top of the wave and trough is the bottom.
  • The distance between two consecutive crests or two consequitive troughs is the 'wavelength'.
  • Wavelength is represented by Greek letter 'λ' (lambda).

(ii) Longitudinal Waves:

  • A longitudinal wave is a travelling wave in which particles of the medium oscillate parallel to the direction of wave propagation.
  • Sound waves in air (and in fluids generally) are the standard example of a longitudinal wave.
  • Waves produced in a spring (slinky) when pushed/pulled along its length.
  • In a longitudinal wave, regions where particle/coils are closer together are called 'compressions', while regions where particles/coils are farther apart are called 'rarefactions'.
  • The distance between two consecutive compressions or two consecutive rarefactions is 'wavelength' (λ).
RarefactionRarefaction
compressioncompression

Direction of wave progation

  • Longitudinal waves are originated in all mediums i.e. solid, liquid & gas.
  • Along with propagating transverse waves on the surface of the liquid, longitudinal waves can be propagated inside the liquid.
  • Longitudinal waves are always mechanical waves. Time Period:
  • In case of a wave propagating in a medium, time taken by the particle for one complete oscillation (one vibration) is known as the time period of the wave. It is denoted by 'T'.
  • Increase in frequency of waves, results into a decrease of time period.

Frequency:

  • During propagation of the wave in the medium, frequency is the number of occurrences of repeating event per unit of time by particle. In other words, the frequency is the number of oscillations per second.
  • Relation between time period (T) and frequency (υ) υ = 1/T
  • It is represented by 'υ'. (Greek letter nu) (also written as 'f').
  • Its SI unit is hertz (Hz).

2. Electromagnetic Waves:

  • Contrast to mechanical waves, some waves need no medium for propagation.
  • These waves are called electromagnetic waves.
  • They are self-sustaining oscillations of electric and magnetic fields in free space, or vacuum.
  • Examples of electromagnetic waves are X-rays, light, radio waves etc.
  • In vacuum, the speed of electromagnetic waves of different wavelengths are the same and all travel equal speed to the speed of light (c ≈ 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s) in a vacuum; in a medium their speed depends on the electric and magnetic properties of the medium.

Electromagnetic spectrum

  • The electromagnetic spectrum stretches in principle over an infinite range of wavelengths.
  • In general tabulation of named regions, the order from shorter to longer wavelength runs roughly from about 10–¹² m to 10⁶ m, with overlaps and non-sharp boundaries.
  • Electromagnetic waves with the shortest range of wavelength have higher energy while with longest wavelength range have less energy.

Chapter 9

Sound

46 facts · 10 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (59 points)

Notes

Sound:

  • Sound is a mechanical disturbance (pressure wave) in a material medium that produces the sensation of hearing.
  • Sound travels in the form of waves.
  • Vibrating objects/matters produce sound.
  • The substance through which sound travels is called a medium.
  • Sound waves are mechanical waves.
  • A medium (solid, liquid, gas, etc.) is necessary for their propagation; sound does not propagate in vacuum.
  • Sound is transmitted through gases, plasma, and liquids as longitudinal waves. Through solids, however, it can be transmitted as longitudinal as well as transverse (shear) waves.

Speed of Sound:

  • Speed of sound depends upon the nature/properties of the medium through which it propagates.
  • Speed of sound varies in different media.
  • Sound propagates slowest in gases.
  • Sound propagates faster than gases in liquids.
  • Speed of sound is fastest in solids.
  • Sound does not propagate in vacuum.
  • Speed of sound in steel is about 17 times to speed of sound in air.
  • Speed of sound depends upon temperature in air.
  • Increase in temperature results to increase in the speed of sound (in summer season the speed of sound is more than that of winter season).
  • Humidity of air plays a very important role in the speed of sound.
  • Speed of sound in humid air is more than that of dry air. Speed of sound in different mediums
S.No. MediumSound speed
1.Air (at 0ºC)331 m/sec.
2.Air (at 22ºC)344 m/sec.
3.Hydrogen (at 25ºC)1284 m/sec.
4.Seawater (at 25ºC)1531 m/sec.
5.Aluminium (at 25ºC)6420 m/sec.
6.Iron (at 25ºC)5950 m/sec.
7.Steel (at 25ºC)5960 m/sec.

Frequency range of Sound:

  • Sound waves have been classified into three types on the basis of their frequency range. These are as follows:

(i) Audible sound Waves:

  • Our ear is only capable to hear such sound waves.
  • Frequency range of such sound waves lies between 20 Hz to 20000 Hz (20 kHz).

(ii) Infrasonic Waves:

  • Frequency of such sound waves is below the frequencies of audible sound i.e. below 20 hz.
  • Sources of infrasound in nature include volcanoes, avalanches, earthquakes and meteorites.
  • Many animals can hear infrasound like whales, elephants, rhinos, hippos, giraffes, alligators, squid/cuttlefish/octopus and even pigeons.
  • Generally, it has been observed that, before the earthquake some animals become abnormal. Earthquake produces infrasounds of low frequency before producing main shock waves, which probably alert the animals.

(iii) Ultrasonic Waves:

  • Ultrasonic waves are such sound waves whose frequency is more than 20,000 Hz.
  • Such sound waves are beyond the normal hearing range of human.
  • A number of animals are capable of emitting ultrasonic frequencies and use it for several purposes; such animals are – bats, whales, dolphins, mice, etc.

Applications of Ultrasonic Waves:

  • A dog whistle (Galton whistle) is a whistle that emits ultrasound used for training and calling dogs.
  • Ultrasonic waves are widely used in the field of industries and medicines.
  • Image of the heart is obtained by reflecting the ultrasonic waves from different angle/part of the heart. This technique is known as Echocardiography (Echo Test).
  • Ultrasound waves may be used to breakdown the kidney stone into smaller pieces. These pieces are excreted through urine outside of the body.
  • Ultrasound is used for cleaning a zig-zag tube.
  • SONAR (Sound Navigation & Ranging) device is helpful in determining the distance of any object positioned in water and to measure the direction and speed of any object by using sound waves (acoustic pulses; many SONAR systems operate at ultrasonic frequencies.

Sound Intensity:

  • Sound intensity is defined as the power carried by sound waves per unit area in a direction perpendicular to that area.
  • The SI unit of intensity, which includes sound intensity, is watt/square metre (w/m²).
  • Sound intensity level (or sound-pressure) is expressed in decibel (db), which is 1/10th part of bel (1dB = 0.1 B) Echo:
  • A sound or sounds caused by the reflection of sound waves from a surface back to the listener is known as an echo.
  • The sensation of sound persists in the brain for about

0.1 second. So, to hear clear echo there must be a time interval of at least 0.1 second between the original sound and reflected sound.

  • At least about 17.2 metre distance between listener and reflector is necessary to hear the clear echo (at about 22°C in air when v ≈ 344 m/sand minimum time gap ≈ 0.1s). Mach Number:
  • It is the ratio of the speed of a body to the speed of sound in the surrounding medium.
  • It is often used with numerals as Mach 1, Mach 2 etc. speed of object
  • Mach Number =

speed of sound in that medium

  • Subsonic Aircraft: An aircraft whose speed is less than the speed of sound.
  • Supersonic Objects: The objects with Mach Number between 1-5, e.g., missiles.
  • Hypersonic Objects: The objects whose Mach number is more than 5, e.g., hypersonic missiles.

Notes

Electric Current:

  • The rate of flow of electric charge in a conductor is termed as electric current.
  • The direction of the flow of positive charge is conventionally considered the direction of flow of electric current.
  • Thus, the direction of flow of electric current is just opposite to that the direction of flow of electrons.
  • If a net charge Q flows through a cross-section in time t, Q

then current I =. t

  • The SI unit of electric current is ampere (A).

1 Ampere = 1 coulomb/second (1A = 1 C/s).

Types of Electric Current:

  • It is of two types –

(i) Direct current

(ii) Alternating current

(i) Direct Current (DC) –

  • An electric current that flows only in one direction (its magnitude may be steady or varying, but direction is not reversed).
  • A battery/cell is a common source of DC supply.

(ii) Alternating Current (AC) –

  • An electric current that periodically reverses direction at regular intervals (used in mains power supply).
  • Practical advantage in power systems: AC voltage can be stepped up/down efficiently using transformers, enabling high-voltage transmission and low-voltage safe utilization. (Modern HVDC is also used and can be more efficient over long distances.)

Electromotive Force (emf):

  • Electromotive force (emf, ε) of a source is the work done per unit charge by the source in driving charge around a complete circuit.
  • emf is not a force; it equals the potential difference between the terminals of the source in open circuit.
  • Its SI unit is volt (V).

Electric Potential (at a point):

  • Electrostatic potential at a point is the work done by an external force in bringing a unit positive test charge (without acceleration) from infinity to that point.
  • Its SI unit is volt (V).

Potential Difference (Voltage):

  • Potential difference between two points is the work done per unit charge in moving a test charge from one point to the other.
  • Ifwork W is done in moving charge Q between two points, then V = W/Q
  • Its SI unit is volt (V), and 1 V = 1 J/C (joule per coulomb). Resistance (R):
  • Resistance is a physical quality of conductor which resists the flow of electric current in the conductor. It is represented by ‘R’.
  • It is defined by R = VI.

V

  • Its SI unit is Ohm (Ω); 1Ω = 1.

  • Ohm’s Law states that for a metallic conductor (or resistor), the potential difference (voltage) across its ends is directly proportional to the current through it provided temperature (and other physical conditions) remain constant.
  • If V potential difference is applied at both ends of conductor and flow of electric current is I then,

Electric Generator:

  • Electric Generator is a device which converts mechanical energy into electrical energy.
  • Its works on the principle of electromagnetic induction. Transformer:
  • It is a device based on electromagnetic induction that transfers electrical energy between AC circuits.
  • It increases (step-up) or decreases (step-down) the voltage of alternating current.
  • Transformers are of two types:

(i) Step-up Transformer– It converts low voltage to high voltage of alternating current (with corresponding reduction in current ideally).

(ii) Step-down Transformer– It converts the high voltage into the low voltage of alternating current.

  • Transformers are used to supply appliances/devices at voltages different from the mains voltage and for efficient power transmission and distribution.

Electric Motor:

  • An electric motor is a device that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy, usually by employing electromagnetic effect.
  • Electric motors are used in electric fans, washing machines, mixers/grinders, water pumps, etc.
  • Electric motors can be powered by DC sources, such as from batteries, motor vehicles or rectifiers, or by AC sources, such as power grid, inverters or electric generators.

Dynamo:

  • A dynamo is an electrical generator that creates direct current (DC) using a commutator.
  • It converts mechanical energy into electrical energy through electromagnetic induction.
