Chapter 11

Conductivity

19 facts · 5 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (40 points)

Notes

Electric Conductivity:

  • Within the atom, electrons nearest to the nucleus are strongly bound to the positively charged nucleus (due to protons) by electrostatic attraction.
  • Electrons farther from the nucleus (outer/valence electrons) are comparatively less tightly bound.
  • Because they are less tightly bound, such outer electrons can be removed more easily (with sufficient external energy).
  • In metals, some outer electrons become delocalized in the solid and act as ‘conduction (free) electrons’.
  • Free (conduction) electrons are electrons not bound to a particular atom and are free to move through the material when an external electric field is applied.
  • In general physics, a free electron is an electron that can move under the influence of an applied electric (and/or magnetic) field rather than remaining bound to an atom or molecule.
  • Metals with a high availability of free electrons/mobile charge carriers (and low scattering) show high electrical conductivity.
  • Silver has the highest electrical conductivity among common metals at room temperature; copper, gold, and aluminium are also good conductors.
  • Electrical conduction is also found in some liquids (e.g., electrolytes) and in gases when the gas becomes ionized (plasma/discharge).
  • In metals, conduction is mainly due to the motion of electrons. In electrolytic liquids, conduction is mainly due to the motion of positive and negative ions. In ionized gases, conduction occurs due to electrons and ions.
  • Gases are generally poor conductors under ordinary conditions, but they conduct when sufficiently ionized. Gas breakdown/discharge depends on the electric field and on conditions such as the pressure-gap product (Paschen-type behaviour); electrical discharges/arcs can occur even at atmospheric pressure (e.g., lightning, arc lamps/welding).

Non-conductor:

  • Materials with very high electrical resistivity (very few free electrons/mobile charge carriers under normal conditions) are called insulators (non-conductors).
  • In insulators, electrons (and ions) are usually tightly bound and do not move easily, so current is extremely small under normal conditions.
  • Under sufficiently strong electric fields, an insulator may conduct due to dielectric breakdown.

Semiconductor:

  • Asemiconductor is a material whose electrical conductivity lies between that of conductors and insulators.
  • Its conductivity can increase due to temperature (thermal generation of charge carriers) and due to controlled impurity addition (doping).
  • Adding controlled impurities to a semiconductor is called doping; doped semiconductors are called extrinsic semiconductors.
  • Semiconductors typically show decreasing resistance with increasing temperature, opposite to most metals.
  • Examples: Silicon, Germanium, Selenium, Tellurium (and α-Tin as a special elemental case).

Superconductivity:

  • Superconductivity is the phenomenon of zero electrical resistance and expulsion of magnetic field from the interior (Meissner effect) in certain materials when cooled below a characteristic critical (transition) temperature.
  • The temperature at which a material’s resistance suddenly becomes zero is called the critical (transition) temperature (T(c)).
  • Examples of elemental superconductors (approx. T(c)):
S.No.Name of MatterApprox. T(c)
i.Mercury (Hg)4.2 K
ii.Tungsten (W)0.015 K
iii.Cadmium (Cd)0.56 K
iv.Aluminium (Al)1.19 K
v.Tin (Sn)3.7 K
vi.Lead (Pb)7.2 K
  • When superconductivity was discovered by Dutch physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes in 1911, it was found only at temperatures close to absolute zero (– 273.15°C). But since then, researchers have steadily uncovered materials that superconduct at higher temperatures. In recent years, scientists have accelerated that progress by focusing on hydrogen-rich materials at high pressure.
  • High-pressure hydrogen-rich materials have shown very high T(c) values. In 2019 it was discovered that lanthanum decahydride (LaH₁₀) shows superconductivity at around 250-260 K under megabar pressures of around 168-180 gigapascals (GPa).
  • A 2020 claim of near room-temperature superconductivity in “carbonaceous sulfur hydride” was later retracted (Nature, 26 Sep 2022), and a 2023 near-ambient claim in N-doped lutetium hydride was also retracted (Nature, 7 Nov 2023). Therefore, as of March, 2026, no room temperature superconductor is confirmed at ambient conditions, and the best-confirmed very-high T(c) results remain in high-pressure hydrides such as LaH₁₀.

Applications of Superconductivity:

a. Powerful superconducting electro magnets (used in certain maglev designs and in research magnets.

b.Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
c.Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) machines.
d. e.Magnetic confinement fusion reactors (e.g. tokamaks). Beam steering and focusing magnets used in particle

accelerators.

f. Low loss power cables (where implemented).

Maglev:

  • Maglev is short for magnetic levitation, in which vehicles (e.g.,Trains) are supported and guided by magnetic forces.
  • Depending on the system, levitation can use magnetic attraction (EMS) or magnetic repulsion (EDS).

Chapter 12

Nuclear Physics

82 facts · 13 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (66 points)

Notes

Nuclear Fission:

  • In general neutron induced nuclear reactions, when bombardment of neutrons are done on an element's atom, lighter particles such as α-particles, β-particles, protons etc. are emitted due to artificial disintegration of the atom's nucleus.
  • Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei (fission fragments) of comparable masses, usually accompanied by neutrons and gamma radiation.
  • Sometimes neutrons are absorbed by a nucleus to form a heavier isotope; this is neutron capture, not nuclear fission.
  • In fission, most energy is released as kinetic energy (heat) of the fission fragments; the remainder is carried by neutrons and gamma rays.
  • Hence, nuclear fission is a process in which a heavy nucleus after accepting a neutron breaks down in two lighter nucleus of comparable masses.
  • In this process –
a.some very fast-moving neutrons; and
b.a huge amount of energy mainly as kinetic energy (heat)

of fragments and neutrons, along with gamma rays are released.

  • The atomic bomb and nuclear reactor's principle depends upon the process of nuclear fission.
  • The main fact relating to nuclear fission is that huge amount of energy is released. This energy is known as 'Nuclear Energy'.
  • During this process on fission of 1 gram Uranium, 5 × 10²³ MeV energy is released which is equal to the energy produced by exploding about 20 tonnes of Trinitrotoluene (TNT).

Atomic Bomb:

  • Nuclear Bomb is a more suitable name for Atomic Bomb.
  • It is such a device in which uncontrolled chain reaction is maintained in the fissile matter by fast-moving neutrons.
  • As a result of this process in a very short time, a huge amount of energy is released.
  • In atomic bomb, highly enriched uranium (U-235) or Plutonium (Pu-239) are used.
  • Historically, uranium fission weapons used a gun-type approach (e.g., Little Boy), while plutonium weapons used an implosion-style approach (e.g., Fat Man).
  • The segments' mass of atomic bomb is less than their critical mass and are kept separately. Critical mass is the smallest amount of fissile material needed for a sustained nuclear chain reaction. The critical mass of a fissile material depends upon its nuclear properties, its density, its shape, its enrichment, its purity, its temperature and its surroundings.
  • The temperature range of10⁷ ⁰C and pressure equivalent to lakhs of atmospheric pressure is produced on the explosion of the atom bomb.

Nuclear Reactor or Atomic Pile:

  • A plant in which self-sustained controlled chain nuclear reaction is maintained and at a fixed rate, energy is obtained.
  • Such energy is utilized for several purposes such as to produce electricity and for research works.
  • A modern reactor has the following main parts –

(i) Fuel:

  • It is the main part of the reactor.
  • The matter which undergoes for fission reaction.
  • For this purpose U²³⁵ or Pu²³⁹ is used.

(ii) Moderator:

  • It reduces the speed of fast neutrons, thereby turning them into thermal neutrons capable of sustaining a nuclear chain reaction.
  • Light water or normal water (H₂O), Heavy water (D₂O), Graphite or Beryllium oxide are used as a moderator. Light water is the most commonly used moderator.

(iii) Coolant:

  • A large amount of energy is released during fission which results in an increase of the plant's temperature. To decrease the temperature of the plant, coolants such as air, water or carbon dioxide is flown through the reactor.

(iv) Control Rods:

  • These absorb the slow-moving neutrons.
  • When these rods are pushed into the reactor, the fission rate slows down and when they are withdrawn from the reactor, fission rate increases.
  • For this purpose generally Cadmium or Boron rods are used.

Nuclear Fusion:

  • When two or more light nucleus, moving with very high speed, mutually fused to form a heavy nucleus, this process is termed as nuclear fusion.
  • The mass of the nucleus formed after fusion reaction is less than that of the masses of original fusing nuclei.
  • The loss in mass is converted into energy.
  • For example – when two deuterons (₁H2 - heavy hydrogen nucleus) fused with each other, a triton (₁H³ - nucleus of tritium) or helium isotope is formed.

H² + H² → H³ + P (Proton)

or H² + H² → He³ + n (Neutron)

  • Energy released by fusion of heavy hydrogen nuclei is much more than the energy released by the fission of equal mass of uranium²³⁵.

Hydrogen Bomb:

  • It is a nuclear fusion bomb.
  • It is based on the fusion of heavy hydrogen nuclei.
  • Since the fusion takes place at very high temperature and high pressure, an atom bomb is used as ignitor along with fusion bomb.
  • In the hydrogen bomb, the process of fusion is uncontrolled reaction whose application may be proved only destructive.
  • In fact, the source of the boundless energy of the sun is the fusion of light nuclei.

Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT):

  • The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (commonly known as the Non-Proliferation Treaty or NPT) is the centrepiece of global efforts to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons, to promote cooperation in the peaceful uses of nuclear energy and to further the goal of nuclear disarmament and general and complete disarmament.
  • The NPT was opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force on 5 March 1970. On 11 May 1995, the Treaty was extended indefinitely.
  • 189 UN member States as well as two observers, namely the Holy See and the State of Palestine (total 191 States), have become parties to the NPT. However, one of these States (North Korea) announced withdrawal from the NPT in 2003, and official NPT documentation describes its membership status as uncertain.
  • NPT is the most widely adhered to treaty in the field of nuclear non-proliferation, peaceful uses of nuclear energy and nuclear disarmament.
  • The treaty defines nuclear-weapon states as those that have built and tested a nuclear explosive device before 1 January 1967; these are the United States, Russia, the United Kingdom, France, and China.
  • North Korea, which acceded in 1985 but never came into compliance, announced its withdrawal from the NPT in 2003; its first nuclear test occurred in 2006, in violation of core obligations.
  • Four UN member states have never accepted the NPT, three of which possess or are thought to possess nuclear weapons: India, Israel, and Pakistan. In addition, South Sudan, founded in 2011, has not joined.
  • The treaty defines nuclear-weapon states as those that have built and tested a nuclear explosive device before 1 January 1967; these are the United States, Russia, the United Kingdom, France, and China.

Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty:

  • The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT) is a multilateral treaty that bans nuclear weapons test explosions and any other nuclear explosions, for both civilian and military purposes, in all environments.
  • It was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on 10 September 1996, but has not entered into force. The ratifications of nine specific nations are still required for the Treaty to enter into force.
  • Of the 44 States included in Annex 2 (of the Treaty) required for entry into force of the CTBT, all have signed with the exceptions of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK-North Korea), India, and Pakistan. Five of the 44 Annex 2 States have signed but not ratified the CTBT (they are China, Egypt, Iran, Israel, and the United States), while Russia signed and ratified the treaty but subsequently withdrew its ratification prior to its entry into force.

Chapter 13

Computer and Information Technology

340 facts · 23 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (199 points)

Notes

  • Computer is a device that can be instructed to carry out sequences of arithmetic or logical operations automatically in computer programming.
  • Data: Data is measured, collected, reported and analyzed, whereupon it can be visualized using graphs, images or other analysis tools.

Data as general concepts refer to the fact that existing information or knowledge is represented or coded in some form suitable for better usage or processing.

  • Information: Information is the meaning assigned to data (facts/ideas/knowledge) using known conventions of representation. Technically data are raw facts and figures that are processed/organized/interpreted into information such as summaries and totals.
  • Bit: A bit (short for binary digit) is the smallest unit of data in a computer. A bit has a single binary value either 0 or 1.
  • Byte: A group of binary digits or bits (usually eight) operated on as a unit. A byte is considered as a unit of memory size.

Development of Computers in India:

  • HEC-2M (Hollerith Electronic Computer-2M): Computer technology came into existence in the decade of 1940 in the decade of the world. Computer age in India began in 1956 with the installation of HEC-2M (a computer designed by A.D. Booth in England) at the Indian Statistical Institute at Calcutta (now Kolkata).
  • TIFRAC (Tata Institute of Fundamental Research Automatic Calculator): It was the first computer developed in India at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research in Mumbai. It was formally commissioned in 1960.
  • PARAM Series: PARAM 8000 (first in the Param Series) was India's first indigenous supercomputer which was unveiled by C-DAC (Centre for Development of Advanced Computing) in 1991. Further more powerful series of computers were developed by C-DAC. Param Shivay (installed in IIT-BHU), Param Shakti (installed in IIT Kharagpur), Param Brahma (installed in IISER, Pune), Param Pravega (installed in IISc, Bengaluru), Param Ganga (installed in IIT-Roorkee), Param Kamrupa (installed in IIT-Guwahati), Param Himalaya (installed in IIT-Mandi), Param Utkarsh (installed at C-DAC, Bengaluru), Param Smriti (installed in NABI, Mohali), Param Yukti (installed in JNCASR), Bengaluru), Param Seva (installed in IIT-Hyderabad), Param Ananta (installed in IIT-Gandhinagar), Param Sanganak (installed in IIT-Kanpur), Param Porul (installed in NIT-Tiruchirappalli), Param Siddhi-AI (installed at C-DAC, Pune) and Param Rudra systems (installed at various institutions including IUAC Delhi, IIT-Bombay, IIT-Madras, NCRA Pune, SNBNCBS Kolkata, IIT-Patna, C-DAC Delhi etc.) are some of the latest versions of Param series of computers.

National Supercomputing Mission (NSM):

  • The National Supercomputing Mission (NSM) is a flagship initiative by the Government of India to empower the country with high-performance computing (HPC) capabilities.
  • Launched in 2015, the mission aims to enhance India’s technological prowess in supercomputing, foster research and development (R&D), and support scientific advancements across academia, industry, and government sectors.
  • NSM was set up to provide the country with supercomputing infrastructure to meet the increasing computational demands of academia, researchers, MSMEs, and startups. It is a first of its kind attempt to boost the country’s computing power.
  • The Mission envisages empowering our national academic and R&D institutions spread over the country by installing supercomputers of various capacities. Access to these supercomputers is provided through the National Knowledge Network (NKN). The NKN is another program of the government which connects academic institutions and R&D labs over a high-speed network.
  • Academic and R&D institutions as well as key user departments/ministries would participate by using these facilities and develop applications of national relevance.
  • The Mission also includes development of highly professional High-Performance Computing (HPC) aware human resource for meeting challenges of development of these applications. HRD activities in this area are steered through five training centres at Pune, Kharagpur, Chennai, Palakkad, and Goa to expand the awareness and familiarization of supercomputing with college students and researchers.
  • Under NSM, as of 30 November, 2025, a total of 37 supercomputers with cumulative compute capacity of 39 Petaflops, have been deployed across various academic institutions, research organizations, and R&D labs, including prominent institutions like IISc, IITs, C-DAC, and other institutions from Tier-II and Tier III cities of the country under NSM.
  • The supercomputing systems commissioned under NSM have achieved an overall utilization rate of over 85%, with many systems exceeding 95%, demonstrating a high level of usage and efficiency in their computational capacity.
  • NSM is steered jointly by Department of Science and Technology (DST) and Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and implemented by Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC), Pune and Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru.

Classification of Computer:

  • On the basis of their size and functioning, computers have been classified into 4 categories –

(a) Microcomputer

(b) Minicomputer

(c) Mainframe computer

(d) Supercomputer

(a) Microcomputer: A microcomputer is a small, relatively inexpensive computer with a microprocessor as its central processing unit (CPU). Many microcomputers (when equipped with keyboard and screen for input and output) are also called personal computers (P.C.). Personal computers has been divided into following –

(i) Desktop computer

(ii) Laptop computer

(iii) Notebook computer

(iv) Tablet computer

(v) Palmtop computer

(b) Minicomputer: A minicomputer is a computer of size intermediate between a microcomputer and mainframe computer. Minicomputers are used for scientific and engineering computations, business transaction processing, file handling and database management and are often referred to as small or midsize server.

(c) Mainframe computer: Mainframe computers are computers used primarily by large organizations for critical applications, bulk data processing such as census, industry and consumer statistics, enterprise resource planning and transaction processing.

(d) Supercomputer: A supercomputer is a computer with a high level of performance compared to a general purpose computer. The performance of a supercomputer is measured in floating-point operations per second (FLOP/s) instead of million instructions per second (MIPS).

  • Supercomputers can combine thousands to millions of processors/cores and they complete suitable compute intensive workloads by parallel processing.
  • Supercomputers are very expensive in cost so smaller companies can not afford it.
  • These are used primarily for scientific and engineering work requiring extremely high-speed computation.
  • Applications of supercomputers commonly include weather/climate modeling, physical simulations, computational chemistry/material science, and complex engineering computations.
  • Supercomputers are used in the following areas –
(i) Weather forecasting(ii) Oil & Gas exploration
(iii) Physical simulations(iv) Quantum mechanics
(v) Climate research(vi) Molecular modelling
  • At present (as per the November, 2025 list of TOP 500 supercomputers), the fastest supercomputer installed in India is Power Edge XE 9680 (installed at Shakti Cloud, Yotta Data Services Pvt. Ltd., Mumbai), which is ranked 28th in the world. Its performance capacity (R(max)) is 84.31 Petaflop/sand maximum capacity (R(peak)) is 102.82 Petaflop/s. However, this supercomputer is not developed/manufactured in India. It is purchased from its manufacturer DELL, USA.
  • AIRAWAT-PSAI (Integration of AIRAWAT & Param Siddhi-AI) is the fastest supercomputer developed in India which is established at C-DAC, Pune. Its performance capacity (R(max)) is 8.50 Petaflop/sand maximum capacity (R(peak)) is 13.17 Petaflop/s. In November, 2025 list of TOP500 supercomputers of the world, it is at 188th rank.
  • According to November, 2025 list of TOP500 super computers, the 3 fastest supercomputers of the world are as follows – 1. El Capitan (U.S.), 2. Frontier (U.S.), 3. Aurora (U.S.).

computers. Supercomputers are typically defined as a class of for scientific/engineering computations. So, the very fastest term 'supercomputer' was coined around the mid-1960s (e.g.,

  • It has two main parts –

(i) Control unit

(ii) Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU)

  • Memory Unit: It functions as storage and retrieval of data and instructions.
  • Generally, computer memory is of two types–

(i) Internal memory

(ii) External memory

  • Memory capacity (in binary) is measured in –

(a) Byte

(b) Kilobyte – 1 KB (KiB) – 1024 bytes (2¹⁰ bytes)

(c) Megabyte – 1 MB (MiB) – 1024 KB (2²⁰ bytes)

(d) Gigabyte – 1 GB (GiB) – 1024 MB (2³⁰ bytes)

(e) Terabyte – 1 TB (TiB) – 1024 GB (2⁴⁰ bytes)

  • Internal Memory or Primary Memory: Primary memory is semiconductor memory; RAM is typically on DIMM/SODIMM modules plugged into the motherboard; firmware is stored on non-volatile flash/EEPROM chips.
  • Internal memories which are used by computers are-

(i) RAM (Random-Access Memory)

(ii) ROM (Read-Only Memory)

(i) Random-Access Memory (RAM)

  • It is a form of computer data storage that stores data and machine code currently being used.
  • RAM allows data items to be read or written in almost the same amount of time irrespective of the physical location of data inside the memory.
  • It contains multiplexing and demultiplexing circuitry, to connect the data lines to the addressed storage for reading or writing the entry. In today's technology, random-access memory takes the form of integrated circuits.
  • It is volatile memory: RAM contents (data) are lost when power is cut unless the data was saved to non-volatile storage such as SSD/HDD.

(ii) Read-Only Memory (ROM)

  • ROM is non-volatile memory used to store firmware. In earlier systems, ROM was the memory from which we can only read but cannot write on it. In modern computers firmware storage is commonly EEPROM/flash, which can be updated/rewritten.
  • This type of memory is non-volatile.
  • The information remains stored even after the computer is switched off; it is not deleted.
  • 'Basic input & output system' (BIOS)/ Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) firmware is stored in system flash memory (EEPROM/flash) and can be updated.
  • External Memory or Secondary Memory: Main examples of secondary memory are–

(i) Hard Disk

(ii) Floppy Disk

(iii) CD ROM

(iv) DVD

(v) Pen Drive

(vi) Blu-ray Disc.

  • Hard Disk – A hard disk has one or more platters/disks. Each disk is divided into the track and each track is divided into the sector.
  • DVD (Digital Versatile Disc or Digital Video Disc) - It is an optical storage device, which is similar to CD, but its storage capacity is much more than that of CD.
  • Its capacity depends on DVD type; commonly about 4.7 GB vs about 650 MB for a CD –about 7 times; and higher for double layer/double sided DVDs.
  • DVD formats include DVD-ROM/DVD-Video (read only), DVD-R and DVD+R (record-once), DVD-RW and DVD+RW (rewritable), and DVD-RAM (rewritable).
  • Pen Drive – Pen Drive is also known as a USB flash drive. It is widely used as a portable data storage device.
  • Blu-ray Disc – Blu-ray Disc is an optical disc, which is the advance version of DVD. In Blu-ray Disc, blue represents the colour of laser and ray represents optical ray.

Input Units:

  • Such devices which are used to enter data and instructions in the computer are known as Input Units.
  • Examples of input devices are – keyboard, mouse, scanner, trackball, and lightpen, etc.

Output Unit:

  • An output device is any device used to send data from a computer to another device or user.
  • Examples of output units are – printer, speakers, headphones, projectors, monitors, plotter, and LCD, etc.
  • Output can be visual (monitor/projector), audio (speakers/ headphones), and hardcopy (printer/plotter), etc.

Computer Software:

  • Computer software has been divided into two parts –

1. System software

2. Application software

1. System Software:

  • System software is used for operating computer system. They are designed to provide a platform for other software.
  • Examples of system software include operating systems like Microsoft Windows, macOS, Ubuntu/Linux, and Android (in smartphones and tablets).
  • It controls the internal operations of the computer.

2. Application Software:

  • Application software is used by the user to perform specific task.
  • These are installed according to user's requirements.
  • There are different application software for different required applications such as, for writing, to keep data, to record the song, calculation of salary and accounts of transactions.
  • Application software include such things as database programs, word processors, Web browsers, spreadsheets, graphic software, computational science software, game engines, industrial automation, etc.

Computer Programming Languages:

  • For functioning, the computer follows the instructions given by the programmer. This set of instructions is called a (computer) program that produces various kinds of output. A program is written in a programming language. Generations of Computer Languages:
  • Programming languages are often classified into ‘generations’as a broad taxonomy (however, the boundaries are not universally fixed). A common classification is:

machine language (1GL), assembly language (2GL), high level languages (3GL), very high-level/nonprocedural languages and tools often used for database/query reporting and application generation (4GL), and logic constraint-based AI-oriented languages sometimes labeled as 5GL.

  • First-Generation Languages (1GL):

Machine Language: The most basic form, consisting of binary code (0s and 1s) that the CPU directly executes. Examples: Machine code specific to a particular computer architecture.

Characteristics: Very difficult for humans to read/write; hardware-dependent, requiring direct interaction with the computer's hardware.

  • Second-Generation Languages (2GL):

Assembly Language: Uses mnemonics and symbolic names that map closely to machine instructions and is translated by an assembler. Examples: Assembly language specific to a particular CPU architecture.

Characteristics: Still low-leveland hardware-dependent; requiring knowledge of the underlying hardware, but easier to program than machine language.

  • Third-Generation Languages (3GL):

High-Level Languages: More human-readable; typically compiled or interpreted into machine code.Examples: C, C++, Java, Python, PHP, Perl, C#, BASIC, Pascal, Fortran, ALGOL, COBOL, etc.

Characteristics: More portable and maintainable than low-level languages.

  • Fourth-Generation Languages (4GL):

Very High-Level / Largely Nonprocedural Languages and Tools: Often used for database querying, reporting, and rapid application development where users specify what result is needed rather than how to compute it. These languages are designed to simplify database management and scripting tasks, often using declarative syntax. Examples: SQL; query-by-example (QBE); report generators and application generators (tooling category). Characteristics: Focus on what needs to be done rather than how, making them more efficient for specific tasks.

  • Fifth-Generation Languages (5GL):

Logic/Constraint-Based AI-Oriented Languages: Often associated with logic programming and AI research; sometimes also defined by natural language understanding and processing. Examples: Prolog, OPS5, Mercury, etc. Characteristics: Emphasize logic/rules/constraints and knowledge representation approaches for problem solving, allowing computers to solve problems in a more human like way.

Computer Network:

  • A computer network is a set of computers/nodes with supporting network links connected together for the purpose of communicating/exchanging data and sharing resources.
  • Types of Network: Following are the types of network-

(i) Local Area Network (LAN): A local area network is a computer network that interconnects computers and other devices within a limited area such as a residence, school, laboratory, university campus/building or office.

(ii) Wide Area Network (WAN): A wide Area Network is a telecommunications network or computer network that extends over a large geographical area (e.g., across cities/ countries/continents). WAN connectivity is often provided using telecommunications infrastructure, including leased circuits and carrier networks.

(iii) Metropolitan Area Network (MAN): A high-speed network spanning a metropolitan area (typically a large city) and commonly used to interconnect multiple LANs across that area using high-speed links and networking equipment.

World Wide Web (www):

  • The World Wide Web (WWW) is an information space of interrelated resources identified by URIs/URLs and accessed over the Internet using web technologies (commonly HTTP- Hyper Text Transfer Protocol).
  • Commonly known as 'the Web', it is an information system on the Internet which allows documents and other web resources to be connected to other documents/resources by hypertext links, enabling the user to search (navigate/ browse) for information by moving from one document to another.
  • British scientist Tim Berners-Lee invented the Web in 1989. He wrote the first web browser while employed at CERN near Geneva, Switzerland.
  • Web resources are commonly represented using HTML (Hyper Text Markup Language) and delivered by web servers to user agents (e.g., web browsers), which render text and link to or embed media such as images, audio, and video.

E-mail:

  • E-mail (electronic mail) is a method of exchanging digital messages over computer networks (today, primarily the Internet).
  • Raymond (Ray) Tomlinson is widely known for inventing network electronic mail and introducing the “@” convention for addressing; however, earlier email-like systems existed on time-sharing computers (e.g., CTSS in the 1960s).
  • Email first entered limited use in early time-sharing systems and later became a major application on computer networks; today it operates primarily over the Internet.
