Chapter 15

Defence Technology

102 facts · 13 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (190 points)

Notes

IGMDP:

  • The Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme (IGMDP) was conceived by renowned scientist Dr. APJ Abdul Kalam (then director of Defence Research and Development Laboratory – DRDL) to enable India to attain self-sufficiency in the field of missile technology.
  • The IGMDP finally got the approval from the Govt. of India on 26 July, 1983. This ambitious project brought together the country’s scientific community, academic institutions, R & D laboratories and industries in giving shapes to the strategic, indigenous missile system.
  • IGMDP was started in 1983 and completed in March, 2012.
  • The missiles developed under this programme are:
a.Short-range surface to surface ballistic missile – Prithvi
b.Intermediate-range surface to surface ballistic missile – Agni

(As re-entry 'Technology Demonstrator' project; technology used for Agni series of missiles)

c. Short-range low-level surface to air missile – Trishul (Technology Demonstrator – not inducted)

d. e.Medium-range surface to air missile – Akash Third Generation anti-tank missile – Nag
  • Dr. Kalam played a major role in the development and operationlisation of Agni and Prithvi Missiles.

Prithvi Missile:

  • Prithvi is a tactical surface to surface short-range ballistic missile developed by DRDO under the IGMDP. It is deployed by India’s Strategic Forces Command.
  • Its first test was conducted on 25 February, 1988 from (SHAR)- Sriharikota High Altitude Range.
  • Its variants are as follows –

(a) Prithvi - I (ss-150) – Army version: 150 km range with a warhead of 1000 kg.

(b) Prithvi - II (ss-250) – Air Force version: 250 km range with a warhead of 500-750 kg.

(c) Prithvi - III (ss-350)/Dhanush – Naval version: 350 km range with a warhead of 1000 kg.

  • Prithvi missiles are operated by liquid propellants. Agni Missile:
  • Under IGMDP, Agni began as a re-entry technology demonstrator. The Agni demonstrator's first flight test was conducted on 22 May, 1989 from ITR Chandipur (subsequent flights followed later).
  • It was double stage missile of which first stage was solid and second stage was liquid.
  • Agni re-entry 'Technology Demonstrator' project has been completed successfully. It was not an operationally inducted missile). Its re-entry technologies were later used in the Agni series of missiles.
  • Its advanced version – ‘Agni-II’was successfully test-fired on 11 April, 1999 from ITR Chandipur, which is capable to carry a warhead of 1000 kg and can strike target up to the distance of 2000 km.
  • It is double stage missile which is 16 tonne heavy and 20 m long.
  • For deployment in Military, solid propellant techniques are preferred because the solid propellants can kept filled before and can be fired.
  • The missile can be fired just after getting any information.
  • The height of Agni-I is 15 m and weight is 12 tonne.
  • It can be fired up to a range of 700 km with a warhead of 1000 kg.
  • It was firstly test-fired on 25 January, 2002 from ITR Chandipur.
  • Agni - II and Agni - I have been deployed in Military. Agni III:
  • After maturation of Agni - II Technology, Agni - III came into existence.
  • Its first successful test-fire was conducted on 12 April, 2007.
  • It is capable to carry a warhead of 1500 kg. and can be fired up to a distance of 3000 km.

Agni IV:

  • It is fourth in the Agni series of missiles.
  • Its operational range is 4000 km.
  • Its weight is 17 tonnes and length 20 metre.
  • It is two-stage, solid propellant missile.
  • It is capable to carry a warhead weighing 1000 kg. Agni V:
  • Agni V is India's Intermediate Range Ballistic Missile (IRBM).
  • Its first test was conducted on 19 April, 2012.
  • Its length is 17.50 m and weight 50 tonne.
  • It is three-stage missile.
  • It is solid propellant operated missile and capable to carry both conventional and nuclear warhead of 1.5 tonne.
  • Its operational range is over 5000 km, which can be extended up to 8000 to 10,000 km as per some sources.
  • On 15 December, 2022, first night trial of Agni V was successfully carried out by the Strategic Forces Command (SFC).
  • Mission Divyastra, conducted by India's DRDO on 11 March, 2024, was the first successful flight test of the indigenously developed Agni-5 missile equipped with Multiple Independently Targetable Re-entry Vehicle (MIRV) technology.
  • On 20 August, 2025, successful test-firing of Agni 5 from ITR Chandipur, carried out under the aegis of the Strategic Forces Command (SFC).

Agni P:

  • Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) successfully flight tested a New Generation Nuclear Capable Ballistic Missile Agni P (Agni Prime) from Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam island offthe coast of Odisha, Balasore on 28 June, 2021.
  • Agni P is a new generation advanced variant of Agni class of missiles.
  • It is a two-stage, canisterised, solid propellant ballistic missile with a dual redundant navigation and guidance system.
  • It has maneuverable re-entry vehicle (MaRV) capability that can alter flight path during re-entry.
  • It has range capability between 1,000 and 2,000 kms.
  • On 18 December, 2021, the second flight test of Agni P was successfully conducted by the DRDO.
  • On 21 October, 2022, Agni P was successfully test fired for the third time to achieve maximum range.
  • A first pre-induction night launch of Agni P was carried out by users on 7 June, 2023.
  • Strategic Forces Command along with DRDO conducted a successful flight-test of Agni P on 3 April, 2024.
  • DRDO in collaboration with SFC carried out a successful launch of Agni P from a rail-based mobile launcher system under a full operational scenario on 24 September, 2025.
  • The road-mobile Agni Phas already been inducted into services after a series of successful flight trials.

RudraM-I:

  • The RudraM-I, previously referred as DRDO's anti radiation missile (ARM) or new generation anti-radiation missile (NGARM) is an air-to-surface anti-radiation missile developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO).
  • It is primarily meant for suppression of enemy air defenses (SEAD), that can be launched from a range of altitudes with large standoffdistance for destroying enemy surveillance radars, tracking and communication systems.
  • It is the first indigenous anti-radiation missile developed by India.
  • It has a range of up to 200 km and it can be launched from altitudes of 500 m to 15 km. Its range varies based on launch conditions.
  • It was successfully flight tested on 9 October, 2020 by DRDO. It was launched from SU-30 MKI fighter aircraft on a radiation target located on Wheeler Island off the coast of Odisha.

RudraM-II:

  • Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) successfully flight-tested the RudraM-II air-to surface missile from Su-30 MKI platform of the Indian Air Force (IAF) off the coast of Odisha on May 29, 2024.
  • The flight-test met trial objectives, validating the propulsion system and control and guidance algorithm.
  • RudraM-II is described as an indigenously-developed, solid-propelled, air-launched missle system meant for Air-to-Surface role to neutralise multiple types of enemy assets.
  • A number of state-of-the-art indigenous technologies developed by various DRDO laboratories have been incorporated in the missile system.
  • It has a range of 300 km and has an additional Imaging Infrared (IIR) seeker.
  • The missile can be launched from a variety of altitudes and has the capability to detect enemy radio frequencies and signals from radars at ranges exceeding 100 km.
  • It is equipped with Lock-On-Before/After-Launch systems, providing flexibility in targeting.
  • Additionally, the missile features an internal guidance system that enables it to autonomously navigate towards the target after launch.

Prahaar Missile:

  • Its weight is 1.28 Tonne with a length of 7.3 metre and diameter of 42 cm.
  • It is single-stage solid propellant missile.
  • It can be launched within 2-3 minutes without any preparation, providing significantly better reaction time than liquid-fuelled Prithvi Ballistic Missile and act as a gap filler in the range between the Pinaka Multi-barrel Rocket Launcher System (MBRLS) and Smerch MBRL in due end and the Prithvi ballistic missile (MRBM) on the other.
  • Rapid and the sharp reaction is the main peculiar feature of Prahar missile.
  • It is capable to carry the warhead of 200 kg.
  • It can strike target up to a distance of 150 km within 250 seconds.
  • Prahaar was first test-fired successfully on 21 July, 2011 from the Integrated Test Range (ITR) at Chandipur. Pragati Missile:
  • India’s DRDO is promoting an indigenously developed short-range ballistic missile called Pragati, designed to strike targets up to ranges of 60-170 km.
  • It is an export variant of the Prahaar missile.
  • It is 7.4 min length with 0.42 m diameter.
  • It is capable to carry a conventional warhead of 200 kg. Nirbhay Cruise Missile:
  • It is a long-range, all-weather, subsonic cruise missile designed and developed by DRDO.
  • It can be launched from multiple platforms and is capable of carrying up to 300 kg conventional or nuclear warheads.
  • It is a surface to surface missile.
  • It is two-stage missile of long-range.
  • It is six meter long, 0.52 m wide and with a wingspan of

2.7 m, it can carry the designated warhead at speed of

0.6-0.7 Mach.

  • Its launch weight is about 1500 kg.
  • It is remarkable that Nirbhay missile is launchedjust like a rocket. Upon reaching the required velocity and height this turbofan engine missile takes over the further propulsion.
  • Defence Experts often compared in analyses, Nirbhay Missile to the Tomahawk of U.S.A. (similar class/role). Amogha ATGM Missiles:
  • Amogha I is a second generation, Anti-Tank, Guided Missile (ATGM) which has pinpoint accuracy for a range upto 2.8 km.
  • It has been designed and developed by Bharat Dynamics Ltd. (BDL) at Hyderabad.
  • Its operational range is 2.8 km.
  • The test firing was carried out on September 10, 2015 at Babina Army Range, Jhansi, Uttar Pradesh.
  • In the test two missile were fired and both hit targets placed at 2.8 km as well as 2.6 km respectively.
  • On 14 October 2017, its upgraded version, the Amogha-II missile was successfully test fired by the BDL for the first time using a launcher on the ground.
  • Amogha-II uses Semi Automatic Command to Line of Sight (SACLOS) with a radio frequency seeker.
  • Amogha-III is an indigenous, third-generation, man portable ‘fire-and-forget’ Anti-Tank Guided Missile (ATGM) designed and developed by the in-house R&D Division of Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL).
  • On 7 February 2020, BDL unveiled Amogha-III ATGM at Defexpo 2020 in Lucknow.
  • It features a tandem warhead, dual-mode Imaging Infra Red (IIR) seeker, and a range of200 m to 2.5 km, capable of top and direct attack modes for destroying modern armored vehicles.
  • BDL successfully test-fired its Amogha-III ATGM on March 26, 2023. The test met all mission objectives, demonstrating fire-and-forget capability with a range of 200 m–2.5 km.
  • On 21 February, 2024, Indian Army's Battle Axe Division (12 Infantry Division, part of XII Corps) tested the 2.5 km range ATGM in Jaisalmer district. The missile was fired from man portable tripod. The missile uses a tandem high-explosive anti-tank (HEAT) warhead to neutralise vehicles with explosive reactive armour (ERA).

K- Missile Family:

  • The K-missile family named after Indian Scientist and former President A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, is a series of submarine-launched ballistic missile developed by India to boost its second-strike capabilities and thus augments its nuclear deterrence.
  • First missile of this series is Sagarika (K-15) which has been tested successfully many times.
  • Its launch platform is Arihant Class Submarine.
  • Its firing range is approximately 700 km (700-750 km in some sources).
  • Its speed is 7.5 Mach.
  • Shaurya has been reported as a land-based version of Sagarika K-15 Missile.

K-4 Missile:

  • It is a nuclear-capable intermediate-range submarine launched ballistic missile under development by DRDO to arm the Arihant class submarines.
  • This missile has a maximum range of 3500 km.
  • It has been developed under a classified DRDO–Navy programme; official technical details are limited in public domain.

BrahMos Missile:

  • The BrahMos is a medium-range ramjet supersonic cruise missile that can be launched from submarine, ships, aircraft, or land.
  • It is a joint venture between the Russian Federation's NPO Mashinostroyeniya and India's Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), who together have formed BrahMos Aerospace. The name BrahMos is a portmanteau formed from the names of two rivers, the Brahmaputra of India and the Moskva of Russia.
  • BrahMos missile's original range was 290 km with speed of 2.8 to 3.0 Mach. In 2019, India upgraded the missile with a new range of450/500 km. The 450/500 km variant of the BrahMos is referred to as BrahMos ER (Extended Range).
  • A hypersonic version of the missile BrahMos-II, is also presently under development with a speed of Mach 7-8 to boost aerial fast strike capability.
  • In February, 2024, the Cabinet Committee on Security has cleared the Indian Navy's proposals to buy 220 BrahMos ER supersonic cruise missiles for its warships.
  • In 2016, as India became a member of the Missile Technology Control Regime (MTCR), India and Russia are now planning and jointly developing a new generation of BrahMos missiles with extended ranges (far beyond 400 km) and an ability to hit protected targets with pinpoint accuracy.
  • In April, 2025 and March, 2026, India has sent the second and third batches of BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles to Philippines. Earlier, in April, 2024, India delivered the first batch of BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles to Philippines. In January, 2022, Philippines concluded a $375-million deal with India for three batteries of shore based, anti-ship variant of the BrahMos becoming the first export customer for thejoint venture missile between India and Russia.

Pralay Missile:

  • Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) successfully conducted maiden flight test of indigenously developed new generation surface-to-surface missile 'Pralay', from Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam Island off the coast of Odisha on 22 December, 2021.
  • Pralay is a canisterised surface-to-surface tactical short-range ballistic missile (SRBM) for battlefield use developed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO).
  • The missile is the amalgamation of technologies developed for exoatmospheric interceptor missile Prithvi Defence Vehicle (PDV) from Indian Ballistic Missile Defence Programme and Prahaar tactical missile.
  • The Missile is powered with solid propellant rocket motor and many new technologies. The missile has a range of 150-500 kilometre and can be launched from a mobile launcher. The missile guidance system includes state-of the-art navigation system and integrated avionics to ensure high precision.
  • The missile is capable of carrying multiple types of warheads against various targets.
  • On 23 December, 2021, DRDO conducted second test of Pralay from the Abdul Kalam Island. For the first time, two consecutive flight tests of a ballistic missile have been conducted successfully on two consecutive days. The second test concluded with a heavier payload and different range to check the precision and lethality of the missile.
  • On December 31, 2025, India successfully conducted a salvo launch of two Pralay missiles, a solid-propellant, surface-to-surface, quasi-ballistic weapon with a 500 km range.
  • Conducted by the DRDO off the Odisha coast, these user evaluation trials validated the missile’s high precision navigation, guidance, and ability to hit targets with conventional warheads, marking its readiness for induction.

Indian Ballistic Missile Defence (BMD) System:

  • Indian Ballistic Missile Defence Programme is an initiative to develop and deploy a multi-layered ballistic missile defence system to protect from ballistic missile attacks.
  • DRDO has developed a two-layer Ballistic Missile Defence (BMD) capability against missiles with range up to the 2000 km-class, with exo-atmospheric and endo atmospheric interception demonstrated.
  • It is a double-tiered system consisting of two interceptor missiles namely the Prithvi Air Defence (PAD) missile for high altitude interception and the Advanced Air Defence (AAD) missile for lower altitude interception.
  • The system also includes an overlapping network of early warning and tracking RADAR, as well as command and control system.
  • The layered BMD concept is based on atmospheric interception layers (endo/exo); for Phase II, DRDO tested the AD-1 interceptor designed for low exo-atmospheric and endo-atmospheric interception.
  • Earlier interception trials are reported as Nov. 27, 2006 (exo-atmospheric) and Dec. 6, 2007 (endo-atmospheric using AAD).
  • On 2 Nov., 2022, DRDO conducted a successful maiden flight-test of Phase II BMD interceptor AD-1, with participation of BMD weapon-system elements at different locations.
  • On 21 April, 2023, DRDO and the Indian Navy conducted a maiden flight trial of a sea-based endo-atmospheric interceptor missile; land-based BMD had been demonstrated earlier.
  • On 24 July, 2024, DRDO successfully flight-tested the Phase II Ballistic Missile Defence System; the test validated the networked weapon system and demonstrated capability to defend against ballistic missiles of the 5000 km class.
  • The Phase II test description includes system elements such as long-range sensors, low-latency communication, and Mission Control Centre (MCC) as part of the network centric BMD weapon system.
  • With the successful tests of BMD, India became the 4th country to have successfully developed an anti-ballistic missile system after U.S.A., Russia and Israel.
  • This anti-ballistic missile defence system has undergone several tests but its operational/commissioning details are not officially disclosed publicly; information is treated as strategic.

Missile Technology Control Regime (MTCR):

  • The Missile Technology Control Regime (MTCR) is an informal political understanding among states that seek to limit the proliferation of missiles and missile technology.
  • MTCR was formed in 1987 by the G-7 industrialized countries (Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the UK, and the United States).
  • There are currently 35 countries that are members (Partners) of the MTCR: Argentina (1993); Australia (1990); Austria (1991); Belgium (1990); Brazil (1995); Bulgaria (2004); Canada (1987); Czech Republic (1998); Denmark (1990); Finland (1991); France (1987); Germany (1987); Greece (1992); Hungary (1993); Iceland (1993); India (2016); Ireland (1992); Italy (1987); Japan (1987); Luxembourg (1990); Netherlands (1990); New Zealand (1991); Norway (1990); Poland (1998); Portugal (1992); South Korea (Republic of Korea) (2001); Russian Federation (1995); South Africa (1995); Spain (1990); Sweden (1991); Switzerland (1992); Turkiye (Turkey) (1997); Ukraine (1998); United Kingdom (1987); United States of America (1987). The date in brackets represents the initial year of membership.
  • The MTCR seeks to limit the risks of proliferation of weapons of mass destruction (WMD) by controlling exports of goods and technologies that could make a contribution to delivery systems (other than manned aircraft) for such weapons. In this context, the Regime places particular focus on rockets and unmanned aerial vehicles capable of delivering a payload of at least 500 kg to a range of at least 300 km and on equipment, software, and technology for such systems.
  • The MTCR is not a treaty and does not impose any legally binding obligations on Partners (members). Rather, it is an informal political understanding among states that seek to limit the proliferation of missiles and missile technology. The Hague Code of Conduct against Ballistic Missile Proliferation (HCoC):
  • The Hague Code of Conduct against Ballistic Missile Proliferation (HCoC) is the result of efforts of the international community to internationally regulate the area of ballistic missiles capable of carrying weapons of mass destruction (WMD).
  • The Hague Code of Conduct (HCoC), was established on 25 November, 2002 as an arrangement to prevent the proliferation of ballistic missiles.
  • The HCoC is the only multilateral code in the area of disarmament which has been adopted over the last years. The HCoC does not ban ballistic missiles, but calls for maximum possible restraint in the development, testing and deployment of ballistic missiles capable of delivering WMD.
  • Along with the MTCR, the HCoC is one of the only multilateral instruments addressing ballistic missile proliferation; the HCOC is the transparency and confidence building measure concerning the spread of ballistic missiles.
  • Since the launch and coming into effect of the HCoC Code in November, 2002 in The Hague (Netherlands), the number of signatories has increased from 93 to 145 (143 UN members, the Cook Islands and the Holy See). In 2024, Qatar became the 145th subscribing State of the HCoC.
  • India joined the HCoC on 1 June, 2016.

Australia Group:

  • The Australia Group (AG) is a multilateral export control regime (MECR) and an informal forum of countries and the European Union (represented by the European Commission) established in 1985 (after the use of chemical weapons by Iraq in 1984) to help member countries to identify those exports which need to be controlled so as not to contribute to the spread of chemical and biological weapons.
  • The Australia Group is an informal forum of countries which, through the harmonisation of export controls, seeks to ensure that exports do not contribute to the development of chemical or biological weapons.
  • The group, initially consisting of15 members and the EU, held its first meeting in Brussels, Belgium, in June, 1985.
  • With the incorporation of India on 19 January, 2018, it now has 43 members, including Australia, New Zealand, the European Union (represented by the European Commission), all 27 member States of the European Union, United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, India, Ukraine, and Argentina.
  • The name comes from Australia's initiative to create the group. Australia manages the secretariat.
  • All States participating in the Australia Group are parties to the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC) and the Biological Weapons Convention (BWC).

Wassenaar Arrangement:

  • The Wassenaar Arrangement on Export Controls for Conventional Arms and Dual-Use Goods and Technologies was formally established in 1996, replacing a previous export control mechanism (The Coordinating Committee for Multilateral Export Controls: CoCom).
  • The Wassenaar Arrangement is a multilateral export control regime (MECR) with 42 participating States.
  • The 42 Participating States in the Wassenaar Arrangement are Argentina, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Canada, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, India, Ireland, Italy, Japan, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Mexico, Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Russia, Slovakia, Slovenia, South Africa, South Korea, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkiye, Ukraine, the United Kingdom, and the United States.
  • The Wassenaar Arrangement promotes transparency, exchanges of views and information, and greater responsibility in transfers of conventional arms and dual use goods and technologies with military applications.
  • Participating States undertake to ensure that exports of these items do not contribute to the development or enhancement of military capabilities which undermine international and regional security and stability.
  • Representatives of Participating States meet regularly in Vienna where the Wassenaar Arrangement's Secretariat is located.

New START (Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty):

  • New START (New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty) is a nuclear arms reduction treaty between the United States and the Russian Federation with the formal name of Measures for the Further Reduction and Limitation of Strategic Offensive Arms.
  • It was signed on 8 April, 2010 in Prague, and, after ratification, entered into force on 5 February, 2011. It was extended for five years in 2021.
  • New START superseded the Treaty of Moscow (SORT), upon entry into force (5 February, 2011). The SORT was to remain in force until 31 December, 2012, unless superseded earlier.
  • It follows the START I treaty, which expired in December 2009; the proposed START II treaty, which never entered into force; and the START III treaty, for which negotiations were never concluded.
  • New START contained limits of1,550 deployed strategic warheads and 700 deployed delivery vehicles, and also limits each Party to 800 deployed and non-deployed launchers. Its verification provisions revise, update, and build upon START’s verification provisions. It does not limit the number of operationally inactive nuclear warheads that can be stockpiled, a number in the high thousands.
  • On 21 February, 2023, Russia suspended its participation in New START. However, it did not withdraw from the treaty, and clarified that it would continue to abide by the numerical limits in the treaty.
  • On 5 February, 2026, the new START officially expired as under its provisions, it could not be extended beyond. The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO):
  • The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), also called the North Atlantic Alliance, is an intergovernmental military alliance of 32 member States – 30 European and 2 North American.
  • Established in the aftermath of World War II, the organization implements the North Atlantic Treaty, signed in Washington, D.C., on 4 April, 1949.
  • NATO is a collective defence alliance: Article 5 treats an armed attack against one as an attack against all, and each Ally will assist by taking action it deems necessary (including the use of armed force).
  • NATO formed with twelve founding members and has added new members ten times, most recently when Sweden joined the alliance on 7 March, 2024. In addition, NATO currently recognizes Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, and Ukraine as aspiring members.
  • NATO's main headquarters are located in Brussels, Belgium, while NATO's military headquarters are near Mons, Belgium.

Notes

Albert Einstein (1879-1955):

  • German-born physicist who developed the special and general theories of relativity and won the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1921 for his services to Theoretical Physics, and especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect.
  • Einstein is generally considered the most influential physicist of the 20th Century.

Einstein miracle year 1905 –

  • While working at the patent office, he did some of the most creative works of his life.
  • First Paper – He applied the quantum theory (Developed by German Physicist Max Planck) to light in order to explain the phenomenon known as the photoelectric effect, by which a material will emit electrically charged particles when hit by light.
  • Second Paper – Einstein's second paper of 1905, titled "On the Motion of Small Particles Suspended in a Stationary Liquid, as Required by the Molecular-Kinetic Theory of Heat", provided a theoretical, mathematical explanation for Brownian motion. it provided crucial evidence for the existence of atoms and molecules, helping to convince skeptical physicists of their reality.
  • Third Paper – In the third and most famous article titled “On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies” Einstein confronted the apparent contradiction between two principal theories of physics: Isaac Newton concepts of absolute space and time and James Clerk Maxwell’s idea (via electromagnetism) that the speed of light is a constant. To do this he introduced his Special Theory of Relativity which held that the laws of physics are the same even for objects moving in different inertial frames (i.e. at constant speeds relative to each other) and that the speed of light is constant in all inertial frames.
  • Fourth paper concerned the fundamental relationship between mass and energy. Einstein famous equation E = mc² (where ‘c’is the constant speed of light) expressed this relationship.
  • In November, 1915 Einstein published four papers that laid out the foundation of the General Theory of Relativity, which explains the law of gravitation and its relation to the forces of nature.

C.V. Raman (1888-1970):

  • Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman was born at Thiruvanaikaval in Tiruchirappalli in Southern India on Nov. 7, 1888. His father was a Lecturer in Mathematics and Physics so that from childhood he was immersed in an academic atmosphere. He entered Presidency College Madras in 1902 and in 1904 he completed his bachelor’s degree winning the first place and the gold medal in Physics and in 1907 he gained his Master degree, obtaining the highest distinctions.
  • His earliest researches in optics and acoustics-the two fields of investigation to which he has dedicated his entire career were carried out while he was a student.
  • Since at that time a scientific career did not appear to present the best possibilities, Raman joined the Indian Finance Department in 1907, though the duties of his office took most of his time, Raman found opportunities for carrying on experimental research in the laboratory of the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science at Calcutta (now Kolkata) of which he became Honorary Secretary in 1919.
  • In 1917 he was offered the newly endowed Palit Chair of Physics at Calcutta University and decided to accept it. After 15 years at Calcutta he became Professor at the

Scientist Main contribution / Invention Native land Indian Institute of Science at Bangalore.

  • He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society early in his career (1924) and was Knighted in 1929. In 1930 he was awarded Nobel Prize for his work Raman-Effect.

Satyendra Nath Bose (1894-1974):

  • Satyendra Nath Bose [Born Jan. 1, 1894, Calcutta (now Kolkata) – died Feb. 4, 1974], was great Indian Mathematician and Physicist noted for his collaboration with Albert Einstein in developing a theory regarding the gaslike qualities of Electromagnetic radiation (Bose Einstein Statistics).
  • Bose, a graduate of the University of Calcutta taught at the University of Dhaka (1921-1945) and then at Calcutta (1945-1956). Bose’s numerous scientific papers published contributed to statistical mechanics and thermoluminescence and unified field theory. Bose’s Planck’s Law and the Hypothesis of Light Quanta (1924) led Einstein to seek him out for a collaboration.
  • A Fellow of the Royal Society, he was awarded India’s second-highest civilian award, the Padma Vibhushan, in 1954 by the Govt. of India.
  • The class of particles that obey Bose-Einstein statistics– bosons– was named after Bose by Paul Dirac.

Notes

Indian Science Congress Association (ISCA):

  • The Indian Science Congress Association is an autonomous scientific society/professional body in the DST (Department of Science & Technology, Government of India) family; supported through grant-in-aid.
  • The ISCA is a premier scientific organization of the country established in 1914, with headquarters at Kolkata (W.B.). It owes its origin to the foresight and initiative of two British scientists, namely, Prof. J.L. Simonsen (chemist) and Prof. P.S. MacMahon (mathematician).
  • ISCA has been promoting science and inculcating the spirit of science through its multifarious activities.
  • The ISCA is a society originally registered under Societies Act XXI of 1860; now deemed registered under the West Bengal Societies Registration Act, 1961.
  • The ISCA vision is to inculcate scientific temper among the common people.
  • The ISCA mission is to make people aware about the recent developments in science and technology and its impact on the society, to establish different centres all over India for spreading scientific knowledge through school / college programs, to provide a common platform where scientists from India and abroad can exchange their views.
  • The first Indian Science Congress was held in 1914 at the premises of the Asiatic Society, Calcutta (Now Kolkata).
  • The 104th ISC conference was held at Sri Venkateshwar University, Tirupati, (A.P.) from 3-7 Jan 2017; 105th conference held at Manipur University (Imphal) from 16-20 March 2018; 106th conference was held at Lovely Professional University, Phagwara, Jalandhar, Punjab from 3-7 Jan. 2019 and its focal theme was– ‘Future India:

Science &Technology’.

  • Its 107th conference was held at University of Agricultural Sciences, GKVK Campus, Bengaluru with the focal theme of‘Science & Technology: Rural Development' from 3-7 Jan. 2020.
  • Due to COVID-19 pandemic annual ISC conference was cancelled in 2021 and 2022.
  • 108th ISC conference was held from 3-7 January, 2023 at Rashtrasant Tukadoji Maharaj (R.T.M.) Nagpur University with the focal theme of 'Science and Technology for Sustainable Development with Women Empowerment'.
  • The 109th edition of the ISC was originally meant to hosted by Lucknow University (LU) on the theme 'Global Perspective on Science and Technology for a Sustainable Future'. However, LU withdrew from the responsibility and the venue was shifted to Lovely Professional University (LPU), Jalandhar but LPU has also backed out from hosting this event. Ultimately it was not held due to a dispute between the Department of Science and Technology (DST) and the Indian Science Congress Association (ISCA).

Nanotechnology:

  • The branch of technology that deals with the dimensions and tolerances of less than 100 nanometres, especially the manipulation of individual atoms and molecules.
  • Nanometre is a unit of length (1 nanometre = 10–⁹ metre)
  • The matter on nanoscale is too small which cannot be seen by the naked eyes, and even with conventional lab/ optical microscopes; nanoscale is studied using advanced tools such as electron microscopes and scanning probe microscopes.
  • To observe matter on nanoscale Scanning Tunneling Microscope or Atomic Force Microscope is used.
  • Eminent physicist Richard Feynman firstly expressed his views on this subject at California Institute of Technology (Caltech) on 29 Dec. 1959 and initiated an era of nanotechnology.
  • The term nanotechnology was firstly defined by Tokyo Science University Professor Norio Taniguchi in 1974. According to him nanotechnology mainly consists of the processing, separation, consolidation and deformation of materials by one atom or by one molecule.
  • In 1986, Dr. K. Eric Drexler wrote a book on nano technology – 'Engines of Creation: The coming era of Nanotechnology', which is the first book on this subject. LASER:
  • A laser is a device that emits light through a process of optical amplification based on the stimulated emission of electromagnetic radiation.
  • The term LASER originated as an acronym for “Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation”.
  • The emission generally covers an extremely limited range of visible, infrared or ultraviolet wavelengths.
  • Laser light is highly directional, highly monochromatic and highly coherent; it is often polarized and forms a narrow, collimated beam. A narrow laser beam can be focused to a small spot; focusing is limited by optics/ diffraction.
  • Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics (Garching near Munich, Germany) works in quantum optics (including laser physics). It is a leading institute in the world regarding fundamental researches on laser.

MASER:

  • A maser is a device using the stimulated emission of radiation by excited atoms to amplify or generate coherent monochromatic electromagnetic radiation in the microwave range.
  • MASER is an acronym for "Microwave Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation."
  • The first maser was built by Charles H. Townes, James P. Gordon, and Herbert J. Zeiger at Columbia University in 1953.
  • Masers are used as the timekeeping device in atomic clocks, and as extremely low-noise microwave amplifiers in radio telescopes and deep space spacecraft communication ground stations.
  • Modern masers can be designed to generate electromagnetic waves at not only microwave frequencies but also radio and infrared frequencies. For this reason Charles Townes suggested replacing "microwave" with the word "molecular" as the first word in the acronym maser.
  • The laser works by the same principle as the maser, but produces higher frequency coherent radiation at optical wavelengths.

Liquid Crystal:

  • A liquid crystal is a thermodynamically stable phase characterized by anisotropy of properties without the existence of a three-dimensional crystal lattice, generally lying in the temperature range between the solid and isotropic liquid phase, hence the term mesophase.
  • Liquid crystal materials are unique in their properties and uses. As research into this field continues and as new applications are developed, liquid crystals will play an important role in modern technology.
  • Liquid crystal materials generally have several common characteristics. Among these are a rod like molecular structure, rigidity of the long axis, and strong dipole and/ or easily polarizable substituents.
  • Liquid crystals find wide use in liquid crystal displays, which rely on the optical properties of certain liquid crystalline substances in the presence or absence of an electric field.
  • Liquid crystals have a multitude of other uses. They are used for nondestructive mechanical testing of materials under stress. This technique is also used for the visualization of RF (radio frequency) waves in waveguides. They are used in medical applications where, for example, transient pressure transmitted by a walking foot on the ground is measured. Low molar mass (LMM) liquid crystals have applications including erasable optical disks, full color "electronic slides" for computer-aided drawing (CAD), and light modulators for color electronic imaging.

Indian Antarctic Programme:

  • The Indian Antarctic Programme is a multi-disciplinary, multi-institutional programme under the control of the National Centre for Polar and Ocean Research (Goa), Ministry of Earth Sciences, Government of India.
  • It was initiated in 1981 with the first Indian expedition to Antarctica.
  • The programme gained global acceptance with India's signing of the Antarctic Treaty and subsequent construction of the Dakshin Gangotri Antarctic research base in 1983- 84, superseded by the Maitri base from 1989.
  • The newest base commissioned in 2012 is Bharati, constructed out of 134 shipping containers.
  • Under the Antarctic programme, atmospheric, biological, earth, chemical and medical sciences are studied by India. Indian Arctic Programme:
  • The Indian Arctic Programme is also under the control of the National Centre for Polar and Ocean Research (Goa), Ministry of Earth Sciences, Government of India.
  • India launched its first scientific expedition to the Arctic Ocean in 2007 and opened a research base named "Himadri" at the International Arctic Research Base at Ny-Alesund, Svalbard, Norway in July, 2008 for carrying out studies in disciplines like Glaciology, Atmospheric sciences & Biological sciences.
  • IndARC is India's first multi-sensor underwater moored observatory in the Arctic region. It was deployed in 2014 at Kongsfjorden fjord, Svalbard, Norway which is midway between Norway and North Pole. Its research goal is to study the Arctic climate and its influence on the monsoon.

Chapter 18

Atomic Structure

34 facts · 5 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (119 points)

Notes

Kanad (कणाद):

  • Kanad, also known as Kashyap, Uluka and Kanabhuk, was an Indian natural scientist and Philosopher, who founded the Vaishesika School of Indian Philosophy.
  • Estimated to have lived sometimes between 6th century to 2nd century BC, little is known about his life. He is known for developing the foundation of an atomistic approach of the universe.
  • He suggested that everything can be subdivided, but this subdivision can not go on forever and there must be smallest entities (Parmanu) that cannot be divided, that are eternal, that aggregate in different ways to yield complex substances and bodies with unique identity, a process that involves heat and this is the basis for all material existence. Dalton’s Atomic Theory:
  • In the beginning of 19th century, Dalton proposed that all matters are composed of atoms which are indivisible and indestructible building blocks.
  • All atoms of an element are identical.
  • Different elements have atoms of different size and mass.
  • Atoms are neither created nor could be destroyed. This implies that during chemical reactions, no atoms are created or destroyed.
  • Atoms of different elements combine in a fixed ratio to form compounds.
  • The formation of new products (compounds) results from the rearrangements of existing atoms.

Drawbacks of Dalton’s Atomic Theory –

  • It was proved that an atom is not indivisible. An atom can be subdivided into electrons, protons and neutrons. But remember that atom is the tiniest particle that takes part in a chemical reaction.

Fundamental Particles of Atom:

(i) Electron–

  • An electron is negatively charged sub-atomic particle.
  • It can be either free (not attached to any atom) or bound to the nucleus of an atom.
  • Electrons in atoms exist in spherical shells of various radii, representing energy levels.
  • The charge on an electron is (–) 1.6022 × 10–¹⁹ coulomb.
  • Its symbol is e–.
  • The electron has a mass that is approximately 1/1837 that of the proton or 9.109 × 10–³¹ kg.
  • It was discovered by J.J. Thomson (1897).
  • Atomic mass unit of the electron is 0.0005486.

(ii) Proton –

  • A proton is a positively charged sub-atomic particle.
  • Its symbol is por p⁺.
  • The charge on a proton is (+) 1.6022 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulomb.
  • Its weight is 1.6726 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.
  • Its atomic mass unit is 1.00727.
  • Eugen Goldstein observed beams of positive ions, including H⁺, as 'canal/anode rays' in 1886; the discovery of the proton as the hydrogen nucleus is generally credited to Ernest Rutherford's work around 1917, and the specific name 'proton' was proposed by Rutherford in 1920.
  • As per the new NCERT (April, 2026 Edition), proton was discovered and named by Rutherford.

Note: The number of electrons is equal to the number of protons in an atom with an equal charge of opposite nature. Hence the atom is neutral.

(iii) Neutron –

  • It is a neutral sub-atomic particle so its name is neutron.
  • It is represented by symbol nor n°.
  • Its mass is slightly larger than that of proton i.e. 1.0087 amu.
  • It was discovered by James Chadwick (1932).

Note: Atomic mass unit (amu) is defined as precisely 1/12 of the mass of an atom of Carbon-12.

Constitution of Atomic Nucleus:

  • The atomic nucleus is the small, dense region consisting of proton and neutrons at the center of an atom.
  • The proton & neutron jointly called nucleon.
  • It was discovered by Ernest Rutherford (1911) based on the Geiger - Marsden gold foil experiment (1909).
  • Protons and neutrons are bound together to form a nucleus by the nuclear force.

Atomic Number (Z):

  • The symbol of atomic number (Z) is a conventional symbol possibly came from the German word Zahl/Atomzahl which means number/atomic number.
  • Atomic number of an element is the number of protons in the nucleus of its atom.
  • It is the characteristic of a chemical element and determines its place in the periodic table.
  • The atomic number of each element is certain and constant.
  • Atoms of different elements are with different atomic number.
  • The atomic number of Hydrogen is 1, it means it has one proton in its nucleus.

Mass Number (A):

  • (A) has been derived from German word Atomgewicht which means atomic weight.
  • The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom’s nucleus is known as its mass number.
  • It is used as the nucleon count and approximates the atomic mass of a nuclide in atomic mass units.
  • Mass number of an atom = No. of protons + No. of neutrons in nucleus of an atom.
  • It represents the total number of nucleons in the nucleus of an atom.
  • The mass number is not a fundamental character of the element.
  • An element may have atoms with different mass number. Atomic Mass and Atomic Weight:
  • The atomic mass refers to a mass of a single atom. In contrast, the atomic weight refers to the weighted average mass of all atoms of an element.

For a single nuclide, the atomic mass is approximately equal to its mass number.

Atomic weight of an element is a weighted average of isotopic masses and is not, in general, equal to a single mass number A.

Isoelectronic:

  • The ions and atoms with an equal number of electrons are known as isoelectronic.
  • The electronic configuration of these ions and atoms are the same. For example –

a. Ne → 2,8

b. Na⁺ → 2,8

c. Mg²⁺ → 2,8

d. F– → 2,8

(Each ion/atom with same electronic configuration of 10 electrons)

Isotopes:

  • Isotopes are atoms of a chemical element that have the same atomic number but are with different mass number.
  • The place of isotopes is same in the periodic table as they have the same atomic number.

Isotopes of Hydrogen (three naturally occurring isotopes) –

IsotopeNo. of protons/No. ofMass
Atomic Number neutronsNumber
Protium (₁H¹)101
Deuterium (₁H²)112
Tritium (₁H³)123

Isotopes of oxygen– There are three known stable isotopes of oxygen viz. O16, O17, O18.

Isobars:

  • Isobars are atoms of different chemical elements having the same number of nucleons (mass number), but their atomic numbers are different.

Example – H³ & He³

  • The place of isobars is different in the periodic table because their atomic number differs.

Isoneutronic or Isotones:

  • Different element’s atom with the same number of neutrons are called Isoneutronic or Isotones.

Example –

a. H³ and He⁴ – Both have same number of neutrons

i.e. 2 neutrons.

b. Si³⁰, P³¹, S³² – All with the same number of neutronsi.e. 16 neutrons.
c. C¹³, N¹⁴– both have the same number of neutronsi.e. 7 neutrons.

Radioactivity:

  • Radioactivity is a nuclear phenomenon in which there is a spontaneous emission of radiations from the nuclei of atoms during their decay. In other words, radioactive decay is the process by which an unstable atomic nucleus loses energy by radiation.

Unstable nuclei that exist in nature are said to undergo natural radioactivity, and the man made unstable nuclei undergo artificial radioactivity.

  • The elements with such atoms have spontaneous disintegration character.
  • Such elements are called radioactive substances.
  • α particles, β particles and γ rays are emitted by radioactive nuclei. These three types of radiation are called ionizing radiation.
  • Radioactivity is a nuclear phenomenon, not a chemical reaction.
  • It was discovered by Henri Becquerel in Uranium.
  • In 1898 Marie Curie and her husband Pierre Curie discovered a radioactive element Polonium.
  • Radium was identified as a new element in 1898 by Marie and Pierre Curie while studying uranium ores such as Pitchblende; in 1902 they isolated radium chloride from pitchblende, a uranium oxide mineral often approximated as U O but also described as mainly UO with variable oxidation.

Chapter 19

Physical and Chemical Changes, Solution

36 facts · 3 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (97 points)

Notes

  • Matter is defined as anything that occupies space and exhibits rest mass or inertia.
  • In physical changes no new substances are formed; the substance retains the same chemical composition while only its physical properties change.

Physical changes may be reversible; some physical changes are irreversible, even though no new substance is formed.

  • In our daily life, we encounter many changes in our surroundings, though we do not notice them, such as souring of milk, rusting of iron, stretching of a rubber band, bread becoming toast, melting of wax, etc.
  • All these changes that take place around us are either a physical change or chemical change.

Physical Changes

  • Physical changes, are the changes that change the physical traits of the substance, without making any change in their internal structure.
  • In physical changes no chemical bonds are broken or formed.
  • Some examples of physical changes are:

(i) Melting of wax

(ii) Melting of ice

(iii) Freezing of water

(iv) Vaporization of water

(v) Dissolving sugar in water

(vi) Chopping of wood

(vii) Crumpling of paper

Chemical Changes

  • A chemical change is defined as the process in which the atoms of one or more substances are rearranged or combine to form a new substance.
  • When a substance undergoes a chemical change, the chemical properties of the substance change and it is transformed into a different substance with different chemical composition.
  • Energy change is one of the characteristics of a chemical change, because of the formation of a new product.
  • Once the chemical change takes place, it is usually not easily reversible, but some chemical changes can be reversed under suitable conditions.
  • Some examples of chemical changes are as follows -

(i) Adding vinegar to baking soda

(ii) Bleaching a stain

(iii) Fermenting of grapes

(iv) Burning of magnesium wire and paper

(v) Nail rusting

(vi) Souring of milk

(vii) Cooking of food

Solution

  • In chemistry, a solution is a special type of homogeneous mixture composed of two or more substances.
  • Other characteristics of the solutions are -

(i) The particles of solute in a solution cannot be seen by the naked eye.

(ii) A solution does not allow beams of light to scatter.

(iii) A solution is stable.

(iv) From a solution, the solute cannot be separated by filtration.

Solvent:

  • Solvents are substances that have the ability to dissolve other substances, known as solutes.
  • A solvent can be solid, liquid or gas.
  • The particles of the solvent work to put the solute particles apart.
  • Eventually, the particles of solute become uniformly distributed throughout the solvent.

Types of Solution:

1. Gaseous Solution:

  • If the solvent is a gas, only gases or vapours are dissolved under a given set of conditions.
  • Example of a gaseous solution is air (Oxygen and other gases dissolved in Nitrogen).

2. Liquid Solution:

  • If the solvent is a liquid, then different gases, liquids and solids can dissolve depending on the nature of solute and solvent and conditions.
  • Examples of liquid solutions are as follows-

(i) Gas in liquid – Oxygen in water.

(ii) Liquid in liquid – Alcoholic beverages are basically solutions of ethanol in water.

(iii) Solid in liquid – Sucrose in water; Sodium chloride in water.

3. Solid solutions:

  • If the solvent is a solid, then gases, liquids and solids can act as solutes in such solid solutions.

(i) Gas in Solid – Hydrogen dissolves in palladium; this is studied as a means of hydrogen storage.

(ii) Liquid in solid – Mercury in gold forming amalgam; Hexane in paraffin wax.

(iii) Solid in solid – Alloys are examples of solid in solid, e.g. bronze is a solution primarily of copper and tin; brass is a solution of copper and zinc.

Unsaturated Solution:

  • An unsaturated solution in chemistry is a solution that can accept more solute, until it becomes saturated, or in which there is a relatively small amount of solute dissolved in the solution.

Saturated solution:

  • A saturated solution is a solution that contains the maximum amount of that solute that can dissolve at a given temperature and pressure; additional solute remains undissolved.

Concentrated Solution:

  • The concentrated solution is a solution that contains a large amount of solute relative to the amount of solvent or solution present.

Dilute Solution:

  • A dilute solution is one that has a relatively small amount of dissolved solute.

Solubility:

  • Solubility is the amount of solute required to form a saturated solution in a given amount of solvent under specified conditions of temperature and pressure, which may be specified by mass or volume.
  • Solubility is expressed commonly as grams of solute per 100 g or 100 mL of solvent, or in other concentration units such as molarity, molality, mole fraction, etc.

Colloids:

  • A colloid is a mixture in which one substance consisting ofmicroscopically dispersed particles of colloidal size, is suspended throughout another substance. Colloids can be classified, among other ways, according to the physical state of dispersed phase and dispersion medium, as well as by the nature of interaction between them.

  • Movement of solvent (such as water) through a semi permeable membrane into a solution of higher solute concentration that tends to equalize the concentration of solute on the two sides of the membrane.
  • The process of osmosis continues until a state of osmotic equilibrium is reached where the chemical potentials across the membrane become equal.

Semipermeable Membrane:

  • A semipermeable membrane is any biological or synthetic polymeric membrane that allows certain molecules or ions to pass through while restricting others.
  • It generally allows the passage of solvent molecules but blocks the passage of solute molecules.
  • A semipermeable membrane has selective pathways such as pores, channels or polymer regions whose permeability depends on factors like pore size, solubility, charge and specific interactions.

Chapter 20

Inorganic Chemistry

12 facts · 1 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (82 points)

Notes

Classification of Elements

  • Periodic Table or Periodic table of elements is a tabular arrangement of the chemical elements, arranged by atomic number, electron configuration and recurring chemical properties, whose structure shows periodic trends. Need for classification of Elements:
  • Before the beginning of the 18th century, only a few elements were known, so it was quite easy to study and remember the properties of those elements and their compounds individually.
  • Later on, with the growing number of known elements, it became more and more difficult to study their properties individually, therefore the need for their systematic classification was felt.

Development of Periodic Table:

  • Several major attempts were made for classification of elements. Some of them are as follows -

(i) Prout Hypothesis (1815-16) –

  • William Prout observed that the atomic weights that had been measured for the elements known at that time appeared to be whole multiples of the atomic weight of hydrogen.
  • He hypothesized that the hydrogen atom was the only truly fundamental object, which he called protyle and that the atoms of other elements were actually groupings of various numbers of hydrogen atoms.
  • Later, more precise measurements of atomic weights showed many values were not exact integer multiples of hydrogen, so chemists rejected this simple form of the hypothesis, even though a modified ‘whole-number rule’ for isotopes remains approximately valid.

(ii) Dobereiner’s Law of Triads (1829) –

  • According to this law, when chemically analogous elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic weight, they formed well-marked group of three called ‘Triads’, in which the atomic weight of middle element was nearly equal to the arithmetic mean of the other.
  • Examples of triads of elements are as follows –

Element Atomic Weight Mean of 1 & 3 (Approx.)

1.Lithium7
2.Sodium23= 23
3.Potassium39
1.Calcium40
2.Strontium88= 88.5
3.Barium137
  • This classification did not receive wide acceptance since only a few elements could be arranged into triads.

(iii) Newlands’ Law of Octaves (1865) –

  • If the chemical elements are arranged according to increasing atomic weight, those with similar physical and chemical properties occur after each interval of seven elements.
  • Arrangement of some elements with their atomic weights (approx.) according to the Law of Octaves:
LiBeBCNOF
(7)(9)(11)(12)(14)(16)(19)
NaMgAlSiPSCl
(23) (24)(27)(28)(31)(32)(35.5)
  • Newlands was among the first to recognize a periodic pattern in elemental properties, anticipating later formulations of the periodic law.

(iv) Lothar Meyer’s Atomic Volume Curve (1870) –

  • Lothar Meyer, a German chemist plotted a graph between atomic weight and atomic volume (i.e. atomic/molar mass divided by the density of the element in the solid state), he found that elements with similar properties occupied the similar position on the graph.

(v) Mendeleev’s Law of Periodicity (1971) –

  • In 1869, Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev arranged 63 elements by increasing atomic weight in several columns, noting recurring chemical properties across them. As per the ‘law of periodicity’ given by him in 1971– “The physical and chemical properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic weight”.

Salient Features of Mendeleev’s Periodic Table:

(i) Mendeleev mainly arranged the elements in increasing order of their atomic weight but deliberately reversed some pairs, such as Co–Ni and Te–I, to keep chemically similar elements together.

(ii) The elements were arranged in horizontal rows called periods. Those were six in numbers (1 to 6 - Arabic numerals). Period 4th, 5th & 6th had two series of elements.

(iii) The vertical columns were called groups. Originally, there were eight groups numbered from I to VIII (Roman Numerals).

(iv) Groups I to VII were further divided into A & B subgroups. However, group VIII contained three elements in each of the three periods.

(v) Elements within each subgroup (A or B) are broadly similar, but subgroup A and subgroup B of the same group can have quite different physical and chemical properties, which is treated as a defect of Mendeleev’stable. They also shown a limited or imperfect gradation in many of their properties from top to bottom, with important anomalies, especially when both subgroups of a group are taken together.

(vi) Mendeleev’s original classification included all the 63 elements known at that time.

(vii) He left blank spaces for elements yet to be discovered, which were filled with the discovery of germanium, scandium and gallium.

(vi) Modern Periodic Table –

  • Keeping in view the drawbacks of Mendeleev’s periodic table such as anomalous pair – placing of heavier element before lighter one and there is no separate place/position for different isotopes of an element in the periodic table, it was felt that the arrangement of elements in the periodic table should be based on some other property which is more fundamental than atomic mass.
  • Moseley (1913) established atomic number as the fundamental basis for arranging elements, leading to the modern tabular arrangement based on increasing atomic numbers.
  • It states that the chemical and physical properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers

i.e. ifelements are arranged in the order of their increasing atomic numbers, the elements with similar properties are repeated after certain regular intervals.

(vii) Long Form of Periodic Table –

  • The most accepted modern periodic table is the long form (18-column) periodic table.
  • The arrangement of elements in this table is also in keeping with their electronic structure (configuration). Columns represent the Groups or families and rows represent the Periods.

Groups:

  • It contains 18 vertical columns. The groups have been numbered from 1 to 18 (in Arabic numerals).
  • All elements present in a group generally have similar electronic configuration in their valence shell and have the same number of valence electrons for main-group elements; transition metals are an important exception. Periods:
  • There are seven horizontal rows in the modern periodic table.
  • The elements in a period have consecutive atomic numbers.
  • The periods have been numbered from 1 to 7 (Arabic numerals).
  • In each period a new shell starts filling up. The period number is also the number of shells that starts filling up as we move from left to right across the period.

(a) The first period is the shortest period of all. It contains only two elements – Hand He.

(b) The second and third periods are called short-periods each with 8 elements.

(c) The 4th & 5th periods are called long periods each with 18 elements.

(d) The 6th & 7th periods are very long periods; both presently have 32 known elements.

Types of Elements:

1. Main Group Elements or Normal Elements –

  • Main Group elements have been placed in groups 1 and 2 on the left side and in groups 13 to 17 on the right side of the periodic table.
  • Their outermost shell is incomplete (their outermost shell has less than eight electrons).

2. Noble Gases –

  • Group 18 contains noble gases. Their outermost shell contains 8 electrons except Helium (only 2 electrons in the outermost shell).
  • These are inert gases (very unreactive gases that were historically called ‘inert’; however, heavier noble gases like xenon, krypton and radon are now known to form compounds with elements such as fluorine and oxygen, so they are not absolutely non-reactive) and with zero valency (their valency is usually taken as zero in basic chemistry because they show almost no chemical activity under ordinary conditions, even though known noble gas compounds imply non-zero oxidation states in more advanced treatments).

Note: NCERT class XI includes group 18 as well in the Main Groups.

3. The d- and f-Block Elements: –

  • The d-block of the periodic table contains the elements of the groups 3-12 in which the d orbitals are progressively filled in each of the four long periods.
  • The f-block consists of elements in which 4 f and 5 f orbitals are progressively filled. They are placed in a separate panel at the bottom of the periodic table.
  • The names transition metals and inner transition metals are often used to refer to the elements of d-and f-blocks respectively.
  • There are mainly four series of the transition metals, 3d series (Sc to Zn), 4d series (Y to Cd), 5d series (La and Hf to Hg) and 6d series which has Ac and elements from Rf to Cn.
  • According to IUPAC, transition metals are defined as metals which have incomplete d subshell either in neutral atom or in their ions.
  • Zinc, cadmium and mercury of group 12 have full d 10 configuration in their ground state as well as in their common oxidation states and hence, are not regarded as transition metals.
  • However, being the end members of the 3d, 4d and 5d transition series, respectively, their chemistry is studied along with the chemistry of the transition metals.
  • The two series of the inner transition metals; 4f(La to Lu) and 5f(Ac to Lr) are known as lanthanoids and actinoids respectively.
  • Lanthanoids, along with the chemically similar elements scandium and yttrium, are often collectively known as the 'rare earth elements'.
  • All actinoids are radioactive and release energy upon radioactive decay.
  • The element Lanthanum (57) and Actinium (89) are the eponyms of Lanthanoid and Actinoid series respectively.
  • Even though lanthanoid means like lanthanum and actinoid means like actinium and as such they should not be included in these groups but IUPAC acknowledges their inclusion based on common usage.
  • Sometimes these groups are considered to have 14 elements each (without lanthanum and actinium).

  • The Earth's crust is the major source of metals.

  • In nature, metals are found in two states:

(ii) Combined state

Ores:

Karat/Carat

  • A karat, when used with gold, is a unit of purity.
  • 24-karat gold is pure (≥ 99.9%) gold.
  • Usually to make jewellery some metals like copper or silver is mixed with it, because pure gold is too soft.
  • 18-karat gold is 75% gold and 25% other metals, and so on.
  • 1 gram of 12-karat gold contains 50% or 0.5 grams of pure gold.
  • Each karat indicates 1/24th of the whole.
  • While 'karat' is commonly used in the USA to describe gold purity, 'carat' is also used in some regions (like, the UK, Australia and India) to describe gold purity.
  • The standard unit of weight for gemstones, including diamonds, is the carat.
  • One carat is defined as exactly 200 milligrams or 0.2 grams.

Non-Metals · Carbon and its Various Forms

28 facts · 7 Must know

Key facts from the book (52 points)

Notes

  • The general properties of non-metals are –

(i) High ionization energies.

(ii) High electronegativities.

(iii) Poor thermal conductors (Graphite is an exception).

(iv) Poor electrical conductors (Graphite is an exception).

(v) Brittle solids-not malleable or ductile.

(vi) Little or no metallic luster (Iodine is an exception)..

(vii) Generally gain electrons easily (except the noble gases).

(viii)Generally dull, although they may be colourful.

(ix) These are generally gases as – Hydrogen, Oxygen, Fluorine, Chlorine, Argon, Krypton, etc.; solids as - Carbon, Phosphorus, Sulfur, Selenium, Iodine, etc.; and liquid – Bromine (only).

Oxocarbon:

  • An oxocarbon is an inorganic compound, consisting wholly of carbon and oxygen.
  • The simplest and most common oxocarbons are carbon monoxide (CO) and carbon dioxide (CO₂).

Carbon has three main allotropes:

(i) Graphite

(ii) Diamond

(iii) Buckminsterfullerene

  • Graphene, Q-carbon, amorphous carbon etc. are some other allotropes of carbon.

Graphite:

  • Graphite word derived from the Greek verb 'graphain' (to write/left a mark). Modern pencil 'lead' is commonly graphite mixed with clay. The mineral was so much like the lead ores found at that time that the residents called it plumbago – which is Latin for lead ore.
  • It is a crystalline form of the element carbon with its atoms arranged in a hexagonal structure.
  • It occurs naturally in this form and is the most stable form of carbon under standard conditions.
  • Under very high pressure and temperature, it converts into a diamond.
  • It is soft and used to prepare lead pencils.
  • This is useful in applications where wet lubricants, such as oil can not be used. So it is called dry lubricant.
  • It is a good conductor of electricity.

Diamond:

  • Diamond is a solid form of carbon with its atoms arranged in a crystal structure called diamond cubic.
  • Diamonds are used as an abrasive because it is very hard. Small particles of diamonds are embedded in saw blades, drill bits and grinding wheels for the purpose of cutting, drilling or grinding hard materials.
  • It has a high index of refraction and high luster. Due to these properties, diamond is a highly valued and widely used gemstone; its value varies and depends on grading/ value factors such as cut, color, clarity and carat weight.
  • Its thermal conductivity is highest with respect to other natural materials.
  • It is used to inscribe words on glass.
  • Hydrofluoric acid (HF) is also used to inscribe words or for etching on the glass. Glass forms silicon fluorides with HF, hence HF is not kept in glass containers.

Note: A carat is a unit of mass equals to 200 mg (0.2 gram) which is used to weigh the diamond.

Buckminsterfullerene:

  • It is a type of fullerene with the formula C₆₀.
  • It has a cage-like fused-ring structure that resembles a soccer ball, made of 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons, with a carbon atom at each vertex of each polygon, and a bond along each polygon edge.
  • It has shown potential for drug-delivery applications. They can carry drug molecules through surface modification/ conjugation. Drug molecules are often conjugated to modified fullerene systems in reported delivery designs. Its free-radical scavenging/antioxidant activity is also under research.
  • It is also used as a lubricant and catalyst.
  • The tube fullerene is called nanotube.

Solid carbon dioxide:

  • Solid (frozen) carbon dioxide is known as dry ice, because it looks like ice and it sublimes straight from solid to gas, without changing in liquid. Dry ice sublimes at –78.5°C (–109.3°F) at earth atmospheric pressure.
  • It is useful for preserving frozen foods where mechanical cooling is unavailable.
  • It does not leave any residue.

Types of Coal:

  • On the basis of the presence of carbon percentage, different varieties of coal mineral have been divided into 4 main types–

(i) Lignite – 25-35% carbon

(ii) Sub Bituminous – 35-45%

(iii) Bituminous – 45-86% carbon

(iv) Anthracite – 86-97% carbon

18 facts · 5 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (51 points)

Notes

  • Hydrogen is a chemical element with symbol H, atomic number 1 and its electronic configuration is 1s¹.
  • It is the lightest element in the periodic table with a standard atomic weight of approx. 1.008.
  • It occupies a unique position in the periodic table.
  • In its properties, it behaves like alkali metals (Li, Na, K etc.) as well as halogens (F, Cl, Br etc.).

Isotopes of Hydrogen:

  • There are three naturally occuring isotopes of hydrogen –

(i) Protium - H¹ (A = 1) Without any neutron – stable form

(ii) Deuterium - H² (A = 2) With one neutron – stable form

(iii) Tritium - H³ (A = 3) With two neutrons – it is unstable and therefore it is radioactive. Like all radioactive isotopes tritium decays. As it decays it gives off or emits beta radiation.

  • Deuterium was discovered (1931) by American chemist Harold C. Urey (for which he was awarded the Nobel Prize for Chemistry in 1934) and his associates F. Brickwedde and G. Murphy.
  • In nature, tritium is found in very less amount. It is prepared in atomic reactors by artificial techniques.
  • The existence of tritium was established by Bleakney and Gould in 1934 during mass spectrograph analysis of heavy water. Tritium was first detected in 1934 by Ernest Rutherford, M.L. Oliphant and Paul Harteck – when they bombarded deuterium with high energy deuterons (nuclei of deuterium atoms).

Properties of Deuterium:

  • It is an isotope of hydrogen.
  • It is colourless, odourless and tasteless gas.
  • It is slightly soluble in water.
  • Its molecule is diatomic.
  • Deuterium is now prepared largely by the electrolysis of heavy water.

Heavy water (D₂O):

  • It is the oxide of deuterium.
  • It was discovered by Harold C. Urey in 1932, while G.N. Lewis and R.T. MacDonald were able to isolate the first sample of practically pure heavy water (D₂O) in 1933.
  • It is a valuable substance. Its uses are as follows–

(i) As neutron moderator – The substance which moderates the fast moving neutrons in atomic reactors is termed as moderator. Heavy water is used as a neutron moderator in atomic reactors. It is also used as a coolant in reactors.

(ii) It is used to prepare deuterium and deuterium compounds. Effect of Heavy Water on livings –

(i) Intake of high concentration of heavy water can be toxic. It reacts more slowly than ordinary water, as a result the physiological reactions of the body become abnormal.

(ii) It inhibits the growth of plants.

(iii) Seed germination inhibited in the presence of high D₂O. Manufacturing of Heavy water in India –

  • The first heavy water plant was set up in India at Nangal (Punjab) in 1962, which was later closed down. Other heavy water plants were established at Baroda (Gujarat), Tuticorin (Tamil Nadu), Kota (Rajasthan), Hazira (Gujarat), Manuguru (Telangana), Thal (Maharashtra) and Talcher (Odisha). Among them, production of heavy water at Baroda and Talcher was suspended later.

Soft and Hard Water:

Soft water –

  • Soft water is characterised by very low concentrations of calcium and magnesium ions (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺); it may be naturally soft or softened by treatment (often increasing sodium ions – Na⁺).
  • It gives froth easily with soap.

Hard water:

  • The water that contains an appreciable quantity of dissolved salts/ minerals (bicarbonates, chlorides, sulfates, etc.) of calcium and magnesium.
  • The hardness of water depends on the concentration of dissolved calcium and magnesium ions.
  • Soap is a salt/mixture of salts of long-chain fatty acids (often sodium/potassium salts).
  • Hard water does not give froth easily with soap.
  • Rainwater is naturally soft. When it goes underneath the ground, it picks up minerals like chalk, limestone and mainly calcium and magnesium salts.

Hydrogen Peroxide:

  • It is a chemical compound with chemical formula H₂O₂.
  • It was discovered by Louis Jacques Thenard in 1818. Properties of Hydrogen Peroxide –
  • It is pale blue-liquid which appears colourless in a dilute solution, slightly more viscous than water.
  • It is soluble in water, alcohol and ether. It is a weak acid.
  • Its relative density is about 1.45 (at 20°C).
  • Its boiling point is 150.2°C and freezing point is – 0.43°C. Uses of Hydrogen Peroxide –
  • Hydrogen peroxide is a natural antiseptic and germicide, therefore one of its most common uses is to clean wounds to prevent infection.
  • It is used for bleaching silk, wool, hair and ivory.
  • It is used to decrease free SO₂ in juice and wine.
  • It is used as fuel or used as an oxidizer, with other fuels.
