Chapter 25

Non-Metals · Sulfur, Nitrogen, Halogen, Inert Gases

28 facts · 5 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (68 points)

Notes

Sulfur (S):

  • It is a nonmetallic, abundant and multivalent element. Elemental Sulfur at room temperature is a bright yellow, crystalline solid.
  • The elemental Sulfur is used in matches, insecticides and fungicides.
  • The main commercial use of Sulfur is the production of Sulfuric acid for sulfate and phosphate fertilizers.
  • It is one of the core elements needed for biochemical functioning and is an elemental macronutrient for all living organisms.
  • It is also called 'brimstone' (burning stone).

Sulfur dioxide (SO₂):

  • It is a toxic colourless gas with a characteristic, irritating, pungent odour.
  • It is released naturally by volcanic activities and is produced as a by-product of the burning of fossil fuels contaminated with Sulfur compounds.
  • It is used as a precursor to sulfuric acid, a preservative for dried fruits, in winemaking, etc. and earlier also as a refrigerant.
  • SO₂ is used as a reducing agent. In the presence of water, it is able to decolorize substances. It can also used as an oxidizing agent.
  • It is a major air pollutant and has significant impacts on human health.

Sulfur Hexafluoride (SF₆):

  • It is an inorganic, colourless, odourless, non-flammable, extremely potent greenhouse gas and an excellent electrical insulator.
  • It has an octahedral geometry, consisting of six fluorine atoms attached to a central Sulfur atom. It is a hypervalent compound.
  • It is used as a gaseous dielectric medium in the electric industry. Its other usages include as inert gas for the casting of magnesium and as an inert filling for insulated glazing windows.

Nitrogen (N):

  • Nitrogen gas (N₂) forms about 78% of the Earth's atmosphere.
  • It is a naturally occurring element that is essential for growth and reproduction in both plants and animals. It is found in amino acids that make up proteins, in nucleic acids that comprise the heredity material and life blueprint for all cells and in many organic and inorganic compounds.
  • Aircrafts tyres are filled with nitrogen because nitrogen gas is mostly inert, meaning that it requires more energy to react with other substances.
  • In relation to this, another reason is that nitrogen is less likely to diffuse through the rubber than oxygen, maintaining tyre pressure stable over the long term.
  • Insectivorous plants have adapted to grow in places where the soil is poor in nutrients especially nitrogen such as acidic bogs. These plants get nitrogen from insects.
  • Approximately 860 species (as of January, 2020) of insectivorous plants have been discovered globally. In India, such plants are found in Darjiling, Nainital, Kashmir, etc.

Nitrous Oxide (N₂O):

  • It is commonly known as laughing gas.
  • Its formula is N₂O.
  • At room temperature, it is colourless, non-flammable gas, with a slightly sweet odour and taste and soluble in water.
  • On the increasing temperature, it is a powerful oxidiser similar to molecular oxygen.
  • It is used in surgery and dentistry, for its anaesthetic and pain-reducing effects.

Ammonia (NH₃):

  • It is a compound of nitrogen and hydrogen.
  • It is a colourless gas with a specific pungent odour.
  • It is a common nitrogenous waste and it contributes significantly to the nutritional needs of organisms by serving as a precursor to food and fertilizers.
  • Ammonia mainly used as fertilizers either as its salts, solutions or anhydrously.
  • Its solution in water is used as a general-purpose cleaner for many surfaces.

Tear Gas:

  • It is also called as lacrymatory agent/riot control agent (RCA).
  • It is treated as a chemical weapon (when used as a method of warfare) that causes severe eye and respiratory pain, skin irritation, bleeding and even blindness.
  • In the eye, it stimulates the nerves of the lacrimal gland to produce tears.
  • Some main tear gases are Alphachloroacetophenone, 2-Chlorobenzalmalononitrile etc.
  • Chlorine can be reagent in synthesis of tear gas.

Halogens:

  • These are a group of elements in the periodic table.
  • These have been kept in Group 17 of the periodic table.
  • Its naturally occuring members are fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine and astatine.
  • The artificially created element tennessine (Ts) with atomic number 117 is also belongs to Group 17.
  • Fluorine and chlorine, are gases. Iodine is a grey/black, shiny, crystalline solid at standard conditions that sublimes to a purple/violet vapour on heating. Bromine is liquid at normal temperature and pressure. Astatine is a radioactive element.
  • Halogens are the most reactive non-metallic elements.
  • Fluorine is the most reactive element among halogens.
  • Bromine compounds (bromides) are used in some analgesic/antipyretic formulations and in treatment of epilepsy.

Inert Gases (Noble Gases):

  • An inert gas or noble gas is a gas that has extremely low reactivity with other substances. These gases generally do not undergo chemical reactions under certain given conditions.
  • The noble gases are – helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon and may be newly found element with atomic number 118–oganesson (Og; predicted solid at 20°C).
  • These are kept in Group 18 of the periodic table.
  • Their outer shell of valence electrons is considered to be full, giving them little tendency to participate in chemical reactions.
  • Helium is used in breathing gas by deep-sea divers to address nitrogen's narcotic effect.
  • Argon is used in incandescent lamps to prevent the hot tungsten filament from oxidizing.

Xenon (Xe):

  • It is a chemical element of Group 17.
  • It is a noble gas with atomic number 54.
  • It is a colourless, dense, odourless gas found in the Earth's atmosphere in trace amounts.
  • It is used in photographic flashes, in high-pressure arc lamps for motion picture projection and in high- pressure arc lamps to produce ultra-violet light. It is used in instruments for radiation detection e.g. neutron and X-ray counters and bubble chambers.
  • It is also used as a general anaesthetic and as the propellant for ion thrusters in spacecraft.
  • It was discovered by William Ramsay and Morris Travers in 1898.
  • It is heavier than air and also known as 'Stranger Gas'. Heliox:
  • It is a breathing gas composed of a mixture of helium (He) and oxygen (O₂). The main reason for this breathing mix is to reduce the proportion of nitrogen below those of air, to allow the gas mixture to be breathed safely on deep dives. A lower proportion of nitrogen is required to reduce nitrogen narcosis. Heliox generates less airway resistance than air and thereby requires less mechanical energy to ventilate the lungs.

Chapter 26

Non-Metals · Acid, Base and Salt

51 facts · 6 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (70 points)

Notes

Acid:

  • The acid name comes from Latin acidus which means sour and refers to the sharp odour and sour taste of many acids.
  • According to Arrhenius, acid is a compound that can increase the hydrogen-ion (H⁺/Hydronium-ion H₃O⁺) concentration in aqueous solution.
  • According to Bronsted - Lowry concept, acid is defined as any hydrogen containing material which can donate a proton (hydron) to other substances.

Properties of Acids:

(i) Acids in solution have a pH below 7.0 (at about 25°C).

(ii) Taste is sour.

(iii) Releases hydrogen-ion (H⁺) in water.

(iv) An acid turns blue litmus paper into red.

(v) Chemicals or substances having the property of an acid are said to be acidic.

Classification of acids:

  • Acids are divided into two main classes:

I. Strong acids: These are completely ionized in water. They are very corrosive and can cause severe skin burns. Examples are hydrochloric acid (HCl), Sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) and nitric acid (HNO₃).

II. Weak acids: These are partially ionized in water. They are mildly corrosive and normally do not affect the skin. Examples are citric acid, acetic acid, tartaric acid etc. Sources of Some Natural Acids

fruits,

in all citrus fruits

(Vitamin C)Stings of ants and Stinging
8.Formic acidNettle (a plant)

Uses of Acids:

(i) Tartaric acid, lactic acid, acetic acid and malic acid are edible acids.

(ii) Oxalic acid is used to remove the rust/iron stains on clothes.

(iii) Conc.-Nitric acid is used in the preparation of explosive substances and for seperation of silver from gold-silver alloys.

(iv) Aqua regia is a mixture of three-part of conc-hydrochloric acid and one part of conc-nitric acid (3 conc-HCl: 1 conc HNO₃). It has capacity to dissolve platinum and gold. It is also known as Royal water. It is primarily used to produce chloroauric acid for refining the highest quality of gold. It is also used in laboratories to remove trace amounts of organic compounds and trace metals from glassware.

(v) Carbonic acid is (through carbonation of water from added CO₂) present in soda and many soft drinks.

(vi) Phosphoric acid is used as acidulant in Coca-Cola.

(vii) Certain acids are used as drugs. Acetylsalicylic acid (Aspirin) is used as a pain-killer and for bringing down fever.

Role of Acids in Human Body:

  • Acids play important roles in the human body.

(i) The hydrochloric acid present in the stomach helps in the digestion.

(ii) Amino acids are the structural unit of protein. For the synthesis of protein, amino acids are required. Protein is very essential for the growth and repair of body cells.

(iii) Fatty acids are also required for growth and repair of body tissue.

(iv) Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) are essential for all known forms of life. Genes/DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) are responsible for transmitting of traits to offsprings from parents; RNA (ribonucleic acid) is involved in protein synthesis.

(v) The carbonic acid/bicarbonate (H₂CO₃/ HCO3⁻) buffer system is essential for the maintenance of pH equilibrium in the body.

Base:

  • According to Arrhenius, a base is a compound that increases the concentration of hydroxide ions (OH–) in aqueous solution.
  • According to Bronsted-Lowry concept, base is any substance that can accept a proton (hydron) from an acid/ proton donor.

Properties of Bases:

(i) Bases have a bitter taste.

(ii) Bases feel slippery.

(iii) Bases conduct electricity in aqueous solution, because they consist of charged particles in solution.

(iv) A water-soluble base is called an alkali ifit produces OH– ions in water.

(v) Bases in solution have a pH above 7.0 (at about 25°C).

(vi) An alkali turns red litmus into blue.

Some bases and their uses are as follows:

(a) Calcium hydroxide Ca(OH)₂–Slaked Lime (Limewater is saturated aqueous solution of this)

(b) Ammonium hydroxide NH₄OH (Aqueous ammonia)–to clean glass windows.

(c) Sodium hydroxide NaOH–used to prepare soap.

(d) Potassium hydroxide KOH – used to prepare soap.

(e) Magnesium hydroxide Mg(OH)₂ – Its aqueous suspension is known as milk of magnesia, a common antacid. It is used to remove the acidity of the stomach and also as a laxative.

pH Scale:

  • In chemistry, pH is a logarithmic scale used to specify the acidic or basic/alkaline nature of an aqueous solution. It approximates the negative of the base 10 logarithm of the molar concentration, measured in units of moles per litre, of hydrogen ions in a solution, meaning each whole pH unit change represents a 10-fold change in acidity/basicity.
  • A pH value is a number generally from 0 to 14 with 7 as the middle (neutral) point (temperature-dependent). Values below 7 indicate acidic nature which increases as the number decreases while values above 7 indicate alkaline/ basic nature which increases as the number increases.
  • As per the NCERT, pin pH is 'potenz' (power) in German.
  • Pure water is neutral. Its pH value is 7 (at about 25°C). Chemical Indicator:
  • Any substance that gives a visible sign, usually by a colour change, of the presence or absence of any substance such as an acid or an alkali in a solution.
  • Turmeric, litmus and shoe flowers (Gurhal) petals are natural chemical indicators.

Natural Indicator - Litmus (a natural dye):

  • Litmus is a water-soluble mixture of different dyes extracted from lichens. It is often absorbed onto filter paper to produce one of the oldest forms of pH indicator, used to test materials for acidity and basicity.
  • It is available in the form of red and blue litmus paper.
  • Acids turn blue litmus into red while alkali solutions turn red litmus into blue.
  • Shoe flower turns the acidic solution into magenta while the basic solution is turned into green.

Chapter 27

Organic Chemistry · Hydrocarbons

17 facts · 4 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (83 points)

Notes

  • In organic chemistry, a hydrocarbon is an organic compound consisting entirely of hydrogen and carbon.
  • Hydrocarbons from which one hydrogen atom has been removed are univalent substituent groups called hydrocarbyls, e.g. Methyl, phenyl etc.
  • In hydrocarbons the carbon atoms join together to form the framework of the compound and the hydrogen atoms attach to them in many different configurations.
  • Hydrocarbons are the principal constituents of petroleum and natural gas.
  • Hydrocarbons serve as fuels and lubricants as well as raw materials for the production of plastics, fibres, rubbers, solvents, explosives and industrial chemicals.
  • Many hydrocarbons occur in nature. In addition to making up fossil fuels, they are present in trees and plants. For example in the form of pigments called carotene (C₄₀H(x) e.g. β-carotene C₄₀H₅₆) that occur in carrots and green leaves.
  • Compressed natural gas (CNG) is natural gas that is compressed; ‘liquefied’ petroleum gas (LPG) is derived from crude oil refining or natural gas processing; many domestic and automobile fuels are refined from crude oil.
  • Besides above substances, diesel, kerosene, lubricants, paraffin waxes are also obtained by the fractional distillation of petroleum.

Classification of Hydrocarbons:

  • On the basis of structure, hydrocarbons can be broadly classified into two classes:
I.Open chain hydrocarbons
II.Cyclic or closed chain hydrocarbons

Hydrocarbons

Open-chain hydrocarbonsClosed-chain hydrocarbons
SaturatedUnsaturatedHomocyclic/Carbocylic

(Alkanes)

Alkenes Alkynes Aromatic Alicyclic Open-chain Hydrocarbons:

  • The hydrocarbons, which contain carbon atoms linked on the non-cyclic (acyclic) open-chain are known as open chain hydrocarbons. In these hydrocarbons, the chain of carbon atoms is not cyclic.
  • Open-chain hydrocarbons are further divided into

(i) Saturated hydrocarbons

(ii) Unsaturated hydrocarbons

(i) Saturated hydrocarbons (Alkanes):

  • Those hydrocarbons, in which the carbon atoms are bonded to each other with a single covalent bond (–C–C–) are called a cyclic saturated hydrocarbons. They are also known as alkanes.
  • They follow the general formula C(n)H₂(n)₊₂ (–ane suffix). For example-methane, ethane, propane, etc.
  • They are also known as paraffin because these are less reactive in normal conditions with acids and other reagents (Parum = too little, Affinis = related → little affinity). Methane (CH₄):
  • Methane is the first member of open chain saturated hydrocarbons.
  • Methane is the primary constituent of natural gas and it is released into the atmosphere from crude oil production and some industrial activities. More of it is released from biological processes. Methane is produced primarily by methanogenic archaea (methanogens) under anaerobic conditions; in termites and ruminants (like cows), methane is produced by gut/rumen methanogens.
  • It is also known as Marsh gas due to its production in the wetland by decomposition of organic materials by anaerobic archaea (methanogens).

Some Alkanes and their Molecular Formula

Molecular FormulaName
CH₄Methane
C₂H₆Ethane

C₄H₁₀Butane

Properties of Alkanes:

  • These are non-polar.
  • Weak van der Waals force exists between molecules.
  • Due to weak forces, the first four members (from C₁ to C₄) are gases, members from C₅ to C₁₇ are liquids and members C₁₈ and onwards are solids at 298.15K (25ºC).
  • Alkanes are chemically inert to most laboratory reagents (like acids, bases etc.) under ordinary conditions, but react with oxygen (combustion) and halogens under appropriate conditions.

(ii) Unsaturated Hydrocarbons:

  • Acyclic hydrocarbons, in which the carbon atoms are bonded to each other with two (= C = C =) or three (– C ≡ C –) covalent bonds and have a tendency to gain more hydrogen atoms are known as unsaturated hydrocarbons. They are of two types – (a) Alkenes, (b) Alkynes.

(a) Alkenes:

  • Acyclic hydrocarbons containing a double bond between carbon atoms are known as alkenes.
  • They have the general formula C(n)H₂(n) (–ene suffix).
  • Alkenes are included within the class olefins.

Name and Molecular Formula of Some Alkenes

Molecular FormulaName
C₂H₄Ethylene (ethene)
C₃H₆Propylene (propene)

Ethylene (C₂H₄):

  • It is prepared by heating ethyl alcohol at 170°C in presence of conc-Sulfuric acid.
  • Sulfuric acid acts as a dehydrating agent in this reaction.
C H OHH²SO⁴ (C°nc.)C H + H O
2 5170°C2 42
  • Ethylene is colourless, sweet smell and less soluble gas in water; high concentration can cause unconsciousness.
  • Its molecular weight/molar mass is 28.
  • Its density is 1.25 gm/litre at S.T.P. (0°C, 1 atm).
  • Its boiling point is –103.7°C at 1 atm.

Uses of Ethylene –

  • Some plants produce ethylene which helps in the ripening of fruits (as a natural plant hormone).
  • It is used on a commercial basis for ripening of fruits.
  • It was historically used as an anaesthetic.
  • It is widely used to manufacture polythene.
  • It is used in the preparation of mustard gas.
  • Mustard gas is a warfare agent known as the Sulfur mustard (HD), which can form blisters on exposed skin and in the lungs.

(b) Alkynes:

  • Acyclic hydrocarbons containing a triple bond between carbon atoms are known as an alkyne.
  • They have the general formula C(n)H₂(n–)₂.
  • Its first member is acetylene or ethyne (C₂H₂).

Acetylene (C₂H₂):

  • When calcium carbide reacts with water, acetylene is formed.
  • It is colourless gas with a faint, ethereal odour and less soluble in water.
  • It sublimes under typical atmospheric conditions. Its boiling point is –84°C.
  • Impure acetylene has smelt like garlic.
  • It is lighter than air.
  • Free acetylene at elevated pressure is unstable and explosive; acetylene is shipped dissolved in acetone.
  • Its mixture with oxygen on ignition may be explosive. Uses of Acetylene –
  • When carbide comes in contact with moisture, it produces acetylene gas. Acetylene acts like ethylene and accelerates the ripening process, but it is inadvisable because calcium carbide has harmful traces of arsenic/phosphorous. The use of this chemical for ripening fruits is illegal in India.
  • Carbide lamps or acetylene gas lamps are simple lamps that produce and burn acetylene which is created by the reaction of calcium carbide. This lamp is used in mines.
  • Oxyacetylene flame is used for welding and cutting of metals.

Cyclic or closed-chain compounds:

  • Those organic compounds, which contain a ring of atoms are known as cyclic ring compounds.
  • They are further classified into homocyclic and hetero cyclic compounds.

(i) Homocyclic hydrocarbons:

  • If the cyclic organic compounds have ring of only carbon atoms, and contain only C and H, they are known as homocyclic/carbocylic hydrocarbons.
  • These are divided into–

(a) Aromatic hydrocarbon: Aromatic hydrocarbons are defined as those cyclic hydrocarbons which have alternate C – C and C = C bond and are similar to the benzene ring in structure. For examples – benzene, naphthalene etc.

(b) Alicyclic hydrocarbons: Those cyclic hydrocarbons which have no alternate C – C and C = C bond and similar properties to aliphatic compounds are known as alicyclic compounds. For example – cyclohexane, cyclopentane etc.

(ii) Heterocyclic compounds:

  • Those cyclic organic compounds (not categorized as hydrocarbons), which have ring of carbon atoms as well as other elements like N, O, S etc. are known as heterocyclic compounds. For example– Furan and Pyridine.

Chapter 28

Organic Chemistry · Alcohol

8 facts · 0 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (57 points)

Notes

  • Alcohol is an organic compound with a hydroxyl (–OH) functional group attached to a saturated carbon atom. Because –OH is the functional group of all alcohols, we often represent alcohols by the general formula R-OH where R is an alkyl group.
  • In other words, the hydroxyl derivatives of alkenes/ aliphatic hydrocarbons are termed as alcohols.
  • Condensed/structural formula and name of some alcohols are as follows:
(i)Methyl Alcohol (Methanol) – CH₃OH
(ii) Ethyl Alcohol (Ethanol)– C₂H₅OH
(iii) n-Propyl Alcohol– CH₃CH₂CH₂OH
(iv) Isopropyl Alcohol– (CH₃)₂CHOH
(v) n-Butyl Alcohol– CH₃ (CH₂)₂CH₂OH
(vi) Isobutyl Alcohol– (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH

Methyl Alcohol (Methanol or Carbinol):

  • Its chemical formula is CH₃OH.
  • It acquired the name wood alcohol or wood naphtha because it was once produced primarily by the destructive distillation of wood.
  • Today it is mainly produced by hydrogenation of carbon monoxide.
  • It is the simplest alcohol, consisting of a methyl group linked to a hydroxyl group.
  • It is light, volatile, colourless, flammable liquid with a distinctive odour similar to that of ethanol (Ethyl alcohol).
  • At room temperature, it is a polar liquid.
  • Its boiling point is 64.7°C (148.5°F) and it solidifies at about –98°C (–144°F).
  • It forms explosive mixtures with air and burns with a nonluminous flame. After burning in the air or in oxygen it forms carbon dioxide and water.
  • It is a very toxic substance. Methanol ingestion is an uncommon form of poisoning that can cause severe metabolic disturbances, blindness, permanent neurologic dysfunction and death.
  • It increases the acidity of the body after ingestion.
  • Due to its toxic property, it is used to denature ethyl alcohol, making it not suitable for drinking.
  • It is soluble in water and some other organic solvents.
  • A crystalline compound CaCl₂.4CH₃OH is formed by the reaction of methyl alcohol and anhydrous calcium chloride, so it can not be dried up by anhydrous calcium chloride. Uses of Methyl Alcohol:
  • It is used as a solvent for paint, celluloid, shellac, etc.
  • The mixture of petrol and methyl alcohol is used as fuel in automobiles.
  • It is used in the preparation of dyes, perfumes, medicines etc.
  • It is used in the preparation of formaldehyde, formic acid, acetic acid, methyl chloride, methyl salicylate, etc.
  • It is used in the preparation of the methylated spirit. A mixture of methyl alcohol and ethyl alcohol is known as methylated spirit or denatured alcohol, which is not suitable for drinking.
  • The mixture of methyl alcohol (40%) and water (60%) is used earlier in radiators of automobiles as antifreeze. Modern automobile engine coolants are predominantly ethylene-glycol based.

Ethyl Alcohol (Ethanol):

  • Ethyl alcohol (C₂H₅OH) is commonly called alcohol.
  • It is found in forms of ethyl esters of carboxylic acids in fruits, plants and fragrant oils.
  • It is the primary constituent of all types of wines, so it is called the spirits of wines.
  • It is generally produced by fermentation of carbohydrates by yeast, so it is also called grain alcohol.

Absolute Alcohol–

  • Absolute alcohol is specified as ≥ 99.5% (v/v) ethanol.
  • The rectified spirit (95.6% ethanol + 4.4% water) is a constant boiling point mixture (Azeotropic solution) and water cannot be removed from it by simple fractional distillation method.
  • DNA is insoluble in alcohol so scientists use absolute alcohol for precipitation of a good amount of DNA.
  • It is extremely hygroscopic, transparent, colourless, volatile liquid used as a solvent and injected into nerves and ganglia for relief of pain.

Power Alcohol -

  • Power alcohol is a mixture of petrol, ethanol and minute amount of aromatic/cosolvent compound. It is used as motor fuel.

Properties of Ethyl Alcohol:

  • It is colourless and inflammable liquid.
  • Its boiling point is about 78.2–78.5°C and melting point is about –114.1°C, which allows it to be used in antifreeze products.
  • It has a special odour (alcoholic odour).
  • Its taste is sharp.
  • It is soluble in water and many organic solvents.
  • It is a neutral compound. It does not affect the pH of water. It is neutral to acid-base indicators.
  • It forms a crystalline solid (e.g. CaCl₂.3C₂H₅OH) with anhydrous calcium chloride, so ethyl alcohol cannot be dried up by anhydrous calcium chloride.

Uses of Ethyl Alcohol:

(i) Ethanol is present in alcoholic beverages such as beer, wine, whisky, etc. So, it is also called drinking alcohol.

(ii) Ethanol is used as antiseptic/disinfectant.

(iii) Ethanol is used in cough syrups, digestive syrups and tonics.

(iv) Ethanol is being mixed with petrol and was used as motor fuel. This mixture is called power alcohol.

(v) A mixture of ethanol and water has a lower freezing point than water. This mixture is known as antifreeze and was used earlier in radiators of vehicles in cold countries and at hill stations.

(vi) Ethanol is used for the preparation of chloroform, iodoform, etc.

(vii) Ethanol is used as a sedative/hypnotic (induces sleep).

(viii)Ethanol is used in the preparation of methylated spirit.

(ix) Ethanol is used to preserve the biological specimens.

(x) Ethanol is used in spirit level and alcohol thermometer.

Chapter 29

Organic Chemistry · Polymer

28 facts · 9 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (39 points)

Notes

Polymerization:

  • In polymer chemistry, polymerization is a process of reacting monomer molecules together in a chemical reaction to form polymer chains or three dimensional networks.

Natural polymers:

1. Sporopollenin: Sporopollenin is one of the most chemically inert biological polymers. It is a major component of the tough outer (exine) walls of plant spores and pollen grains. It is chemically very stable and is usually well preserved in soils and sediments. The chemical composition of sporopollenin is not exactly known, due to its unusual chemical stability and resistance to degradation by enzymes and strong chemical reagents. However, recent studies have proposed detailed molecular structures for sporopollenin from some species, while key features such as aromatic content and cross-linking patterns are still debated.

2. Protein: Protein is the polymer of amino acids. They are large biomolecules or macromolecules, consisting of one or more long chain of amino acid residues. They are building material of organism's body and silk, wool, hair etc.

3.Starch, cellulose, glycogen are the polymers of glucose.
4.Chitin: Chitin is the polymer of N-acetylglucosamine

(an amino-sugar derivative of glucose) which contains nitrogen. It is hard, tough substance that occurs widely in nature, particularly in the exoskeleton of arthropods such as crabs, insects and spiders. The walls of hyphae (microscopic filaments of fungi) are composed of chitin.

5.Nucleic acid (DNA/RNA): Polymers of nucleotides.
6.Natural Rubber: Natural rubber is the polymer of organic

compound isoprene. Commercially, natural rubber latex is obtained almost exclusively from the rubber tree Hevea brasiliensis; other plants such as guayule and Russian dandelion are herbaceous alternative rubber crops under development.

7. Wood, cotton, silk, wool, leather, enzymes and cellulose are all examples of natural polymers.

Artificial polymers:

  • Some man-made/artificial polymers of unsaturated hydrocarbons and their derivatives are as follows:

(a) Polyethylene or Polythene:

  • Polythene is the polymer of ethylene. It is the most common plastic.
  • Polythene is thermoplastic, non-conductor of electricity. It has a high ductility and impact strength as well as low friction.
  • Polythene is water resistant.
  • Polythene is used in packaging, plastic bags, plastic films, geomembranes, containers including bottles etc.

(b) Teflon:

  • Teflon is a brand name most commonly used for poly tetrafluoroethylene (PTFE). It is a synthetic fluoropolymer of tetrafluoroethylene (C₂F₄)(n).
  • Chemically it is unreactive and heat resistant.
  • Melting point of teflon is about 327°C.
  • Teflon is used as a non-stick coating for pans and other cookware because it has very low surface energy and a very low coefficient of friction.
  • Teflon is non-reactive, partly because of the strength of carbon-fluorine bonds, and so it is often used in containers and pipe work for reactive and corrosive chemicals such as conc. nitric acid, conc. Sulfuric acid, conc. hydrochloric acid, aqua regia and strong sodium hydroxide.

(c) Polyvinyl chloride (PVC):

  • Polyvinyl chloride is a synthetic thermoplastic polymer made by polymerizing vinyl chloride.
  • Polyvinyl chloride is non-conductor of electricity, brittle in its unplasticized resin form and waterproof.
  • Rigid/unplasticized PVC is characteristically used for pipes and many moulded structural articles, while flexible PVC is used mainly for cable insulation, hoses/tubing, flooring and flexible items such as shoes and garments.
  • Some PVC formulations contains dangerous chemical additives including phthalates, lead, cadmium and/or organotins, which can be toxic to child's health. These toxic additives can leach out or evaporate into the air overtime, posing unnecessary dangers to children.

(d) Neoprene:

  • Neoprene is also called polychloroprene or pc-rubber. It is a family of synthetic rubbers that are produced by polymerization of chloroprene.
  • Neoprene exhibits good chemical stability and maintains flexibility over a wide temperature range.
  • Neoprene is used to prepare pipes, belts and other things.

(e) Polypropylene:

  • It is produced through chain-growth polymerization of the monomer propylene.
  • It is also known as polypropene. It is a thermoplastic polymer used in a wide variety of applications.
  • Its properties are similar to polyethylene, but it is still harder and more heat resistant.
  • Polypropylene is the second-most widely produced plastic (after polyethylene) and it is often used in packaging and labeling.
  • It belongs to the group of polyolefins and is partially crystalline and non-polar with a high chemical resistance.

Natural rubber → polymer of isoprene (monomer). Polymer = many small monomer molecules joined into one big molecule. Must know

Chapter 30

Organic Chemistry · Organic Acids

22 facts · 5 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (47 points)

Notes

  • A carboxylic acid is an organic compound that contains a functional carboxyl group (C(=O)OH).
  • The general formula of a carboxylic acid is R-COOH with R referring to the rest of the molecule.
  • Carboxylic acids occur widely and include the amino acids (which make up proteins) and acetic acid (which is part of vinegar).
  • Salts and esters of carboxylic acids are called carboxylates.
  • On basis of the presence of carboxyl group in acid, carboxylic acids have been divided into three main types–

1. Monocarboxylic Acid: contains one carboxyl group, example – acetic acid (CH₃COOH).

2. Dicarboxylic acid: containing two carboxyl groups, example – adipic acid (one of the monomers, along with hexamethylenediamine, used to produce nylon 6,6).

3. Tricarboxylic acid: containing three carboxyl groups, example – citric acid.

Note: Carboxylic acids with four or more –COOH groups (tetracarboxylic/other polycarboxylic acids) also exist.

  • Carboxylic acids with a long aliphatic chain, which is either saturated or unsaturated are also called fatty acids because higher members of this group as palmitic acid (C₁₅H₃₁COOH) and stearic acid (C₁₇H₃₅COOH) were firstly derived from the fats.
  • Fatty acids have usually even number of carbons, examples – docosahexaenoic acid and eicosapentaenoic acid (nutritional supplements). Odd-chain fatty acids also naturally occur.
  • Fatty acids occur in organisms, mainly in esterfied from rather than as free acids, especially in three main classes of esters – triglycerides, phospholipids and cholestreryl esters.
  • They are important dietary sources of fuel for animals and important structural components for cells.

Formic acid:

  • Formic acid (HCOOH) is simplest monocarboxylic acid. It was firstly obtained by the distillation of ants (formica = ant), so its name is formic acid.
  • Formic acid is an irritating chemical present in the sprayed venom of some ant species and in the secretion released from some stinging nettles.
  • Formic acid is dangerous, but at low concentration it is very useful.
  • Formic acid is an antibacterial substance, hence it is used as a food preservative in some countries and foods.
  • Formic acid is also used to control pest, to produce food and cosmetic additives.

Properties of Formic acid -

  • Formic acid has a strong odour and is often described as having a 'pungent' smell.
  • Formic acid is a colourless liquid.
  • Formic acid freezes at about 8.4°C and boils at about 100.8°C.
  • Formic acid is a corrosive liquid. It makes blisters on the skin.
  • Formic acid is miscible with water, alcohol & ether. Acetic Acid:
  • Acetic acid (CH₃COOH) is also called ethanoic acid.
  • Acetic acid is the most important acid among carboxylic acids.
  • A dilute (approximately 4-8% by volume) solution of acetic acid produced by fermentation and oxidation of natural carbohydrates is called vinegar.
  • Vinegar is sour due to presence of acetic acid.

Properties of acetic acid -

  • Anhydrous acetic acid is a colourless liquid with pungent smell.
  • Boiling point and melting point of acetic acid is about 117.9°C and 16.6°C respectively.
  • Acetic acid when contains a very low amount of water (less than 1%), is called anhydrous acetic acid or glacial acetic acid. The reason it is called glacial is because it solidifies into solid acetic acid crystals, at just below the room temperature (around 16-17ºC).

Chapter 31

Organic Chemistry · The Explosive Substances

10 facts · 3 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (43 points)

Notes

  • An explosive is a chemical compound/mixture/device intended to function by explosion and capable (by chemical reaction) of producing rapidly expanding gases; initiation can involve fire, friction, concussion, percussion, etc.
  • Explosives contain highly reactive chemicals that are full of potential energy, which can be released with a bang.
  • A good explosive should contains following properties–

(i) Explosive should not be volatile.

(ii) Explosive generally should not be hygroscopic.

(iii) Explosive should be stable.

  • Explosive reaction may be detonation (high explosives) or deflagration/burning (low explosives).
  • Some explosives are as follows–

Trinitrotoluene (TNT):

  • TNT is made by combining toluene with a mixture of nitric acid and sulfuric acid.
  • It is a chemical compound with the formula C₆H₂(NO₂)₃ CH₃.
  • This is a yellow solid material.
  • TNT is used in military shells, bombs and grenades. Its industrial uses include deep well and underwater blasting, chemical manufacturing as an intermediate in the production of dye-stuffs and photographic chemicals.
  • Amatol is an explosive made by mixing TNT with ammonium nitrate.

Trinitroglycerine (TNG):

  • It is a dense, colourless, oily, explosive liquid most commonly produced by nitrating glycerol with white fuming nitric acid in presence of Sulfuric acid.
  • It is also known as nitroglycerine or Nobel oil.
  • Trinitroglycerine is a high explosive itselfbut is extremely shock-sensitive and may degrade overtime to even more unstable forms.
  • Trinitroglycerine is used to make dynamite.

Trinitrophenol (TNP):

  • It is also known as picric acid with the formula (O₂N)₃ C₆H₂OH.
  • It is one of the most acidic phenols.
  • It is prepared via multi-step routes e.g., involving sulfonation of phenol followed by nitration.
  • It is used as a laboratory reagent as well as an explosive.
  • It has also been used in medicine (antiseptic, burn treatments) and dyes.
  • It is a light yellow, crystalline solid.

Dynamite:

  • It was invented by Alfred Nobel in 1867.
  • It is made by absorbing nitroglycerine in sawdust or kieselguhr (diatomaceous earth also known as D.E. or a naturally occurring soft, siliceous sedimentary rock that is easily crumbled into a fine white powder).
  • Dynamite is mainly used in the mining, quarrying (excavation), construction and demolition industries. Blasting Gelatin:
  • Blasting gelatin is a mixture of 6-8% nitrocellulose, 91- 93% of nitroglycerine and bout 1% of an acid acceptor.
  • It is used in quarries and mining as an explosive.

RDX:

  • RDX was discovered by George Friedrich Henning of Germany. It is an organic compound with the formula (O₂NNCH₂)₃.
  • Its chemical name is cyclonite or cyclotrimethylene trinitramine.
  • It is a high explosive in a pliable plastic matrix.
  • RDX is a white solid substance, widely used as explosive.
  • RDX is known as hexogen in Germany, T-4 in Italy and cyclonite in United States of America.
  • It is the primary explosive agent in C-4 plastic explosive. Gun cotton:
  • Nitrocellulose or gun cotton is a highly flammable compound formed by nitrating cellulose (cotton or wood fibres) through exposure to nitric acid in the presence of sulfuric acid.
  • It is a mild explosive (but its combustion could prove too violant). It is used in rockets, propellants, printing ink bases, leather finishing and celluloid. A mixture of nitrocellulose, camphor and alcohol was first used to manufacture denture plates.

Chapter 32

Organic Chemistry · The Fuel

46 facts · 8 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (97 points)

Notes

  • A fuel is any material that can be made to react with other substances so that it releases energy as heat energy or to be used for work. Some common fuels are wood, coal, petrol, diesel etc. Uranium and Plutonium are nuclear fuels used to produce nuclear energy.

Ideal fuel:

  • An ideal fuel is a fuel which produces adequate amount of heat and very less amount of pollutants.
  • An ideal fuel has following characteristics–

(a) It is readily available.

(b) It is less expensive.

(c) It burns easily in air at a moderate rate.

(d) It produces a large amount of heat.

(e) It can transport easily.

(f) It has high calorific value.

(g) It does not leave behind any undesirable substances. Heating value of fuel:

  • Heating value or calorific value of fuel is the amount of heat producedby a complete combustion of fuel andit is measured as a unit of energy per unit mass or volume of substance (e.g. kcal/kg, kJ/kg and Btu/m³).

Heating value of some fuels

FuelHeating value (kJ/kg)
Cow dung cake6,000 – 8,000
Wood17,000 – 22,000
Coal25,000 – 33,000
Petrol45,000
Kerosene45,000
Diesel45,000
Methane50,000
CNG50,000
LPG46,000 – 51,000
Biogas23,700 – 26,300
Hydrogen120,000 – 141,900
  • The heat energy released by reactions of fuels is converted into mechanical energy via an engine. Other times the heat itself is valued for warmth, cooking, illumination, in industrial processes etc.

Harmful effects of burning of fuel:

1. Incomplete combustion of fuels like wood, coal and petroleum products can release carbonaceous particles/ root (black carbon) in the air. These fine carbon particles are dangerous pollutants which can cause respiratory diseases.

2. Incomplete combustion of fuels produces a very poisonous gas called carbon monoxide. Excessive inhaling of carbon monoxide gas can kill a person. We should never sleep in a room with closed door and windows and having a coal fire burning inside. This is because when coal burns in an insufficient supply of air in the room, then a lot of carbon monoxide is produced and when the persons sleeping in that room breathe in poisonous carbon monoxide gas, they may all die.

3. Burning of fuels releases carbon dioxide in the environment. Increased percentage of carbon dioxide in air is causing global warming. Carbon dioxide gas in the air traps the Earth's emitted longwave/infrared heat (radiation) by producing greenhouse effect.

4. Sulfur dioxide is produced when sulfur-containing fuels are burned. It is an extremely suffocating and corrosive gas. It may damage our lungs. The burning of petrol and diesel in the engines of vehicles also releases oxides of nitrogen in the air. These oxides produced by the burning of fuels dissolve in reacts in the atmosphere with water, oxygen and other chemicals to form acids. The wet deposition such as rain/snow/fog/hail containing acid is called acid rain, which is very harmful to crops, buildings and soil.

  • The use of petrol and diesel as fuels in automobiles is being replaced by compressed natural gas (CNG) because–

(i) It produces lower emissions of pollutants than petrol/ diesel.

(ii) It burns without smoke, so it is a clean fuel.

  • Disadvantages of burning wood as fuel are as follows:

1. It produces a lot of smoke which is very harmful for human beings.

2. When trees are cut down to obtain wood for use as fuel, then many useful products/benefits and ecosystem services from standing trees are lost or reduced.

3. Deforestation is very harmful for environment.

  • LPG (Liquefied petroleum gas) is a better domestic fuel than wood due to:

1. It has higher calorific value, so it produces much more heat on burning than an equal mass of wood.

2. It burns completely without leaving behind any solid residue but wood leaves behind a lot of ash on burning. Fossil fuel:

  • Fossil fuels are a general term for buried combustible geologic deposits of organic materials, formed from decayed plants and animals that have been converted to crude oil, coal, natural gas, or heavy oils by exposure to heat and pressure in the Earth's crust over millions of years.
  • Fossil fuels are non-renewable sources of energy. As we are excessively dependent on these, alternative forms of energy need to be developed in order to deal with the imminent energy scarcity. These alternative sources of energy also need to be more eco-friendly.
  • The main fossil fuels are as follows–

(a) Coal:

  • Coal is one of the most important fossil fuels.
  • Coal is a carbon-rich sedimentary rock. In addition to carbon it contains hydrogen, Sulfur, oxygen & nitrogen.
  • Coal is usually brown or black.
  • Coal often occurs in stratified sedimentary deposits.
  • On burning in air, coal produces carbon dioxide along with other principal emissions such as sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides.
  • By processing of coal some beneficial products are obtained as coke, coal tar and coal gas.
  • There are 4 main types of coal –

1. Peat coal,

2. Lignite coal (brown coal),

3. Bituminous coal (soft coal), and

4. Anthracite coal (hard coal)

  • Peat coal has excessive quantity of moisture and impurities. It is considered as a precursor to coal.
  • Lignite is a soft, brown, combustible, sedimentary rocks formed from naturally compressed peat.
  • Bituminous coal or black coal is a relatively soft coal containing a tar like substance bitumen or asphalt.
  • It is of higher quality than lignite coal, but ofpoorer quality than anthracite.
  • It is formed under high heat and pressure during coalification.
  • Anthracite coal often referred to as hard coal, is a hard, compact variety of coal that has a submetallic lustre.
  • It has the highest carbon content, the fewest impurities.
  • It is the highest ranking of coals.
  • It is with low Sulfur content, that makes it a good burning fuel.

(b) Coke:

  • Coke is a fuel with few impurities and a high carbon content.
  • It is a solid, hard, porous and grey material derived from destructive distillation of low ash, low Sulfur bituminous coal in the absence of oxygen.
  • It is used in industrial manufacturing of steel and in extraction of several metals.

(c) Coal tar:

  • Coal tar is a thick dark liquid with bad smell.
  • It is a by-product of the production of coke and coal gas from coal.
  • It has both medical and industrial uses.

1. Medical uses of coal tar:

  • It may be applied to the affected area to treat psoriasis and seborrheic dermatitis.

2. Industrial uses of coal tar:

  • It is used in preparation of synthetic colors, explosive substances, plastics, photographic material and road manufacturing materials etc.

(d) Coal gas:

  • Coal gas is a flammable gaseous fuel made from coal.
  • It is produced when coal is heated strongly in the absence of air.
  • The main components of coal gas are hydrogen, methane and carbon monoxide.
  • It is used as fuel in different industries established near to the coal process plants.

(e) Petroleum:

  • Petroleum is a complex mixture of hydrocarbons that occurs on Earth in liquid, gaseous, or solid form; the liquid form is commonly called crude oil.
  • It is also known as black gold.
  • It also contains Sulfur, oxygen and nitrogen in small quantity.
  • It is also known as conventional oil.
  • The word petroleum comes from the Latin petra meaning rock and oleum meaning oil.
  • It can be separated (through distillation) into fractions including natural gas, gasoline, naphtha, kerosene, diesel fuel heating oil, bitumen, lubricating oils, paraffin wax and asphalt.
  • Petrochemicals are chemical products derived from petroleum and natural gas as acetylene, benzene, ethane etc., from which other chemicals, pesticides, plastics, synthetic fibres, paint and medicines are derived.

(f) Natural Gas:

  • Natural gas is a fossil fuel.
  • Like other fossil fuels such as coal and oil, natural gas formed from the buried plants, animals and micro organisms that lived millions of years ago.
  • Natural gas is a mixture of gaseous hydrocarbons as methane, ethane, propane and butane and other gases like nitrogen, carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulphide.
  • Natural gas is found in deep underground rocks formations or associated with other hydrocarbon reservoirs.
  • Helium is also found in natural gas of some area.
  • The percentage of methane in natural gas is highest i.e. about 70-90%.
  • Natural gas used as a source of energy for heating, cooking, and electricity generation. It is also used as fuel for vehicles and as a chemical feed stock in the manufacturing of plastics and other commercially important organic chemicals.

(g) Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG):

  • LPG is made during natural gas processing and oil refining.
  • Propane and butane are separated from the natural gas and liquefied at high pressure and stored in cylinders or tanks.
  • It is used as fuel in houses and hotels.
  • LPG gas is odourless. To detect its leakage, ethyl mercaptan (a clear liquid with a distinct odour) is mixed. (h) Compressed Natural Gas (CNG):
  • In CNG mainly methane is stored at high pressure.
  • It is a fuel which can be used in place of gasoline, diesel fuel and LPG.
  • CNG combustion produces fewer undesirable gases than the fuels mentioned above. So it is clean-burning and eco friendly fuel than gasoline/diesel for many pollutants in many uses.

Chapter 33

Food Preservation, Nutrition, Medicine, etc.

31 facts · 5 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (60 points)

Notes

Food Preservation:

  • Food preservation may be defined as the process of treating and handling food in such a way as to stop, control or greatly slow down spoilage and, of course, to minimize the possibility offoodborne illness, while maintaining the optimum nutritional value, texture and flavour.

Principles of Food Preservation:

  • The principles of food preservation are as follows–

1. Control/inhibit microbial growth: This is done by removing air, water (moisture), lowering or increasing temperature, increasing the concentration of salts, sugar or acids in food. For the preservation of green leafy vegetables, the water should be removed from the leaves so that the microorganisms cannot grow/thrive.

2. Inactivating enzymes: Enzymes found in food can be inactivated by changing its conditions such as temperature and moisture. One of the methods of blanching peas (as a pre-freezing step) is to put them for a few minutes in boiling water. This method inactivates enzymes.

Methods of Food Preservation:

  • Pasteurization: Pasteurization of milk requires temperatures of about 63°C (145°F) maintained for 30 minutes or alternatively heating to a higher temperature i.e. 72°C (162°F) for 15 seconds. This method kills harmful bacteria.
  • Freeze: The colder a food is, the slower is its rate of deterioration. In cold storage refrigerated air is used for food preservation.
  • Use of strong concentrations: Use of strong concentration of salts, inhibit the growth of bacteria.
  • Canning: Canning is most widespread and effective means of long term food storage. In canning food is cooked under pressure to attain a temperature high (around 100- 121°C) to destroy endospores.
  • Organic acids: Organic acids used to preserve food include benzoic acid, sorbic acid and propionic acid. These acids are added as salts such as sodium benzoate, potassium sorbate, sodium propionate. These acids are used primarily to inhibit yeasts/moulds and/or mold. Some other organic compounds as cinnamon and cloves contain the benzene derivative eugenol, a potent anti-microbial agent.
  • Drying method: Food drying is a method of food preservation in which food is dried (dehydrated or desiccated). It inhibits the growth of bacteria, yeasts and mold (fungi) through the removal of water.
  • Most fruits & vegetables age less rapidly when the level of oxygen in the atmosphere surrounding them is reduced. This is because the reduced oxygen slows down the respiration and metabolic rate of the product and, therefore, slows down the natural aging process.

Food Preservatives:

  • Food preservatives / additives are chemical substances used to prolong shelf-life by protecting against deterioration caused by microorganisms; and in some regulations also by controlling oxidation.
  • Some common food preservatives are as follows:

(i) Sodium meta bisulphite (Na₂S₂O₅) – It is used in preservation of jams, sauce and pickles.

(ii) Sodium benzoate (C₇H₅NaO₂) – It is widely used food preservative. It is used to preserve soft drinks and acidic foods.

(iii) Sorbic acid (C₆H₈O₂) and its salts – Sorbic acid or (E, E)–2,4-hexadienoic acid, is a naturally occuring organic compound (usually produced synthetically) used as a preservative. It is a white powder or crystals that is slightly soluble in water and sublimes readily. Its sodium and potassium salts are used as preservative to inhibit primarily the growth of yeasts and molds (and some bacteria) in cheese, cooked foodstuffs, pickles and food products of flesh and fish.

(iv) Epoxides - Epoxide of ethylene (ethylene oxide– C₂H₄O) and epoxide of propylene (propylene oxide– CH₃CHCH₂O) are used as post-harvest fumigants/sterliants to preserve food stuffs with little amount of water as dry fruits and spices. Drugs:

  • Drugs are natural or synthetic substances, when taken into a living body, affects its functioning or structure, and are used in the diagnosis, mitigation, treatment or prevention of a disease or relief of discomfort.
  • The term ‘drug’ can include medical as well as non medical/illegal substances.
  • In medical science drugs have been classified on the basis of their functions, which are as follows–

1. Antipyretics:

  • Antipyretics are substances that reduce fever. Examples:

Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid), paracetamol, etc.

2. Analgesics:

  • The term Analgesics encompasses a class of drugs that are designed to relieve pain without causing the loss of consciousness. It has been divided into two groups –

(a) Non-narcotic analgesics: Aspirin (2- acetoxybenzoic acid) and Paracetamol (4- acetamidophenol).

(b) Narcotic analgesics: Drugs which are administered in small quantity to relieve pain and promoting sleepiness/ sedation, are called narcotic analgesics.

  • Excessive doses may cause loss of consciousness and slowed breathing and can lead to overdose deaths.
  • Examples ofnarcotics analgesics are opium products such as morphine, heroin and codeine. These are also called opioids/opiates because these are derived from opium. These are habit forming substances.

3. Antiseptic:

  • Antiseptics are antimicrobial substances that are applied to living tissue/skin to reduce the possibility of infection, sepsis or putrefaction (the process of decay or rotting in body).
  • Antiseptics are generally harmless to living tissues and are used on cuttings and wounds.
  • Examples of antiseptics are alcohol, iodine, hydrogen peroxide, boric acid, potassium permanganate, iodoform etc.
  • Garlic has powerful antiseptic properties.

4. Disinfectants:

  • Disinfectants are antimicrobial agents that are applied to the surface of non-living objects to destroy microorganisms that are living on the objects.
  • These are harmful to living tissues and cannot be applied on skin.
  • Examples of disinfectants are phenol, methylphenol, chlorine, bleaching powder, formaldehyde etc.

5. Tranquillizer:

  • A medicinal drug taken to reduce tension or anxiety is known as tranquillizer.
  • It acts on the central nervous system and is used to calm, decrease anxiety or help a person to sleep.
  • Reserpine is a strong tranquillizer which is obtained from the plant Rauwolfia serpentina. It is used for the treatment of high blood pressure.
  • Barbiturates such as Seconal and Luminal are some other tranquillizers.

6. Antibiotics:

  • Antibiotics are such chemicals that inhibit the growth of microorganisms or destroy them.
  • Antibiotics are generally obtained or formed from living cells.
  • Most modern antibiotics are semisynthetic i.e., chemically modified derivatives of natural antibiotics, but some are made completely through chemical synthesis.
  • The first antibiotic penicillin was discovered by Alexander Flemming (1928; published 1929) from Penicillium notatum, a fungus.
  • Antibiotics do not work on viruses.

7. Anaesthetics:

  • A substance that induces insensitivity to pain or a temporary loss of sensation is known as an anaesthetic.
  • Its effect is reversible. It means that full sensation should return when the medicine has worn off.
  • Anaesthetics may be divided into two broad classes:

'general' anaesthetics, which result in a reversible loss of consciousness, and 'local' anaesthetics, which cause a reversible loss of sensation for a limited region of the body without necessarily affecting consciousness.

Chapter 34

Detergent and Soap

7 facts · 0 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (23 points)

Notes

Detergent:

  • Detergent is a water soluble cleansing surfactant (or a mixture containing one or more surfactants) which removes oily dirt by emulsifying/entrapping it is micelles and keeping it dispersed/suspended in water. It differs from soap as it does not form a scum with the salts in hard water.
  • Detergent helps to remove dirt and grease from porous surfaces such as fabrics, clothes, non-treated wood and/ or non-porous surfaces such as metals, plastics and treated wood.
  • Soap is used preferably for soft water but detergent can be used for soft water as well as hard water, because the calcium and magnesium salts of detergents are soluble in water.
  • Chemically detergents include ionic, non-ionic and zwitterionic surfactants with higher molecular weight, whose anion or cation has a long chain of carbon atoms from 12 to 18.
  • For example– Sodium Lauryl Sulphate is an anionic surfactant with a long chain of 12 carbon atoms.
  • The aqueous solution of detergent is usually neutral so it is used to clean the clothes made from delicate fibres.
  • The solution of soap is alkaline due to hydrolysis, so it is harmful for cleaning delicate clothes.

Soap:

  • Soaps are salts of fatty acids whereas fatty acids are aliphatic monocarboxylic acids (saturated or unsaturated) that have long carbon chains e.g. palmitic acid (C₁₅H₃₁COOH) and stearic acid (C₁₇H₃₅COOH).
  • Soap is made by the process of saponification. It is a process that involves conversion of fat or oil into soap and glycerol by the action of heat in the presence of alkali.
  • Common soaps are the mixture of salts of higher fatty acids (Generally C₁₂ to C₁₈) which are manufactured by the saponification of fats.
  • Saturated fats give hard soap and unsaturated vegetative oils give soft soap.

Raw materials used in manufacturing of soap:

(i) Vegetable oils or fats– For manufacturing of soap oils of peanut, mahua, castor oil and coconut are used.

(ii) Caustic soda or caustic potash– The saponification of oil or fat is performed with the aqueous solution of caustic soda (NaOH) or caustic potash (KOH).

(iii) Fillers– Fillers are substances that are added to soap to make it more useful for particular applications. For example:

a. Sodium rosinate is added to laundry soap to increase its foaming capacity.

b. Glycerol is added in shaving soaps to prevent them from rapid drying.

Chapter 35

The Fertilizers

19 facts · 2 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (68 points)

Notes

Fertilizers:

  • Fertilizer is any material of natural or synthetic origin that is applied to soils or to plant tissues to supply one or more plant nutrients essential to the growth of plants.
  • Fertilizers are used by farmers and families to help crops and gardens grow.
  • With the global population steadily growing, it is necessary that enough crops are produced each year to provide adequate food, clothing and other agricultural products to people around the world. These crops deplete soil nutrients in different ways and rates.
  • Fertilizers play an important role in providing crops with the nutrients they need to grow and be harvested for nutritious food.

Manure:

  • Manure is an organic material that is used to fertilize land, usually consisting of the feces and urine of domestic animals, with or without accompanying litter such as straw, hay, etc.
  • Animals manure is less rich in nitrogen, phosphorus and potash than synthetic fertilizers and hence must be applied in much greater quantities than the latter.
  • Manure is rich in organic matter and improves the soil's capacity to absorb water and store water, thus helping reduce runoff and erosion.
  • Much of the potassium and nitrogen in manure can be lost through leaching, if the material is exposed to rainfall before being applied to the field. These nutrient losses may be minimized/reduced by such methods as stacking manure under cover or in pits to prevent leaching.
  • Compost is a managed aerobic decomposition product of manure.
  • Green manure is a type of cover crop, grown to add nutrients and organic matter to the soil. Typically, a green manure crop is grown for a specific period of time, and then ploughed under and incorporated into the soil while it is green or shortly after flowering.
  • The legumes (mainly pea family plants) used as green manuring crops have nitrogen fixing symbiotic bacteria in their root nodules that fix atmospheric nitrogen in a form that plant can use as well as providing organic matter (humus) to the soil. Such plants are clover and vetch.
  • Continuous use of chemical fertilizers on soil can destroy soil fertility because the organic matter in the soil is not replenished. As a result, the food produced in these soils may have less vitamins and nutrient contents. The number of microorganisms in soil may decrease. Repeated ammonium-based nitrogen fertilizers may acidify soil. So the application of organic manure has been recommended along with artificial manure.

Vermicompost:

  • Nowadays vermicompost is widely used as an organic soil amendment. The most significant benefit of vermicompost is that the nutrients in it are generally very easily absorbed by the roots of plants. Vermicompost is not easily flushed from the soil because of the worm mucus that it contains. Plants have longer time to obtain the nutrients and get the maximum benefit.

Kinds of Synthetic Fertilizers:

  • There are three main categories of synthetic fertilizers:

(1) Nitrogenous fertilizers

(2) Phosphatic fertilizers

(3) Potassic fertilizers

(1) Nitrogenous fertilizers:

  • Nitrogen is absorbed by the plant roots in two forms– nitrate form (NO₃–) and ammonium form (NH₄⁺).
  • Most of the crop plants prefer nitrogen in nitrate form; but paddy and few other plants prefer nitrogen in ammonium form. Ammonium form of nitrogen is however, easily convertible into nitrate form.
  • Based on the forms of nitrogen they contain, nitrogenous fertilizers are classified into four categories, viz. (i) nitrate fertilizers (ii) ammonium fertilizers (iii) ammonium nitrate fertilizers and (iv) amide fertilizers.

(i) Nitrate fertilizers: These are three main nitrate fertilizers–

(a) Sodium nitrate –20.6% N
(b) Calcium nitrate –15.5% N

(c) Potassium nitrate – 13% N

(ii) Ammonium fertilizers: The following ammonium fertilizers are in use–

(a) Ammonium sulphate –20.6% N min.
(b) Ammonium chloride –25.0% N min.

(c) Monoammonium phosphate– e.g. MAP 12: 61: 0 grade;

12.0% N min. and 61.0% water-soluble Phosphate as P₂O₅ min.

(d) Diammonium phosphate (DAP) – 18% Nand 46% water soluble phosphate as P₂O₅ min.

(iii) Ammonium nitrate fertilizers: Following fertilizers are of this category–

(a) Ammonium nitrate – 34% N

(b) Calcium ammonium nitrate – 26% N

(c) Ammonium sulphate nitrate – 26% N

(iv) Amide fertilizers: Amide group fertilizers are agronomically very significant. They are readily soluble in water and easily decomposed by microorganisms in the soil. In the soil, they are quickly changed into ammonium form and then nitrate form and become available to the plants. The two main amide fertilizers are used –

(a) Urea – 46% N

(b) Calcium cyanamide – 20.6% N

(2) Phosphatic Fertilizers:

  • The nutrient phosphorus present in phosphate fertilizers are usually expressed in terms of phosphoric anhydride or simply as phosphorus pentaoxide (P₂O₅).
  • Some phosphatic fertilizers are as follows:
(a) Super phosphate–16-47% P₂O₅
(b) Basic slag–10-15% P₂O₅
(c) Bone meal–20-35% P₂O₅
(d) Rock phosphate–15-35% P₂O₅
(e) Monocalcium phosphate–45-50% P₂O₅
(f) Calcium metaphosphate–60-62% P₂O₅
(g) Ammophos–41-52% P₂O₅

(3) Potassic fertilizers:

  • It is also called potash fertilizer.
  • Potassium (K) is one of the essential nutrients for plants, along with nitrogen and phosphorus.
  • Potassium is vital for a plant to resist drought and disease as well as for promoting healthy growth.
  • The two main types of potash are – Muriate of Potash (MOP) and Sulphate of Potash (SOP).
  • Muriate of potash is also known as potassium chloride.
  • Potash application should be based on soil-test K; excess application when not needed can cause nutrient buildup.
  • Some potassic fertilizers are as follows:
(a) Potassium chloride–60-63% K₂O
(b) Potassium sulphate–50% K₂O
(c) Potassium nitrate–44-46% K₂O
(d) Wood ash–1-10% K₂O

Biofertilizers:

  • Biofertilizers are living microorganisms of bacterial, fungal and algal origin.
  • Biofertilizers add nutrients through the natural processes of nitrogen fixation and solubilizing phosphorus and stimulate plant growth through the synthesis of growth promoting substances.
  • Biofertilizers may be cost-effective (depending on conditions) as compared to chemical fertilizers.
  • The microorganisms in biofertilizers restore the soil's natural nutrient cycle and build soil organic matter and they may help reduce dependence on synthetic fertilizers and pesticides in some contexts.

Chapter 36

Miscellaneous (Chemistry)

115 facts · 10 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (18 points)

Notes

  • Allethrin is a pyrethroid (type I) insecticide. A pyrethroid is a synthetic chemical compound similar to the natural chemical pyrethrins. Pyrethrins are natural, fast-acting insecticides derived from chrysanthemum flowers (Tanacetum cinerariifolium) that act as neurotoxins to insects. Pyrethroid insecticide are used against mosquitoes.
  • A fire extinguisher is an active fire protection device used to extinguish to control fires, often in emergency situations. In the soda-ice fire extinguisher carbon dioxide is produced by the reaction of sodium bicarbonate and conc. Sulfuric acid.

2NaHCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O + 2CO₂

  • Rodenticides are pesticides that kill rodents. It is also called rat poison. Rodenticides are made from the chemicals such as warfarin or zinc phosphide. These are very poisonous chemicals.
  • Aluminium phosphide is a cheap, easily available agricultural pesticide which causes lethal poisoning by liberation of phosphine gas which causes cell hypoxia due to inhibition of oxidative phosphorylation, leading to circulatory failure. Aluminium phosphide is also used as fumigant for preservation of cereals.
  • Mustard Gas is the prototypical substance of the Sulfur based family of cytotoxic and vesicant chemical warfare agents known as the sulfur mustards. Mustard gas can form large blisters on exposed skin and cause severe, delayed burns/injury to the respiratory tract. Mustard gas may be fatal in large exposures and affects extremely to the cells of skin, eye, lungs and DNA. Mustard gas was used in first World War as chemical weapon. Its chemical name is dichloro diethyl sulphide.
  • Uranium dating is one of the ways of determining the age of ancient objects such as earth and rocks.
  • Carbon dating is a method for the determining the age of an object containing organic material.
  • Crookes glass is made by mixing of cerium and some other rare earth metals. Crookes glass has capacity to absorb the ultraviolet rays. It is used to make sunglasses.
  • Soda-lime glass is produced on a large scale and used for bottles, drinking glasses, and windows. Its light transmission properties, as well as low melting temperature, make it suitable for use as window glass. Its smooth and non-reactive surface makes it excellent as containers for food and drinks.
  • Jena glass is a shock-and heat-resistant glass used in scientific and technological applications, especially in chemistry.
  • Pyrex glass is a low-thermal-expansion borosilicate glass used for laboratory glassware and kitchenware.
  • Zinc Oxide (ZnO) is also known as flowers of zinc, a white powder used as a pigment in manufacturing of cosmetics, inks and ointments.
  • Cloud seeding is the process of spreading either dry ice or more commonly, silver iodide aerosols, into the upper part of the clouds to try to stimulate the precipitation process and induce rain or snow. These chemicals are sprayed over clouds by planes. The above chemicals are also burned/ released from ground-based generators or anti-aircraft guns.
  • In a match ignition is initiated via red phosphorus converting to white phosphorus and igniting. The chemical present on the tip of match stick is potassium chlorate, Sulfur, starch and glue. Antimony trisulfide is also used as the fuel in match tip. Match box striking surface contains red phosphorus, powdered glass and glue.
  • Nickel and Cadmium pairs of material serves as electrodes in chargeable batteries commonly used in devices such as torch light and electric shaver.

Chapter 37

Subdivisions of Biology

25 facts · 5 Must know

Test mode is on: tap a grey box to reveal the answer.

Key facts from the book (63 points)

Notes

  • The word ‘Science’ comes from the Latin word ‘scientia’, meaning ‘knowledge’.
  • Science is the systematic knowledge of the physical or material world gained through observation and experimentation.
  • Science has been classified into– (1) Natural Sciences and

(2) Social Sciences.

  • The natural sciences comprise the physical sciences, Earth and space sciences, and life (biological) sciences; life sciences (biology) are further divided into many branches and sub-branches.
  • Lamarck and Treviranus introduced the term ‘biology’ independently in modern sense in 1802.

Branches and Subbranches of Biology

Zoology – Detailed study of the members of the animal kingdom and animal life in general.

Botany – Detailed study of plants and their life.

Palaeontology – The study of history of life on Earth as based on fossils. Fossils are preserved remains, impressions, or traces of plants, animals, and other organisms from the geologic past; they may be preserved in Earth’s crust and also by processes such as drying, freezing, and entrapment in amber or asphalt. Palaeobotany – Study of plant fossils.

Ecology – The branch of biology that deals with the relation of organisms to one another and to their physical surroundings. Genetics – The study of heredity or how the characteristics of living things are transmitted from one generation to the next. In living organisms, DNA is the genetic material. This material is passed on when organism reproduces. The basic unit of heredity is ‘Gene’.

Physiology – Study of normal functions of living creatures and their parts.

Pedology – It is the study of soils in their natural environment. It deals with pedogenesis, soil morphology and soil classification. Edaphology – It concerns with the influence of soils on living things, particularly plants.

Gerontology – Study of the social, cultural, physiological, cognitive, and biological aspects of ageing, or the scientific study of old age, the process of ageing and the particular problems of old people.

Ethology – It is the scientific and objective study of non-human animal behaviour usually with a focus on behaviour under natural conditions, and viewing behaviour as an evolutionary adaptive trait.

Bionics – It is the study of mechanical systems that function like living organisms or parts of living organisms. Bionics is the application of biological methods and systems found in nature to the study and design of engineering systems and modern technology. The word ‘bionic’ was coined by Jack E. Steele in 1958.

Bionomics – The study of the mode of life of organisms in their natural habitat and their adaptations to their surroundings. Bionomics is the comprehensive study of an organism and its relation to its environment. It is also referred as ‘ecology’. Bionomy – Branch of biology concerned with the laws of life. Biometry – It is also known as biostatistics. It is the development and application of statistical and mathematical methods to analyse the data results from biological observations and phenomenon.

Phrenology – The detailed study of the shape and size of the cranium as a supposed indication of character and mental abilities.

Anthology – Study of flowers. It is also used for a collection of selected writings/works.

Agrostology – It deals with the scientific study of true grasses. It is also called Graminology – scientific study of grasses (the family Poaceae or Gramineae).

Palynology – The study of pollen grains and other spores especially as found in archaeological or geological deposits. Pollen extracted from such deposits may be used for radiocarbon dating and for studying past climates and environments by identifying plants then growing.

Oncology – A branch of biology (Medicine) that deals with the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of tumours/cancer. Teratology – The scientific study of congenital abnormalities and abnormal formations.

Osteology – It is the scientific and detailed study of the bones/bony structure of an organism, skeletal elements, teeth, microbone, morphology etc.

Chondrology – A branch of anatomy that deals with cartilage. Serology – The scientific study or diagnostic examination of blood serum, especially with regard to the response of the immune system to pathogens or introduced substances. Pathology – The science of the causes and effects of diseases, especially the branch of medicine that deals with the laboratory examination of samples of body tissue for diagnostic or forensic purposes.

Parasitology – Parasitology is the study of parasites (protozoa, helminths and ectoparasites), their hosts and the relationship between them. Parasites are organisms that use other species of plants and animals as a host. The hosts provide the environment in which the parasite lives.

Virology – Virology is the study of viruses– submicroscopic, parasitic particles of genetic material contained in a protein coat and virus-like agents.

Bacteriology – Study of the morphology, ecology, genetics and biochemistry of bacteria as well as many other aspects related to them.

Entomology – A branch of zoology that deals with insects. Malacology – Malacology is the branch of invertebrate zoology that deals with the study of the Mollusca, the second-largest phylum of animals in terms of described species after the arthropods. Molluscs include snails and slugs, clams, octopus, and squid (e.g., colossal squid is often cited as the heaviest invertebrate) and numerous other kinds, many of which have shells made of calcium carbonate.

Ichthyology – Ichthyology, also known as fish science, is the branch of zoology that deals with fishes.

Serpentology – A branch of zoology that studies snakes. Herpetology – Herpetology is the branch of zoology which deals with the study of reptiles and amphibians such as snakes, turtles, lizards, tortoises, crocodilians etc. It deals with their behaviour, geographic ranges, physiologies, development, genetics etc.

Ornithology – Ornithology is a branch of zoology that deals with the study of birds.

Dermatology – A branch of medicine concerned with the diagnosis and treatment of skin, nails and hair diseases. Trophology – Study of nutrition. (i.e., a branch of science dealing with nutrition).

Cell biology – Cell biology is a branch of biology that studies the structure and function of the cell, which is the basic unit of life.

Histology – The branch of biology dealing with the study of the microscopic structure of tissues.

Embryology – A branch of biology concerned with the study of embryos and their development.

Phycology or Algology – A branch of biology which deals with the scientific study of seaweeds and other algae.

Mycology – A branch of biology which deals with the scientific study of fungi.

Lichenology – It is the study of lichens, symbiotic organisms made up of an intimate symbiotic association of a microscopic alga (or a cyanobacterium) with a filamentous fungus (mycobiont).

Main Terminologies and related by-products

Apiculture – The raising and care of bees for honey and other hive products and agricultural purposes (pollination services, including cross pollination).

Aviculture – The breeding and rearing of birds.

Aquaculture – The farming of aquatic organisms–fish, molluscs, crustaceans and aquatic plants–for food and other commercial/public purposes, often with intervention to enhance production.

Algaculture – A form of aquaculture involving the farming of algae. Algae can be used in wastewater treatment and nutrient recovery; harvested algal biomass can be used as fertilizer. Phytoplankton are free-floating microscopic algae (often referred to as microalgae) and, in many classifications, include cyanobacteria in sunlit waters.

Pisciculture – The controlled breeding and rearing of fishes. Agriculture – The science or practice of farming, including cultivation of the soil for the growing of crops and the rearing of animals to provide food, wool and other products.

Sericulture – The production of silk and the rearing of silkworms for this purpose.

Silviculture – Silviculture is the practice of controlling the growth, composition, health and quality of forests to meet diverse needs and values.

Spongiculture – The cultivation and growing of (marine) sponges.

Horticulture – Horticulture is the science and art of growing fruits, vegetables, flowers and crops like spices/condiments and other plantation crops.

Floriculture – Floriculture or flower farming, is a discipline of horticulture concerned with the cultivation of flowering and ornamental plants for gardens and for floristry, comprising the floral industry.

Olericulture – Olericulture is the science of vegetables growing, dealing with the culture of non-woody (herbaceous) plants for food.

Arboriculture – Cultivation and management of trees and shrubs.

Pomology – The science that deals with fruit and fruit growing. Agronomy – A branch of agriculture dealing with crop production and soil management.

Vermiculture – The cultivation of earthworms, especially in order to use them to convert organic waste into fertilizer (vermicompost).

Oyster culture – The breeding and farming of oysters (primarily for food). Pearls are produced through pearl culture using pearl oysters.

Heliculture – It is also known as snail farming. It is the process of raising land snails especially for human use, either to use their flesh to eat or to obtain snail slime for use in cosmetics and snail eggs for human consumption as a type of caviar. Viticulture – Cultivation and harvesting of grapes.

Mariculture – Mariculture is a specialized branch of aqua culture involving the cultivation of marine organisms (animal and plant) for food and other products.

Moriculture – Moriculture is the science of mulberry cultivation for silk production, because silkworm (Bombyx mori) is reared on mulberry leaves.

Citriculture – Cultivation of citrus fruit trees.

Vegeculture – Agricultural systems producing mainly vegetatively propagated root and tuber crops; crops are reproduced asexually by planting parts of the parent plant. Aeroponics – A plant-cultivation technique without soil, in which the roots hang suspended in the air while nutrient solution is delivered to them in the form of a fine mist.

Aeroculture – A method of growing plants without soil by suspending them above sprays that constantly moisten the roots with water and nutrients.

Hydroponics – It is the cultivation of plants in nutrient enriched water, with or without the mechanical support of an inert medium (e.g. soil).
